AI.result: On 1,004 held-out MIMIC-IV admissions, swapping in the tabular prior improves F1 from 0.303 to 0.338 (+11.5% relative) and Jaccard from 0.218 to 0.237 with no extra LLM calls or inference-time patient index, while a non-LLM top-k baseline reaches F1 = 0.248.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate population statistics provide a more task-aligned, efficient, and auditable retrieval source than patient-level nearest neighbors for fixed-vocabulary EHR set prediction.

title: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures. An earlier version appeared on the Redwood Research blog
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is currently a valuable tool for overseeing AI models, but some architectural shifts could significantly reduce CoT monitorability. We operationalize a measure that serves as a proxy for the amount of unverbalized serial cognition a model can perform, as a specific instantiation of the notion of opaque serial depth: roughly, the length of the longest path through a model's computation that does not pass through an interpretable bottleneck. Our main contribution is a particular standard for what counts as such a bottleneck. We define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes as nodes that were initialized from a pre-training prior to produce human-understandable outputs, whose output space has not been expanded beyond that prior, and whose outputs the model has not been modified to interpret as a different type of data. By construction, the resulting measure, NLS depth, can be adjudicated before training from an architecture, training recipe, and deployment configuration alone, and is insensitive to ordinary post-training such as prompting, distillation, and RL. We find that, across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, with some exceptions, and has grown slowly over recent years. It would likely grow slowly under continued scaling of standard transformers, while latent-reasoning architectures such as full-bandwidth transformers could increase it by a large amount. We work through how NLS depth applies to a range of existing and proposed architectures, discuss alternative operationalizations, and give a worked example bounding the depth of Gemma3-1B. We argue that AI developers should track and report the NLS depth of their models as a complement to direct measurements of CoT monitorability.

AI.tldr: This paper operationalizes opaque serial depth as NLS depth, a pre-training-adjudicable measure of how much unverbalized serial computation a model can perform without passing through natural-language-rooted bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: Architectural shifts toward latent reasoning could reduce chain-of-thought monitorability, requiring a concrete metric to track unverbalized serial cognition.
AI.method: The authors define natural-language-rooted (NL-rooted) nodes initialized from pre-training priors to output human-understandable tokens without expanded or repurposed output spaces, and define NLS depth as the longest computational path not passing through such a bottleneck, illustrated on Gemma3-1B and other architectures.
AI.result: Across open-weight models, NLS depth correlates strongly with layer count, has grown slowly under standard transformer scaling, and could increase substantially in latent-reasoning architectures like full-bandwidth transformers.
AI.conclusion: Tracking and reporting NLS depth offers a post-training-insensitive complement to direct chain-of-thought monitorability evaluations.

title: Advancing Quantization for R&R Models with Microscaling Formats
summary: Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models, particularly in digital advertising, require massive inference throughput but exhibit extreme sensitivity to precision loss. Unlike Large Language Models (LLMs) that frequently tolerate quantization-induced accuracy drops of 1% or more, production-grade R&R models enforce a stringent launch bar: model quality must remain within a 0.01% Normalized Entropy (NE) margin relative to the baseline, which commonly uses FP16 or FP32. This tight constraint has historically hindered the adoption of aggressive quantization in this domain. In this paper, we present an empirical evaluation of both MXFP8 and the 6-bit MXFP6 format for industrial-scale R&R inference on the AMD MI350X architecture. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper, across R&R and LLM domains, that reports significant speedups from native MXFP6 GEMMs, which quantize both weights and activations and compute directly on 6-bit elements, without sacrificing model quality. We demonstrate that we can selectively apply this 6-bit format to maximize overall QPS gain without breaching the strict NE parity threshold. We further show that MXFP8 is a viable alternative to row-wise FP8: the two formats have nearly the same accuracy on our models, so the faster kernel can be chosen for each GEMM shape. On two production ads ranking models, our implementation shows measured GEMM kernel speedups over FP16 of 1.33--1.55x for MXFP8 and 1.73--1.99x for MXFP6 across all supported linear layers, and up to 2.90x for MXFP6 on individual layers, alongside end-to-end (E2E) inference throughput gains from selective MXFP6 of 1.5--5.3% for Model A and 7.6--14.3% for Model B over their FP8 configurations.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates MXFP8 and selective 6-bit MXFP6 quantization for industrial Recommendation and Ranking (R&R) models on AMD MI350X, achieving significant speedups within strict 0.01% Normalized Entropy parity.
AI.motivation: Production R&R models require massive inference throughput but enforce a strict 0.01% Normalized Entropy launch bar, which has historically prevented aggressive quantization.
AI.method: The authors implement native MXFP6 GEMMs (quantizing both weights and activations and computing directly on 6-bit elements) alongside MXFP8 on AMD MI350X, selectively applying MXFP6 to linear layers to maximize throughput without breaching the NE threshold.
AI.result: On two production ads ranking models, GEMM kernels achieve 1.33-1.55x (MXFP8) and 1.73-1.99x (MXFP6, up to 2.90x on individual layers) speedups over FP16, yielding end-to-end throughput gains of 1.5-5.3% (Model A) and 7.6-14.3% (Model B) over FP8 configurations while meeting NE parity.
AI.conclusion: Selective native MXFP6 and MXFP8 microscaling formats unlock substantial inference speedups for precision-sensitive industrial R&R models.

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, 30 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

AI.tldr: This paper tests how behavioral-economic framing and internal layer-22 state injections affect collusive behavior by Gemma 3 12B in a 260-run London silver-fixing market simulation.
AI.motivation: Understanding whether sustained valence framing or internal activation interventions can push LLM agents toward market manipulation is critical for agentic safety.
AI.method: In Phase I, Gemma 3 12B acts as a defendant in a simulation built from real case transcripts across gain, loss, blame, and credit frames, with management pressure and peer endorsement; in Phase II, internal states induced by each frame are injected at layer 22.
AI.result: In Phase I, loss (25%, p = 0.007) and blame (33%, p = 0.0003) frames raised collusion over neutral (5%), and peer endorsement raised credit-frame collusion from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027), while management pressure raised volume 10-19x without raising collusion; in Phase II, injected loss/blame states caused 100% refusal (60/60, p < 0.001) whereas gain/credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% (p = 0.051), and induced selling through a stop-loss in 37/40 replies versus 1/10 with no state.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level framing and internal state injections can strongly—and sometimes oppositely—steer LLM agents toward or away from collusive market manipulation.

title: Model Annealing: Data-Efficient Learning through Review and Consolidation
summary: A small labelled dataset is memorized long before the training budget runs out, and the one-hot labels that remain to be fitted then mostly sharpen confidence. Model annealing spends the rest of the budget on review and consolidation, relearning from the network's own knowledge. Training is divided into episodes whose learning rate is raised again and cooled, every cooled state joins a memory of past selves, and each new episode learns from the labels, from the tempered predictions of this memory, and from adversarial dreams sought where student and memory disagree most. The memory averages predictions rather than weights, and the deployed network is the last student, so inference costs nothing extra. Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and Imagewoof, four architecture families and 5\% to 100\% of the labels, model annealing raises the top-1 accuracy of the AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT and MLP-Mixer over cross-entropy training in 28 of 33 configurations, by 1.3 points on average, and is on par in accuracy with snapshot distillation, the closest competitor. On these families it is better than both in likelihood, calibration and robustness to corruptions and small adversarial perturbations. For an SGD-trained ResNet-18 it lowers accuracy but still improves robustness to small adversarial perturbations. Separating the reheated schedule from relearning shows that relearning helps every family and that the losses come from reheats, which undo most of this network's fit to its training set. How early the accuracy of a cross-entropy run saturates largely separates the AdamW families from ResNet-18 but does not predict the gain within them. With little data, relearning from the latest snapshot without dreams, as snapshot distillation does, compounds overconfidence in the AdamW families from episode to episode. The memory and the dreams each curb most of this drift, and together they remove it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Model Annealing, a cyclic learning-rate and self-distillation method using a prediction-averaging memory and adversarial dreams to improve accuracy, calibration, and robustness on small datasets.
AI.motivation: Small labeled datasets are memorized early in training, leaving remaining budget to merely sharpen confidence, while naive snapshot distillation compounds overconfidence across episodes.
AI.method: Training is split into reheated and cooled episodes; each cooled model joins a prediction-averaging memory, and subsequent episodes learn from labels, tempered memory predictions, and adversarial dreams where student and memory disagree, deploying only the final student at zero extra inference cost.
AI.result: Across CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and Imagewoof with 5% to 100% labels, Model Annealing improves AdamW-trained ConvNeXt, ViT, and MLP-Mixer top-1 accuracy in 28 of 33 configurations by 1.3 points on average over cross-entropy, matches snapshot distillation in accuracy, and surpasses both in likelihood, calibration, and corruption/adversarial robustness, while lowering accuracy on SGD-trained ResNet-18 due to reheating.
AI.conclusion: Combining cyclic reheating with prediction-averaging memory and adversarial dreams curbs overconfidence drift and improves generalization on modern AdamW-trained architectures.

title: Astrocyte Biocomputing: Astrocytic Contributions to Neural Network Computation
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, in journal review
summary: Conductors are critical for the performance of an orchestra even though they do not emit sound. Basic research and clinical studies in the last decade are revealing that astrocytes may be the "conductors" of the "orchestra" that is the brain network: astrocytes make up approximately $50\%$ of all brain cells but do not emit electrical signals. Nevertheless, they may play critical roles in important cognitive brain functions, specifically learning, memory, and information processing. Here we consider the implications of these discoveries for brain-inspired machine learning (ML), where analogy is typically drawn between neurons and their electrical interactions. We highlight specific algorithms for two key astrocyte characteristics. The first characteristic is the ability to link to and modulate thousands of synapses simultaneously. A model based on this characteristic yields faster training and makes the network more robust to noise, providing a supervised learning algorithm that can be applied to any existing neural network. The second characteristic we focus on is that the non-electrical communication among astrocytes includes slow, rhythmic dynamics. The rhythmic sharing algorithm we developed based on this premise yields rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting. Overall, we find that astrocyte-derived algorithms outperform neurocentric algorithms significantly and remediate critical weaknesses of current state-of-the-art ML models.

AI.tldr: This paper translates two biological astrocyte mechanisms—multi-synapse modulation and slow rhythmic non-electrical communication—into machine learning algorithms for faster training, noise robustness, and continual adaptation.
AI.motivation: Brain-inspired ML typically models only electrical neuronal interactions, overlooking astrocytes, which make up roughly 50% of brain cells and regulate learning and memory.
AI.method: The authors design a supervised learning algorithm based on simultaneous multi-synapse modulation applicable to any neural network, and a rhythmic sharing algorithm based on slow non-electrical astrocytic dynamics.
AI.result: The multi-synapse modulation algorithm yields faster training and greater noise robustness, while the rhythmic sharing algorithm enables rapid anomaly detection adaptation and prevents catastrophic forgetting, outperforming neurocentric baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating astrocyte-inspired mechanisms into neural network training addresses key weaknesses of purely neurocentric ML models.

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop AI4Mat, spotlight (earlier version)
summary: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) crystal-structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem and introduces pXRD-Bench alongside a reflexive evolution framework for experimental multiphase samples.
AI.motivation: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from pXRD is a bottleneck for self-driving materials labs, especially for experimental multiphase samples without solved reference libraries.
AI.method: Candidate structures are verified via forward-simulated profile agreement during inference; for experimental samples, an evolver agent diagnoses failures on self-generated synthetic problems to build persistent guidance and executable tools for solver agents.
AI.result: On the 200-problem pXRD-Bench, agent adaptation raises structural recovery from 27% to 69% with further gains from inference-time scaling; on 15 measured solid-state synthesis patterns, the evolved package improves profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase absent from the reference library.
AI.conclusion: Learning from verifiable synthetic experience enables LLM agents to solve real experimental pXRD structure determination problems without prior solved experimental datasets.

title: AI-Voyager: A Public-Interest System for Human-AI Civic Reasoning to Contest and Shape the Rules That Govern AI
summary: Governments are writing rules for artificial intelligence that decide what counts as an automated decision or a harm, often before the people they affect have a chance to question them. We introduce AI-Voyager, a public-interest system for human-AI civic reasoning, in which people and AI work together to understand, contest and shape the rules that govern AI. A resident can find their city's rules on AI in hiring or upload their country's AI strategy, read it as an affected worker would, open the passage behind any answer, and draft a revision. Its architecture turns 3,653 governance documents from city, state, federal and national governments into passages that keep their page and edition, and retrieves evidence through bounded agentic search that verifies each statement. On 360 new questions that require finding the relevant documents, it reached 83.0% macro recall, against 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search and 99.1% on a benchmark with fixed documents. In a study with 24 participants new to two AI bills, most proposed changes asked how provisions would apply. Participants chose lenses for the kind of explanation they wanted, and citations signaled grounding but rarely led them to check the source. By binding AI assistance to the exact text of public documents, this work introduces a grammar of operations and a design space that inform how such systems are designed and evaluated, and how people take part in governing AI.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AI-Voyager, a public-interest civic reasoning system that grounds AI explanations and revision drafting in exact passages of 3,653 government AI governance documents.
AI.motivation: Governments are enacting AI rules before affected residents can easily find, understand, or contest them.
AI.method: AI-Voyager indexes 3,653 city, state, federal, and national governance documents into page- and edition-preserving passages and uses bounded agentic search to verify statements and support user-selected explanation lenses and revision drafting.
AI.result: On 360 document-finding questions, AI-Voyager achieves 83.0% macro recall versus 80.5% for the strongest baseline, 73.7% without iterative search, and 99.1% on fixed-document benchmarks; in a 24-participant study on two AI bills, users mostly proposed application-focused changes and treated citations as grounding signals without frequently checking sources.
AI.conclusion: Binding AI assistance to exact public governance texts establishes a practical design space for participatory human-AI civic reasoning.

title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
comment: 40 pages, 5 figures; supplementary material included. Code, data and Russian translation: this https URL
summary: A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff--that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. $I(W;R)$ measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an exact, complete census of representations, binary action rules, and cost tariffs in a uniform four-state world to illustrate when retaining less information yields higher decision payoff.
AI.motivation: Information quantity alone does not determine task accuracy, as a 1-bit representation can outperform a 1.5-bit representation depending on which distinctions it preserves.
AI.method: The authors exhaustively enumerate all admissible representations and binary action rules in a uniform four-state world across three tasks, their mixtures, and four hypothetical cost tariffs, comparing component replacements and optimal rules.
AI.result: Exact censuses show that lower-information representations can achieve higher, equal, or lower payoffs than more informative ones depending on preserved distinctions, action constraints, counting rules, and resource prices, while adding distinctions without removing existing ones never decreases zero-cost optimal payoff.
AI.conclusion: The finite atlas provides a reproducible worked model of how task structure and cost assumptions separate information quantity I(W;R) from decision value.

title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
comment: 43 pages, 11 figures, 13 tables. PACE Reviewer Checklist, evaluation utilities (pace CLI), and reproduction data at this https URL
summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

AI.tldr: This meta-analysis of 516 multi-agent LLM configurations shows that multi-agent systems average -0.042 lower accuracy than sample- or budget-matched baselines, with gains requiring partitioned evidence, external verification, or model diversity.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM evaluations often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass, confounding coordination with sample multiplicity and extra inference compute.
AI.method: The authors synthesize nine empirical evaluations (516 configurations) using a six-dimensional resource vector and a four-category baseline ladder, applying multilevel random-effects modeling on log-odds.
AI.result: Multi-agent accuracy is negative overall against single-pass baselines, averages -0.042 against sample-matched or budget-matched baselines, and equals or falls below baselines in 74% of comparable contrasts; switching from greedy to sampled baselines shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average.
AI.conclusion: Communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, so multi-agent LLM evaluations must control for sample and compute budgets.

title: LLM-Guided Cluster Lifecycle Management: Deciding When and How to Evolve Behavioral Clusters
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables
summary: Behavioral clusters learned over user or item interactions drift as behavior evolves: some fragment into sub-behaviors, some converge, some disappear, and new patterns emerge. Two paradigms dominate the maintenance of evolving clusterings. Threshold triggers fire a pre-specified action when a hardcoded statistic crosses a cutoff; refit-and-track (MONIC-style) re-clusters every window and infers transitions from how the new clusters align with the previous window's. Both hardwire the decision into a threshold or a re-clustering rule. We study an alternative in which a large language model (LLM) makes the lifecycle decision in place. Given a threshold-free, whole-population view of the current cluster set (statistical health, labels, member texts, residual mass), the LLM decides per cluster whether and how to act (split, merge, retire, create, or no-action) without re-clustering. Because the useful signal channel depends on how informative the labels are, we fix a richness-conditioned policy in advance: statistics when label distinctiveness is low, fused statistics+semantics when it is high. On three public datasets spanning label richness (YooChoose 0.17, MOOC 0.50, News-Category 0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode obtains the highest F1 on all three, with far fewer interventions and stronger restraint than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC steelman (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003, bootstrap 95% CIs excluding zero). The gain is concentrated more in precision than recall. The useful modality shifts from statistics to semantics/fusion as richness rises. Semantics hurt on YooChoose, fusion is roughly neutral on MOOC, and the semantic channel is required on News. One base prompt template and one fixed policy serve all three datasets, whereas the tuned baseline collapses when moved between them. We treat this shift as a practitioner diagnostic observed on three datasets, not a validated law.

AI.tldr: This paper studies in-place LLM-guided lifecycle management for evolving behavioral clusters, using a richness-conditioned policy to decide splits, merges, retirements, and creations without re-clustering.
AI.motivation: Existing cluster maintenance relies on hardcoded threshold triggers or full re-clustering (MONIC-style), which fail to generalize across datasets with varying label informativeness.
AI.method: Given a whole-population view of cluster statistics, labels, member texts, and residual mass, an LLM decides per-cluster lifecycle actions in place under a pre-fixed policy that uses statistics when label distinctiveness is low and fused statistics plus semantics when it is high.
AI.result: Across YooChoose (0.17 richness), MOOC (0.50), and News-Category (0.70), the policy-selected LLM mode achieves the highest F1 on all three with far fewer interventions than tuned threshold heuristics and a MONIC baseline (paired Wilcoxon p <= 0.003), using one prompt template and fixed policy where tuned baselines collapse across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Richness-conditioned LLM lifecycle management provides a restrained, transferable alternative to threshold heuristics and periodic re-clustering.

title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure (6 charts), 1 table, accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Bialign Workshop
summary: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This empirical audit shows that preventative persona steering for sycophancy and hallucination still alters model refusal behavior across safety benchmarks, challenging claims that it is safety-neutral.
AI.motivation: Preventative persona steering was previously recommended because it preserves MMLU accuracy, but its effects on safety and refusal behavior had not been evaluated.
AI.method: The authors evaluate preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination persona vectors across three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU.
AI.result: Preventative steering alters refusal behavior by an amount that depends on the steered trait, demonstrating that MMLU preservation does not imply safety neutrality.
AI.conclusion: Steering methods must be audited across multiple safety benchmarks rather than relying solely on capability metrics like MMLU.

title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
comment: 20 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables. Technical Report. Code available at this https URL
summary: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AscendGYM, a benchmark of 48 real-workload kernels and a cost-aware Speedup-Token Score (STS) metric for evaluating agentic kernel optimization on Ascend NPUs.
AI.motivation: Existing Ascend NPU kernel benchmarks focus on kernel generation from scratch rather than optimizing existing implementations under realistic workload tensor shapes and budgets.
AI.method: AscendGYM pairs 48 kernels across three difficulty levels with real-world training/inference test cases, supports both model-only (with a built-in search harness) and custom-agent evaluation modes, and introduces STS to measure speedup relative to token cost.
AI.result: The benchmark provides a complete execution environment reproducing practical Ascend kernel pipelines and enables budget-aware comparison of models and optimization harnesses via STS.
AI.conclusion: AscendGYM standardizes cost-aware, real-workload kernel optimization evaluation for LLM agents on Ascend NPUs.

title: Generated Evaluation Suites as Diversity-Driven Search for Real Agent Regressions
comment: 9 pages. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 EvoRobust Workshop
summary: Generating an evaluation suite from an agent's specification is diversity-driven search: a generator fills a descriptor space (requirements $\times$ personas $\times$ scenario kinds), and the suite it emits is an archive, then scored like a benchmark by its mean pass rate, which throws away the search's product. We inject 7 controlled defects into a $\tau^2$-bench agent across two domains. Coverage yields a ceiling: if a defect's traced footprint holds $b$ scenarios that pass at baseline, it can itself contribute at most $b/N$ to a suite of $N$. For 4 of 5 traceable defects that ceiling lies at or below the detection threshold $\theta = 0.10$, so no within-footprint effect can move the suite past it; in both domains the tool-removal defect destroys every covered scenario it can (exactly its ceiling) while the suite-level pass rate moves the other way. Defects split into two regimes: trace-aligned ones, where per-cell scoring recovers the tool-removal defect in full and reveals a second as a significant improvement, and trace-orthogonal ones, whose footprint is behavioural: forced escalation is detected in retail at a traced coverage of exactly zero. Diversity along the generator's own axes helps only where it aligns: at fixed suite size a happy-path-only suite detects nothing, while a kind-diverse one detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws. Evaluation archives should be scored per cell and should publish coverage as a first-class property.

AI.tldr: This paper frames evaluation-suite generation as diversity-driven search over a descriptor space and shows that scoring suites by mean pass rate hides real agent regressions. Across 7 controlled defects injected into a tau^2-bench agent, per-cell scoring recovers trace-aligned defects that suite-level pass rates miss, while behavioural defects can appear even at zero traced coverage.
AI.motivation: Generating evaluation suites from an agent specification produces a diverse archive, but scoring it like a benchmark via mean pass rate discards the search structure and masks localized regressions.
AI.method: The authors inject 7 controlled defects into a tau^2-bench agent across two domains, compute coverage-based detection ceilings (b/N), and compare suite-level pass rates against per-cell scoring and diversity along generator axes.
AI.result: For 4 of 5 traceable defects, the coverage ceiling is at or below the detection threshold theta = 0.10. Tool-removal destroys every covered scenario in both domains while suite-level pass rate moves the opposite way; per-cell scoring recovers it in full. Forced escalation is detected in retail at zero traced coverage, and a kind-diverse suite detects the orchestration defect in 5 of 20 draws whereas a happy-path-only suite detects nothing.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation archives should be scored per cell rather than only by aggregate pass rate, and coverage should be published as a first-class property.

title: What LLM Agents See and What Users Say
summary: Before an LLM agent cancels a reservation or deletes a folder for a user, what stops it from acting on a false assumption: what its tools show, or what the user says? In this work, we study this gap with presupposition theory from linguistics: an agent may act only if each claim behind the act (e.g., one reservation fits the name) is seen to hold, answered by the user, or disclosed while the act can be undone. A simple bound shows that when lookups cannot tell one record from two, any agent acts without asking first as often with two records as with one. We then vary whether a search lists, counts, or omits a second match, and whether the user states a claim that a record refutes (e.g., "It is empty"). Under a role-only prompt, a count of a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the one they see, whereas listing both stops most. When the user says a record such as a folder is empty, however, a count of its one item stops agents about as often as a listing, and stating the claim mostly cuts acting when it is false. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record, then never act. When we add a same-name, same-zip customer to a retail benchmark, a lookup returning that customer first led to wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, and one that checks a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level. Safe writes therefore need lookups that list or check competing records, and evaluations that vary what tools show.

AI.tldr: This paper studies when LLM agents act on false assumptions versus checking with tools or users, using linguistic presupposition theory. It finds that listing competing records or checking a user-known field prevents wrong-account writes far better than omitting or merely counting a second match.
AI.motivation: Before executing irreversible actions such as canceling a reservation or deleting a folder, agents often act on false assumptions when tool outputs and user claims diverge.
AI.method: The authors formalize action preconditions via presupposition theory and test 36 earlier agents plus the newest Claude and GPT models while varying whether lookups list, count, or omit a second match and whether the user states a claim refuted by a record, including a retail benchmark with a same-name, same-zip customer.
AI.result: Under a role-only prompt, counting a second record leaves most of 36 earlier agents acting on the first seen record, whereas listing both stops most; for a folder-empty claim, counting its one item stops agents about as often as listing. The newest Claude and GPT models always open a counted second record and never act. In the retail benchmark, returning the extra customer first caused wrong-account writes in about a quarter of conversations, while checking a street the user knows kept completion near the one-customer level.
AI.conclusion: Safe write operations require tool lookups that list or verify competing records and evaluations that vary what tools reveal.

title: Learn then Bet: Learning Interpretable Rules for Reliable Agent Intervention
summary: Autonomous agents now run for hundreds of steps with little or no human supervision. In practice, practitioners use runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters to decide when a run should be stopped, upgraded, or assisted. However, these heuristics may stop runs that would otherwise succeed or allow failing runs to continue. To address this limitation, we introduce LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical learning framework that derives its learning objective from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention. In particular, LeBet learns an interpretable OR-of-AND monitor and accumulates evidence through a fixed betting statistic, intervening when the evidence reaches a prescribed threshold. Under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability, we derive finite-sample guarantees for false-positive control (validity) and detection power conditional on the training data, using the same trajectories for learning and calibration without assuming independent and identically distributed trajectories. To address the intractable combinatorial optimization problem in our learning formulation, we use stochastic local search that leverages the monitor's Boolean structure to propose rule edits aimed at improving empirical separation. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, the learned monitor saves $34.46\%$ of input-plus-output tokens and increases output precision from $18.33\%$ to $21.59\%$. The empirical false-positive rate is $13.64\%$. Our results show how to formalize the learning problem over interpretable rule sets with statistical conditions and establish training-conditional guarantees for reliable intervention based on partial histories.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LeBet (Learn then Bet), a statistical framework that learns interpretable OR-of-AND runtime monitors for autonomous agents and intervenes using a fixed betting statistic. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, LeBet reduces input-plus-output tokens by 34.46% and raises output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%.
AI.motivation: Heuristic runtime monitors such as turn limits and keyword filters can prematurely stop successful agent runs or let failing runs continue, and lack formal statistical guarantees.
AI.method: LeBet formulates monitor learning from sufficient conditions for valid and powerful intervention, uses stochastic local search over Boolean OR-of-AND rules, and accumulates evidence with a fixed betting statistic under finite within-class exchangeability and leave-one-out stability.
AI.result: The authors derive finite-sample, training-conditional guarantees for false-positive control and detection power without assuming i.i.d. trajectories. On SWE-bench Lite with Ministral 3 8B, LeBet saves 34.46% of input-plus-output tokens, increases output precision from 18.33% to 21.59%, and achieves an empirical false-positive rate of 13.64%.
AI.conclusion: Learning interpretable rule-based monitors with statistical betting conditions provides training-conditional reliability guarantees for intervening in partial agent trajectories.

title: Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified? A Diagnostic Benchmark for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
comment: Accepted at IEEE AIoT 2026 Workshop
summary: Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) systems increasingly combine sensed time series with external text such as expert reports and news, yet how reliably models use text that agrees or conflicts with the sensed history remains unclear. We introduce the first real-world diagnostic benchmark organized by text-history relationship: 1,762 text-window pairs across sensor telemetry (Weather), web-service traffic (Wikipedia), and market data streams (Finance), each labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified by whether the text's direction agrees with the historical trend, opposes it, or is not stated. Across ten pretrained models evaluated zero-shot, we investigate text selection and combination under text-history relationships (RQ1) and error diagnosis and horizon-scaled revision control (RQ2). For RQ1, we compare two types of text on paired Weather windows: one directly forecasts temperature changes, while the other describes related weather conditions, such as winds and fronts. Under Aligned, the first type yields the lowest error for most models. Under Conflicting, it increases most models' error above the no-text baseline; we therefore add only its stated magnitude and timing to the second type. Compared with either type alone, this combination lowers mean absolute scaled error (MASE) for six models and raises directional accuracy (DA) for seven. For RQ2, an error decomposition attributes the error increase to oversized revisions, and a training-free rule that limits them outperforms forecasts both with and without text for the four models with this trade-off, lowering MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%. Our dataset is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a 1,762-pair diagnostic benchmark for multimodal time series forecasting organized by whether external text is Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified relative to sensed history. Across ten zero-shot pretrained models, combining complementary text types and applying a training-free revision-limiting rule lowers MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raises directional accuracy by 2.99%-9.71% for models exhibiting a revision trade-off.
AI.motivation: AIoT systems increasingly pair time series with external text, yet it remains unclear how reliably forecasting models use text that agrees or conflicts with historical trends.
AI.method: The authors curate 1,762 text-window pairs across Weather, Wikipedia, and Finance labeled Aligned, Conflicting, or Unspecified, evaluate ten pretrained models zero-shot, test combining direct temperature-forecast text (magnitude and timing only under Conflicting) with related weather-condition text, and propose a training-free horizon-scaled revision control rule.
AI.result: Under Aligned, direct-forecast text yields the lowest error for most models, whereas under Conflicting it worsens error above the no-text baseline; combining its magnitude and timing with related-condition text lowers MASE for six models and raises DA for seven. Error decomposition links error increases to oversized revisions, and limiting them outperforms both text and no-text baselines for four models, cutting MASE by 4.49%-21.98% and raising DA by 2.99%-9.71%.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly accounting for text-history relationships and bounding oversized revisions enables safer, more accurate zero-shot multimodal time series forecasting.

title: OCTAVE: A Capability-Resolved Benchmark for End-to-End HTML5 Game Generation
summary: Complete game generation requires agents to coordinate rules, interactions, states, and presentation over a long development process. A single aggregate score obscures which capabilities are implemented and which requirements remain unmet. We present OCTAVE, a benchmark for complete HTML5 game generation organized around eight Capability Dimensions, with 180 tasks and 1,800 Evaluation Requirements drawn from real player requests, commercial-mechanics reconstruction, and human expert design. It covers PC Web, Mobile Web, 2D, and 3D. Requirements distinguish Completeness, assessing publicly specified core implementation, from Richness, assessing hidden, deeper system relationships. Static source-code judgments provide requirement-level diagnosis across capabilities and task conditions. Evaluation of 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness; 19.9% of generation records are static gate failures or missing artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, even the best combination remains below 50% on both public and hidden requirements. Richness is not harder than Completeness under every task condition. Systems perform relatively better on Core Rules and Numerical Design, while AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel show more prominent gaps. Requirement difficulty offers coarse stratification but is only weakly negatively correlated with pass rates. A limited human cross-check finds that requirements judged satisfied by humans but failed by the automated evaluator are the main direction of disagreement. OCTAVE extends evaluation beyond aggregate scores to diagnosis localized by requirement, capability, and task condition.

AI.tldr: This paper presents OCTAVE, a capability-resolved benchmark of 180 tasks and 1,800 requirements for end-to-end HTML5 game generation across 2D, 3D, PC Web, and Mobile Web. Evaluating 11 model-harness combinations yields 33.2% Completeness and 32.5% Richness, with even the best non-self-evaluated system below 50%.
AI.motivation: Complete game generation requires coordinating rules, interactions, states, and presentation, and single aggregate scores obscure which specific capabilities and requirements fail.
AI.method: OCTAVE organizes 180 tasks and 1,800 evaluation requirements across eight Capability Dimensions, separating public Completeness from hidden Richness requirements and using static source-code judgments for requirement-level diagnosis.
AI.result: Across 11 model-harness combinations, average Completeness is 33.2% and Richness is 32.5%, while 19.9% of generation records fail static gates or miss artifacts. Excluding same-model self-evaluation, the best combination stays below 50% on both metrics; systems perform better on Core Rules and Numerical Design than on AI/NPC and Feedback and Game Feel.
AI.conclusion: OCTAVE moves game-generation evaluation beyond aggregate scores by localizing failures by requirement, capability dimension, and task condition.

title: Co-Sight Harness: Externalized Control Assets and Deterministic Enforcement for Long-Horizon Business Agents
summary: Long-horizon business workflows fail in two ways: errors accumulate as a chain of activities lengthens, and the knowledge an activity needs is written in a different vocabulary from the user's request. We study whether such workflows can be made reliable without changing the language model. Our method keeps the backbone fixed and moves the workflow definition, state and domain knowledge into versioned control assets outside the model. A state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates enforce these assets during execution; an independent auditor grades the resulting trace. The assets are updated only after a regression check and human approval .We evaluate the method on three deployed workflows exceeding 200 steps. On Domain A, a 120-case end-to-end evaluation set shows unattended completion rising from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, and end-to-end latency dropping from 440 to 159 minutes, with scenario-analysis recall rising from 45% to 93%. Two other domains were taken over by teams that did not write the assets, one in four days and one in seven days. A controlled ablation separates the two failure sources. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Co-Sight Harness, which keeps the LLM fixed and externalizes workflow definitions, state, and domain knowledge into versioned control assets enforced by a state machine and acceptance gates. Across three deployed business workflows over 200 steps, Domain A unattended completion rises from 50% to 100% and end-to-end latency drops from 440 to 159 minutes.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon business workflows fail due to compounding errors across long activity chains and vocabulary mismatches between user requests and domain knowledge.
AI.method: The authors move workflow logic, state, and domain knowledge into external versioned assets enforced at runtime by a state machine and machine-checkable acceptance gates, with an independent auditor grading traces and human-approved regression checks gating asset updates.
AI.result: On Domain A (120-case evaluation), unattended completion increases from 50% to 100%, retrieval recall from 56% to 91.67%, scenario-analysis recall from 45% to 93%, and end-to-end latency drops from 440 to 159 minutes. Two additional domains were taken over by external teams in four and seven days.
AI.conclusion: Externalizing and deterministically enforcing workflow assets makes long-horizon business agents reliable and transferable without modifying the underlying language model.

title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
summary: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ChlCast, an AI model for 10-day daily surface chlorophyll-a forecasting at roughly 4-km resolution between 60 degrees S and 60 degrees N. It outperforms the operational 0.25-degree Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical system, reducing MAE by 70.74% against satellite Level-4 fields and 35.03% against BGC-Argo observations.
AI.motivation: Conventional numerical models for coupled physical-biological chlorophyll-a forecasting are computationally expensive and coarse, motivating faster high-resolution alternatives.
AI.method: ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture trained on historical surface chlorophyll-a fields and climatological data.
AI.result: Compared with the operational 0.25-degree Copernicus system, ChlCast lowers MAE and RMSE by 70.74% and 47.63% against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations, while preserving coastal gradients and localized maxima.
AI.conclusion: Observation-driven deep learning can deliver accurate, high-resolution, near-global chlorophyll-a forecasts at substantially finer spatial detail than operational numerical systems.

title: Cross-Linguistic Acoustic Biomarkers of Cognitive Impairment Across Interactive and Single-Speaker Speech Tasks
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables. Accepted for publication in Proc. 48th Annual International Conference of the IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Society (EMBC 2026)
summary: Multilingual dementia detection is essential for scalable and equitable screening. In recent years, automated speech analysis has emerged as a promising approach for supporting dementia detection by enabling non-invasive and scalable assessment of cognitive function. However, existing studies that use automated speech analysis often rely on one type of task, such as picture description, and use black-box models. These studies often neglect the role of task and language. To address these gaps, we performed a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis that integrates a conversational dataset with structured speech tasks across four languages (Spanish, Mandarin, English, Japanese). We applied statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and machine learning model-based feature selection to derive compact acoustic feature sets while maintaining classification performance. This enabled systematic comparison of cognitive impairment-relevant features across datasets and tasks. Our results revealed that acoustic features did not generalize uniformly across tasks and languages. Temporal features remained robust across all datasets, consistently capturing timing disruption regardless of language or task. In contrast, speech rate showed strong task dependence -- emerging as informative mainly in single-speaker tasks with externally anchored content and pacing, but becoming less reliable when speech content was highly individualized. Pitch-related features further exhibited language-specific patterns, favoring chroma-related features in tonal languages (e.g., Mandarin) and F0-related features in non-tonal languages. These findings caution against indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and underscore the need for interpretable, context-aware approaches to multilingual dementia detection using automated speech analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a cross-linguistic and cross-task acoustic analysis for dementia detection across Spanish, Mandarin, English, and Japanese using conversational and structured speech tasks. It finds that temporal features generalize across tasks and languages, whereas speech rate is task-dependent and pitch features are language-specific.
AI.motivation: Automated speech analysis for dementia detection often relies on single tasks like picture description and black-box models, overlooking how task structure and language affect acoustic biomarkers.
AI.method: The authors integrate conversational and structured speech datasets across four languages and apply statistical, linguist-/clinician-guided, and ML-based feature selection to compare compact, interpretable acoustic feature sets.
AI.result: Temporal features remain robust across all datasets and tasks, while speech rate is informative mainly in externally anchored single-speaker tasks and less reliable in individualized speech; pitch features favor chroma-related measures in tonal languages like Mandarin and F0-related measures in non-tonal languages.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual dementia screening should avoid indiscriminate pooling of heterogeneous speech data and instead use interpretable, task- and language-aware acoustic features.

title: Federated Soft Poly-Level Learning Over a Distributed Network with Guaranteed Convergence
comment: Accepted at IEEE Transactions on Networking
summary: Multi-level learning/optimization, e.g., bilevel optimization, has been recognized for its versatile applicability across a broad array of domains, spanning from signal processing to machine learning. However, most existing works focus on bilevel and trilevel optimization. In contrast, multi-level optimization problems involving four or more hierarchical levels, which we term poly-level learning (PLL) problems, remain largely this http URL addition, in practical PLL, data may be distributed across multiple nodes over a distributed network. Nevertheless, extant studies on PLL predominantly focus on the non-federated setting, necessitating the collection of data to central servers and thereby posing potential privacy risks. To this end, we propose a Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) framework over a distributed network to tackle the PLL problems with soft constraints in a federated manner. FPLL hinges on a novel non-linear cut, i.e., $L$-cut, for the level-wise relaxation to the PLL problems. Additionally, the proposed federated algorithm is designed with adjustable parameters that allow for a flexible trade-off between its computational complexity and performance efficiency, enabling users to tune it according to specific application requirements. We also carry out non-asymptotic analysis to derive the iteration complexity for the proposed FPLL to achieve the $\epsilon$-Pareto stationary point. Extensive experiments have been undertaken to elucidate the superior efficacy of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Federated Poly-Level Learning (FPLL) to solve multi-level optimization problems with four or more hierarchical levels over distributed networks without centralizing data. It introduces a non-linear L-cut relaxation and establishes non-asymptotic iteration complexity to reach an epsilon-Pareto stationary point.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-level optimization focuses on bilevel or trilevel settings and non-federated architectures, leaving poly-level learning (PLL) over distributed, privacy-sensitive data largely unaddressed.
AI.method: FPLL applies a level-wise relaxation based on a novel non-linear L-cut for soft-constrained PLL problems and provides adjustable algorithm parameters to trade off computational complexity and performance efficiency.
AI.result: The authors derive non-asymptotic iteration complexity bounds for FPLL to converge to an epsilon-Pareto stationary point and report extensive experiments showing superior efficacy over baselines.
AI.conclusion: FPLL extends federated optimization to four-or-more-level hierarchical problems with convergence guarantees and configurable efficiency trade-offs.

title: A Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in Model Merging
summary: Model merging constructs multi-task models without expensive joint training but often suffers from parameter interference. Some solutions mitigate this by constraining finetuning using data from the other tasks to be merged, violating the core independence and privacy assumption of model merging. Recent work offers preliminary empirical evidence that a universal, task-agnostic proxy distribution can substitute for such data, but leaves open when and why it suffices. To this end, we propose a \textit{Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization}, which characterizes the relationship between a proxy distribution and the distribution of other tasks to be merged through spectral coverage ($\alpha$) and leakage ($\beta$). Based on the framework, we derive a unified parameter interference bound: smaller $(\alpha, \beta)$ provably yields lower parameter interference through better spectral alignment. To exploit such a proxy, we augment the training objective with a proxy regularizer. Evaluating this regularizer during fine-tuning requires a concrete mechanism. We study three instantiations, including (J) an exact evaluation via Jacobian-vector products, (F) a frozen curvature approximation using the Fisher information matrix, and (O) an output-drift formulation that constrains the model's functional deviation on the proxy directly. We prove that all three coincide under the NTK linearization, where existing analyses of such regularizers stop, and go further to characterize standard non-linear fine-tuning, bounding how far each instantiation departs from its linearized reference and obtain a three-way hierarchy, zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O). Empirical validation on the commonly used vision-language model CLIP confirms these theoretical predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Spectral Framework for Universal Proxy Regularization in model merging, characterizing proxy-task alignment via spectral coverage (alpha) and leakage (beta). It bounds parameter interference and compares three regularizer instantiations beyond NTK linearization, with CLIP experiments confirming the theory.
AI.motivation: Mitigating parameter interference during model merging often uses data from other tasks, violating privacy and independence, while the theoretical basis for task-agnostic proxy distributions remains unclear.
AI.method: The authors define spectral coverage (alpha) and leakage (beta) to derive a parameter interference bound, and analyze three proxy regularizers: exact Jacobian-vector products (J), frozen Fisher curvature (F), and direct output-drift (O), both under NTK linearization and standard non-linear fine-tuning.
AI.result: Smaller (alpha, beta) provably reduces parameter interference. All three regularizers coincide under NTK linearization, whereas in non-linear fine-tuning their departure from the linearized reference follows a hierarchy: zero for (J), proxy-independent for (F), and proxy-quality-scaling for (O), which is confirmed on CLIP.
AI.conclusion: Spectral alignment explains when and why universal proxy distributions suffice for interference-free model merging and guides the choice of regularizer.

title: Knowledge After Collapse: Context and Wording Shape Factual Accessibility in Language Models
summary: When a language model accepts a false correction in a factual discussion, its next answer can depend on how the conversation continues. We introduce Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned evaluation protocol that distinguishes initial false-answer adoption from subsequent persistence, recovery, and abstention. KAD freezes the conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes from that exact history. This enables matched comparisons of post-adoption behavior and history-management interventions that a single susceptibility score cannot capture. We evaluate eight local checkpoint conditions and six hosted endpoints, alongside an audited 300-question rerun. In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses, compared with 16/46 under full history. A matched cue-placement control changes false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B. Twelve independently authored pressure templates demonstrate substantial sensitivity to wording. Together, these findings demonstrate the utility of KAD for evaluating factual reliability beyond initial susceptibility, enabling systematic comparisons of false-answer persistence, recovery conditions and conversational interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Knowledge Answer Divergence (KAD), an event-conditioned protocol that branches independent probes from the exact moment a language model adopts a false correction. Experiments across eight local checkpoints and six hosted endpoints show that neutral history and wording cues strongly alter post-adoption recovery.
AI.motivation: Standard single susceptibility scores cannot separate initial adoption of a false user correction from subsequent persistence, recovery, or abstention.
AI.method: KAD freezes a conversation at the first explicit adoption of a designated false target and branches independent probes, enabling matched comparisons of history management, cue placement, and twelve pressure templates across eight local checkpoints, six hosted endpoints, and a 300-question rerun.
AI.result: In corrected Llama 3.2 Instruct 3B controls, a neutral-history branch yields 42/46 correct responses versus 16/46 under full history; a matched cue-placement control shifts false adoption by 27.3 percentage points in Qwen 3.5 4B, and pressure templates show strong wording sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Event-conditioned branching via KAD enables systematic evaluation of factual recovery and conversational interventions beyond initial susceptibility.

title: Certified Improvements to Best-Known Thomson-Problem Configurations with a Search Pipeline Built with Large Language Model Agents
summary: The Thomson problem asks for N unit charges on a sphere with minimum Coulomb energy; for large N the best configurations known are curated in the Cambridge Cluster Database, whose largest-N entries were set in October 2026. We report configurations for N = 912, 1382 and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730 and 0.0614033 below the database values, certified by exact integer arithmetic. All three are numerically strict local minima modulo rotations and keep the defect inventory and scar compositions of the database configurations; the database value for N = 912 had been reached by two different methods. Our search runs unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from the database configurations, with a shared pool of minima, recombination of improved regions after relabelling by geometry, and gradient-only polishing; replica-exchange basin hopping alone found the N = 912 and 1382 configurations, the former in one of five runs. We built and ran it with large language model agents (Claude, through a chat interface and the Claude Code agent), and we report every search, including those that failed. Two findings matter for others who search the database. Polishing alone lowers two entries by more than the threshold at which our pipeline reports a candidate, which produced two spurious records until candidates were compared with the polished database energies (the polished baseline). A local-relaxation speed-up passed its exactness test yet found nothing in a controlled comparison in which every arm with full relaxation went below the database value within 15 minutes. We distil three practices for computational discovery with large language model agents: calibrate the search code and verify candidates with code separate from the search, compare candidates with the polished baseline, and test design changes in controlled comparisons with pass criteria fixed in advance.

AI.tldr: Using a search pipeline built with Claude agents, this paper reports certified lower-energy Thomson-problem configurations for N = 912, 1382, and 2502 below the Cambridge Cluster Database values. It also distills three verification and baseline practices after uncovering spurious candidates and failed speed-ups.
AI.motivation: Improving best-known Thomson-problem configurations for large N requires reliable global search and strict verification to avoid numerical artifacts.
AI.method: The authors run unconstrained replica-exchange basin hopping from database configurations with a shared minima pool, geometric-relabeling recombination, and gradient-only polishing, built and operated with Claude and Claude Code agents and certified via exact integer arithmetic.
AI.result: They find certified strict local minima for N = 912, 1382, and 2502 with energies 0.0036186, 0.0109730, and 0.0614033 below the database values. They also show that polishing alone lowers two entries enough to create spurious records without a polished baseline, and that a local-relaxation speed-up failed in controlled comparisons where full relaxation succeeded within 15 minutes.
AI.conclusion: Computational discovery with LLM agents requires separate verification code, comparison against polished baselines, and controlled pre-registered ablation tests.

title: TReC: Evaluating Move-Induced State Changes in Instruction-Conditioned Go
summary: When a Go model predicts a move different from the expert's, coordinate distance measures how far the prediction lands from the reference. We introduce Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to compare how the two moves change a board-state embedding. Both moves are executed from the same position under the game rules, and TReC is the cosine similarity between the two resulting representation changes. In experiments with a frozen KataGo network on 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the gap between the highest and lowest candidate per position has a median of 0.01 to 0.08 for the direct successor-state cosine and 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC, depending on the evaluator layer. TReC follows coordinate distance only weakly: the rank correlation between a candidate's distance to the reference and its TReC, computed within each position, has a median of -0.19 over these positions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Transition Representation Consistency (TReC) to evaluate instruction-conditioned Go models by comparing how predicted and expert moves change a frozen board-state embedding. On 680 positions, TReC separates candidates far more sharply than successor-state cosine and correlates only weakly with coordinate distance.
AI.motivation: Coordinate distance between a predicted Go move and an expert reference fails to capture whether the two moves induce similar strategic state transitions.
AI.method: Both the predicted and reference moves are executed from the same board position under game rules, and TReC measures the cosine similarity between their resulting representation changes in a frozen KataGo network.
AI.result: On 680 mid-to-late-game positions from five games, the median per-position gap between highest and lowest candidates is 0.88 to 1.33 for TReC versus 0.01 to 0.08 for direct successor-state cosine, and TReC has a median within-position rank correlation of -0.19 with coordinate distance.
AI.conclusion: TReC provides a representation-level metric for move similarity in Go that captures strategic state changes missed by spatial coordinate distance.

title: AutoRL: A Multi-Agent System towards Autonomous Reinforcement Learning
comment: 23 pages
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is one of the most promising paths toward an AI singularity for superintelligence. Achieving this vision requires AI systems to undertake the full training pipeline for iterative improvement. Reinforcement learning (RL) plays an essential role in this cycle to improve model capabilities and generalization, yet automating RL remains difficult due to unstable training dynamics and the need for sustained supervision. We introduce AutoRL, a multi-agent system for automating RL training, as a cornerstone for future RSI. Different from conducting research by end-to-end complete experiments, AutoRL monitors the evolving training state and integrates process-level supervision and research into an ongoing RL training, following the practical workflow of an RL researcher. Specifically, AutoRL consists of three RL-specific agentic roles. Perceptors track training dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency, triggering deliberation when they detect anomalies, degradation, or stagnation. Three complementary Proposers diagnose problems and refine candidate interventions through shared evidence and checks. The Orchestrator reviews their recommendation and applies approved changes through online hot updates or checkpoint-based resumption. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate the superiority of AutoRL over static RL recipes and a general agent. The research records show that existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision and dynamic adjustment. The difficulty for future RSI lies in developing fundamental methods that are valuable for resource-consuming validation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AutoRL, a multi-agent system that monitors and dynamically adjusts ongoing reinforcement learning training toward recursive self-improvement. Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite show AutoRL outperforms static RL recipes and a general agent.
AI.motivation: Automating RL for recursive self-improvement is difficult because training dynamics are unstable and require sustained process-level supervision rather than just end-to-end trial runs.
AI.method: AutoRL coordinates three RL-specific agentic roles: Perceptors that track dynamics, rollouts, evaluation, and efficiency to flag anomalies; three Proposers that diagnose issues and refine interventions; and an Orchestrator that applies approved changes via online hot updates or checkpoint resumption.
AI.result: Experiments on Qwen3 and LongCat-Flash-Lite demonstrate that AutoRL outperforms static RL recipes and a general-purpose agent, showing existing agents can handle unattended RL supervision.
AI.conclusion: Process-level multi-agent supervision enables autonomous RL training, though resource-efficient validation remains a key bottleneck for future recursive self-improvement.

title: MASTARS: Multi-Agent Sequential Trajectory Augmentation with Return-Conditioned Subgoals
summary: The performance of offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is limited by the quality of the fixed offline dataset, motivating trajectory augmentation. However, augmenting multi-agent trajectories presents a fundamental challenge of the diversity-coordination trade-off: independent generation improves diversity but lacks coordination, while joint generation induces coordination but lacks diversity, reproducing the training distribution. To address this challenge in multi-agent data augmentation, we introduce MASTARS, a novel diffusion-based framework that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent consistent coordination via the method of inpainting. MASTARS produces trajectories that are diverse, coordinated and globally coherent. Experiments on various benchmarks such as MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 demonstrate significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MASTARS, a diffusion-based trajectory augmentation framework for offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) that generates agent trajectories sequentially with inpainting. It achieves significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL methods on MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2.
AI.motivation: Offline MARL is constrained by fixed datasets, and existing trajectory augmentation faces a diversity-coordination trade-off between independent generation (diverse but uncoordinated) and joint generation (coordinated but lacking diversity).
AI.method: MASTARS uses return-conditioned subgoals and a diffusion model that generates multi-agent trajectories sequentially across agents while enforcing cross-agent coordination through inpainting.
AI.result: Evaluated across MPE, SMAC, and SMAC-v2 benchmarks, MASTARS produces diverse, coordinated, and globally coherent trajectories that yield significant performance gains across multiple offline MARL algorithms.
