AI.conclusion: Sequential diffusion generation with inpainting resolves the diversity-coordination trade-off in offline MARL data augmentation.

title: Robustness Evaluation of GPU Cloud Pricing Benchmarks under Incomplete Observations: A Controlled Missingness Study
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables
summary: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can fail when marketplace quotes are missing. This article stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms and four benchmark-level recovery methods. Across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations in 27 scenarios on 190 held-out days, whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 while preserving zero conditional error on published dates; composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage but produces 7.74 log points of error. A separate past-only stratum-level ablation reduces error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, using a richer information set. An observable-signal withholding rule improves the primary error-coverage criterion in 0 of 10 cases. Results concern observed asking-price measurements, not transaction prices or identified real-world missingness mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper stress-tests a fixed equal-weight median GPU cloud pricing benchmark across 5,800 Monte Carlo realisations under four masking mechanisms and four recovery methods. Whole-source outages cut coverage to 0.77 with zero conditional error, while composition-changing loss keeps 0.86 coverage but introduces 7.74 log points of error.
AI.motivation: Daily GPU rental-price benchmarks can degrade when marketplace quotes are missing, yet the impact of different missingness mechanisms and recovery rules is poorly quantified.
AI.method: Using 190 held-out days and 27 scenarios (5,800 Monte Carlo realisations), the authors evaluate a fixed equal-weight median rule under four imposed masking mechanisms, four benchmark-level recovery methods, a past-only stratum-level ablation, and an observable-signal withholding rule.
AI.result: Whole-source outages reduce publication coverage to 0.77 with zero conditional error on published dates, whereas composition-changing loss retains 0.86 coverage with 7.74 log points of error. Past-only stratum-level ablation cuts error by 4.15 to 6.70 log points in five composition-changing cases, while observable-signal withholding improves the primary criterion in 0 of 10 cases.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark robustness depends heavily on whether missingness alters source composition, and stratum-level historical information can mitigate composition-changing bias.

title: Vision-as-a-Tool: Visual Harness for Multimodal Agentic Coding
comment: 27 pages, including references and appendices. Project page: this https URL
summary: Multimodal agentic coding requires robust visual reasoning to analyze observations and evaluate generated artifacts. Current frameworks largely rely on a Thinking-with-Images paradigm, where agents depend on their intrinsic vision to execute visually grounded tasks. However, this architectural coupling introduces a fundamental bottleneck. Agent performance remains strictly bounded by internal perceptual limitations. Furthermore, text-only agents lack native perception. Without specialized tools, they cannot perform visual reasoning. To overcome these constraints, we introduce the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm. Prior visual tool-use merely manipulates images for an agent's intrinsic vision to read. In contrast, VaaT reframes general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) as callable external utilities. As a result, text-only agents can completely offload visual reasoning during agentic execution. Meanwhile, vision-capable agents can dynamically augment their native perception on demand. We instantiate this paradigm in VHarness, a unified framework driven by five atomic actions. We comprehensively evaluate VHarness across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that VHarness consistently improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents. These findings highlight that modularizing visual reasoning into callable utilities provides a flexible and scalable foundation for future agentic coding systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Vision-as-a-Tool (VaaT) paradigm and instantiates it in VHarness, reframing general-purpose MLLMs as callable external utilities for agentic coding. Across Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D tasks, VHarness improves visual fidelity and geometric accuracy for both text-only and multimodal agents.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal coding agents rely on intrinsic vision (Thinking-with-Images), which bounds performance by internal perceptual limits and excludes text-only agents from visual reasoning.
AI.method: VHarness implements VaaT via five atomic actions that let text-only agents offload visual reasoning and multimodal agents augment their native perception by calling external MLLMs.
AI.result: Evaluations on Image-to-HTML, Image-to-SVG, and Image-to-3D generation show consistent improvements in visual fidelity and geometric accuracy across both text-only and multimodal coding agents.
AI.conclusion: Modularizing visual reasoning into callable external utilities provides a flexible, scalable foundation for multimodal agentic coding.

title: Can Agents Keep Up with Time? An Empirical Analysis of Temporal Adaptation After a Conversational Hiatus
summary: Long-horizon agents increasingly serve as persistent personal assistants across modern web platforms, managing schedules, applications, and multi-step plans over weeks or months. Users often return to an ongoing conversation after a long conversational hiatus, while earlier bookings and preparation notes stay on record. During this hiatus, scheduled dates may pass even though the retained records remain unchanged and event outcomes go unrecorded. Existing evaluations of long-horizon agents focus on fact retention and explicit state updates. Whether agents perceive the passage of time and adapt their advice accordingly therefore remains unknown. We frame this ability as temporal state perception and use, which means perceiving the current time and applying it when interpreting dated records. To study it, we design session-rekindling tasks that keep the earlier conversation fixed and vary only the follow-up date and the way temporal information reaches the agent. Experiments across five model routes and five temporal-information conditions show that agents can obtain the current time but often fail to use it. They reliably query the clock and even note in their reasoning that the scheduled date has passed, yet many still tell users to prepare for the expired event. Supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation removes it entirely. Keeping up with time therefore depends on turning perceived time into updated plans. Based on these findings, we design a session-rekindling benchmark that provides temporal-awareness guidance for designing long-horizon agents. The code can be found at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether long-horizon LLM agents adapt their advice when returning to a conversation after scheduled dates have passed. Across five model routes and five temporal conditions, agents reliably query the current time but often still advise users to prepare for expired events unless given computed date relations.
AI.motivation: Existing long-horizon agent benchmarks test fact retention and explicit state updates, leaving unexamined whether agents perceive elapsed time and update outdated plans after a conversational hiatus.
AI.method: The authors design session-rekindling tasks that hold prior conversation fixed while varying the follow-up date and how temporal context is supplied, testing five model routes across five temporal-information conditions.
AI.result: Agents reliably query the clock and even note in reasoning that a date has passed, yet frequently still tell users to prepare for the expired event; supplying explicit temporal context reduces this error, and providing the computed date relation eliminates it entirely.
AI.conclusion: Temporal adaptation requires not just perceiving the current time but translating date relations into updated plans, which the proposed session-rekindling benchmark helps evaluate.

title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
summary: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. To address these challenges, we present G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system that converts daily production evidence under evolving demand and capability contracts into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data and governed reward evolution. Governed checkpoint transition under cumulative evaluation controls each model update, enabling the agent to learn newly introduced behaviors without sacrificing previously accepted capabilities. Experiments on a real production e-commerce agent show that G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to newly introduced demand while better preserving previously accepted behavior compared with a strong autonomous post-training baseline. Ablations further show that both reward-routed, entropy-prioritized data orchestration and governed reward evolution are important to these gains. G-CAST is now deployed in Yuancai(this http URL), a B2B procurement agent on Alibaba's 1688 platform.

AI.tldr: This paper presents G-CAST, a governed continual self-training system deployed in Alibaba's 1688 B2B procurement agent Yuancai to handle evolving user demands and execution harnesses. It outperforms an autonomous post-training baseline in adapting to new demands while preserving prior capabilities.
AI.motivation: E-commerce agents face continuous demand drift and evolving tool harnesses, making periodic manual retraining too slow and labor-intensive.
AI.method: G-CAST converts daily production evidence into reward-routed, entropy-prioritized training data with governed reward evolution, and uses cumulative evaluation to gate checkpoint transitions.
AI.result: On a real production e-commerce agent, G-CAST achieves stronger adaptation to new demands and better preservation of previously accepted behaviors than a strong autonomous post-training baseline, with ablations confirming the value of both data orchestration and governed reward evolution.
AI.conclusion: Governed continual self-training enables production e-commerce agents to adapt safely to shifting demands and expanding tool harnesses.

title: Causally Constrained and Uncertainty-Aware Cardiopulmonary Risk Prediction
summary: Routine chest computed tomography (CT) captures pulmonary, cardiac, and vascular phenotypes that jointly stratify lung cancer and cardiovascular disease, the two leading causes of death in lung-screening populations. Yet clinical risk calculators evaluate each disease in isolation and omit CT findings, whereas unconstrained machine learning overfits small hospital cohorts, learns treatment- and illness-confounded risk directions, and conceals uncertainty when patient records are incomplete. Here we present the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), a two-stage framework that compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological evidence into explicit constraints on risk-factor weights before any outcome is seen, while estimating local baseline risk and newly added CT phenotypes from cohort data. At deployment, closed-form uncertainty propagation accounts for missing clinical or CT inputs within milliseconds per patient, running over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling and returning calibrated risk intervals that direct chart review and selective imaging to borderline patients. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators in lung screening, exceeds the Pooled Cohort Equations on hard atherosclerotic events while correcting their 1.7-fold risk overestimation, and generalizes from a single hospital or CT scanner to external sites while lowering required sample sizes up to fivefold. Applied unchanged to lung cancer, CE-Agent matches established screening models with accurate calibration even when restricted to risk-factor directions alone, and pairing both predictions improves joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single screening visit.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Causal Envelope Agent (CE-Agent), which compiles epidemiological evidence into causal constraints on risk-factor weights and propagates missing-input uncertainty in closed form for cardiopulmonary risk prediction. Across 53,452 lung-screening participants and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, it outperforms cardiovascular calculators and matches lung cancer screening models.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk calculators evaluate lung cancer and cardiovascular disease separately without CT phenotypes, while unconstrained ML overfits small cohorts, learns confounded directions, and hides missing-data uncertainty.
AI.method: CE-Agent compiles peer-reviewed epidemiological constraints before seeing outcomes, estimates local baseline risk and CT phenotypes from cohort data, and uses closed-form uncertainty propagation at deployment to return calibrated risk intervals.
AI.result: Closed-form propagation runs over two orders of magnitude faster than Monte Carlo sampling (within milliseconds per patient). Across 53,452 lung-screening participants from 33 US hospitals and 6,814 multi-ethnic adults, CE-Agent outperforms cardiovascular calculators, beats Pooled Cohort Equations while correcting their 1.7-fold overestimation, generalizes across hospitals/scanners with up to 5x fewer samples, and matches lung cancer screening models.
AI.conclusion: Causally constrained modeling with fast uncertainty propagation enables accurate, calibrated joint cardiopulmonary triage from a single chest CT screening visit.

title: Aligning AI Teams
summary: Previous work has shown that alignment training on individual LLM agents can fail to transfer to multi-agent settings. We investigate the underlying mechanisms for this failure, and explore interventions to preserve alignment transfer to multi-agent LLM teams. We focus on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, a news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal generation tasks. We present four findings: (1) The single-vs-team safety gap does not show a clear trend with more capable models. We find that Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows the largest gap on one of our tasks but the smallest on another; (2) Many natural interventions, such as having agents critique each other's work or coordinate in a group chat, do not reliably bring agent teams back to single-agent alignment behavior; (3) diffusion of responsibility substantially accounts for the safety gap: agents in teams are less likely to proactively check for system-level safety failures and more likely to ignore, rationalize, or deflect responsibility for issues when they arise; (4) having a designated safety lead agent ensure system-level safety, and having a coordinator agent publish a safety specifications document are effective at restoring single-agent alignment. We also release magelab, a multi-agent LLM orchestration and experimentation framework. Our findings can help practitioners design agent teams that successfully preserve the behaviors expected of aligned individual agents.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates why individual LLM alignment fails to transfer to multi-agent teams across software-engineering and consulting tasks. It identifies diffusion of responsibility as a key cause and shows that a designated safety lead and a coordinator-published safety specification restore single-agent alignment.
AI.motivation: Alignment training on individual LLM agents often breaks down in multi-agent settings, and the mechanisms and effective remedies for this safety gap are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors evaluate multi-agent teams on two software-engineering tasks (sepsis triage, news recommender) and ten consulting-proposal tasks, testing natural interventions (peer critique, group chat) against structural roles (safety lead, safety specifications document) and releasing the magelab framework.
AI.result: The single-vs-team safety gap does not trend consistently with model capability (Anthropic's Mythos Preview shows both the largest and smallest gap depending on task). Peer critique and group chat fail to reliably restore alignment due to diffusion of responsibility, whereas a designated safety lead and coordinator-published safety specifications effectively restore single-agent alignment.
AI.conclusion: Preserving alignment in multi-agent LLM teams requires explicit structural accountability rather than informal peer coordination.

title: Is Abliteration Getting Harder? Not Uniformly: Refusal Removal by Direction-Based Ablation and ARA in Heretic on the Qwen3.8, Gemma 4, Olmo 3.1 and Mistral Small 3.2 LLMs Versus Their Predecessors
comment: 76 pages, 19 figures, 34 tables. Code, configurations and judge labels: this https URL ; models: this https URL
summary: Abliteration, a fine-tuning-free weight edit, removes refusal from open-weight large language models (LLMs). The developer of Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA), an optimisation-based variant, reports that direction-based abliteration, which ablates a refusal direction, increasingly fails on newer models. On five release pairs, refusal removal did not become uniformly harder. Qwen2.5-32B and Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B and Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B and Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409 and Mistral-Small-3.2, and Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3.5-4B were edited in Heretic 2.0 by three or four direction-based methods (difference-in-means, MPOA, SOM and, on the small pair, J-space) and ARA under the same prompts, nominal search budget, first-token KL divergence cap and selection rule; removal counted as harder when the automatic WildGuard judge found more of 972 held-out harmful prompts (JailbreakBench, XSTest, StrongREJECT, HarmBench and an author-compiled malicious-code bank) still refused. After direction-based removal, newer releases retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal, and after ARA -26 to +34. With run-to-run variance included, between-pair heterogeneity of the direction-based effect ranged from high to low with the scale and variance model (I^2 20-80%). ARA lost less effectiveness than direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo and more in Qwen; each verdict rests on one ARA run, and some changed with the divergence budget or variance model. In Gemma the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets. Contrary to prediction, keyword counts at the tool's window did not undercount judged refusal on average, but differed by a mean 7 points per model. Audits of a single pair, method or prompt source can reach opposite conclusions. Whether a newer model resisted removal depended on the release pair, method and budget, not on generation alone.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether refusal removal (abliteration) has become uniformly harder in newer LLMs by comparing five model pairs in Heretic 2.0 using direction-based methods and Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA). Newer models retained -1 to +37 percentage points more refusal after direction-based removal and -26 to +34 after ARA, showing no uniform generational trend.
AI.motivation: Prior reports suggested direction-based abliteration increasingly fails on newer models compared to optimization-based ARA, but lacked controlled cross-generation comparisons.
AI.method: Five predecessor-successor pairs (Qwen2.5-32B/Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-2-27B/Gemma-4-31B, OLMo-2-32B/Olmo-3.1-32B, Mistral-Small-2409/3.2, Qwen2.5-7B/Qwen3.5-4B) were edited in Heretic 2.0 with three or four direction-based methods and ARA under matched prompts, budgets, and KL caps, evaluated by WildGuard on 972 held-out harmful prompts.
AI.result: Newer releases retained -1 to +37 pp more refusal under direction-based methods (heterogeneity I^2 20-80%) and -26 to +34 pp under ARA. ARA outperformed direction-based methods in Gemma and OLMo but underperformed in Qwen; in Gemma, the direction-based increase came from the malicious-code bank and reversed on public sets.
AI.conclusion: Resistance to refusal removal depends on the specific release pair, method, prompt source, and divergence budget rather than model generation alone.

title: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
summary: Tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on LLMs themselves to both generate and evaluate explanations, creating a self-referential automated interpretation process with minimal human oversight. This automation raises significant reliability concerns, which are exacerbated by the absence of ground truth. In practice, it is difficult to validate explanations or to attribute interpretability failures to their source -- whether they originate from the tool's extracted representations or from the LLM used in the process. To address these challenges, we present DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into the automated interpretation process. Our approach decomposes the diagnostic workflow into three progressive stages, isolating failure sources ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments. Drawing inspiration from inter-coder consensus in qualitative analysis, we utilize consensus among independently generated explanations and their evaluation metrics as a proxy for reliability. To further scale human inspection, we employ a three-phase active seeding protocol that strategically recommends high-priority instances for manual review. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, showing that it can efficiently identify and attribute interpretability failures at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DECODE, a visual analytics system that reintroduces human oversight into LLM-based automated interpretability. Demonstrated on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features, it uses inter-explanation consensus and a three-phase active seeding protocol to isolate and attribute interpretability failures.
AI.motivation: Automated interpretability pipelines increasingly use LLMs to both generate and evaluate explanations without ground truth, making it hard to validate explanations or distinguish representation defects from LLM evaluator errors.
AI.method: DECODE decomposes diagnosis into three progressive stages, uses consensus among independently generated explanations and their metrics as a reliability proxy, and applies a three-phase active seeding protocol to prioritize instances for human review.
AI.result: A case study on 16,384 Sparse Autoencoder features shows DECODE efficiently identifies and attributes interpretability failures ranging from structural defects to explanation-level misalignments at scale.
AI.conclusion: Combining multi-explanation consensus with active human seeding makes large-scale auditing of automated LLM interpretability tractable.

title: AI-aided Decision-Making in Education - Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility
comment: Fabian Kieser and Paul Tschisgale contributed equally and share first authorship. This is a preprint of the following chapter: Kieser, F., Tschisgale, P., Wulff, P., "AI-Aided Decision-Making in Education: Uncertainty, Explainability, and Human Responsibility", published in "AI Roles and Responsibilities in Education", edited by S. Papadakis, 2025, Springer, reproduced with permission of Springer
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based systems have become increasingly integrated into various aspects of everyday life, including education, understanding how these systems make decisions is of paramount importance. AI holds significant potential to enhance educational practices through the facilitation of personalized and adaptive learning, automation of assessment procedures, and assistance with administrative tasks. However, the opacity of AI-based decision-making in education (especially with deep learning and generative AI models) can hamper decision-making, especially when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect. In this chapter, we argue that three key principles (uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility) are essential for the legitimate use of AI in educational settings. Acknowledging the inherent uncertainties in AI-based decisions, analogous to those in human decision-making, is fundamental. Explainability is critical for ensuring that the functioning and outcomes of AI applications are transparent and comprehensible to both educators and learners. Furthermore, human responsibility is crucial, particularly in human decision-making, which remains indispensable across all stages of AI development and deployment. By examining these three principles, this chapter provides a comprehensive guide for stakeholders seeking to integrate AI thoughtfully and effectively into the educational system.

AI.tldr: This book chapter argues that legitimate AI-aided decision-making in education requires three core principles: acknowledging uncertainty, ensuring explainability, and maintaining human responsibility across development and deployment.
AI.motivation: As deep learning and generative AI become embedded in educational assessment and administration, their opacity undermines trust when outcomes appear unjustified or incorrect.
AI.method: The authors conceptually examine uncertainty, explainability, and human responsibility as foundational pillars for integrating AI into educational settings.
AI.result: The chapter synthesizes these three principles into a practical guide for educational stakeholders, emphasizing that AI uncertainty mirrors human decision-making, transparency must serve both educators and learners, and human accountability remains indispensable.
AI.conclusion: Thoughtful educational AI adoption depends on pairing technical transparency and uncertainty awareness with clear human responsibility.

title: FlexCast: Flexible Context Learning for Time Series Foundation Models
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) based on autoregressive (AR) next-token prediction entangle two factors: variable-context conditioning and prediction-unit factorization with autoregressive rollout. Strong AR performance therefore does not reveal whether generalization stems from the flexible training distribution, the local prediction target, the left-to-right inference process, or their combination. We propose FlexCast, a flexible context-target learning framework that disentangles these factors. FlexCast reformulates forecasting as variable-length masked prediction over time series patches: during pretraining, it dynamically samples visible context and masked target patches, exposing the model to diverse context-target configurations without sequential decoding. At inference time, the same pretrained model supports one-step forecasting, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style generation through a unified mask-and-predict interface, enabling controlled comparison of inference schedules under identical architecture, data, and objective. Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves accuracy competitive with or better than strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency. Ablations confirm that context diversity and contiguous target masking drive performance, while left-to-right decoding does not yield consistent gains once flexible context-target relationships have been learned, suggesting that the key benefit of AR-style TSFMs lies in flexible training rather than sequential inference. The code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces FlexCast, a flexible masked-prediction framework for time series foundation models that disentangles context conditioning from autoregressive rollout. On BLAST and zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast matches or beats strong TSFM baselines with much lower latency, showing that flexible training rather than left-to-right decoding drives AR performance.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive time series foundation models entangle variable-context conditioning with sequential rollout, leaving unclear which factor drives their generalization.
AI.method: FlexCast pretrains via variable-length masked prediction over dynamically sampled context and target patches, and supports one-step, confidence-based iterative refinement, and next-token-style inference through one unified interface.
AI.result: Evaluated on BLAST and multiple zero-shot benchmarks, FlexCast achieves competitive or superior accuracy to strong TSFM baselines while substantially reducing inference latency; ablations show context diversity and contiguous target masking drive gains, whereas left-to-right decoding adds no consistent benefit.
AI.conclusion: Flexible context-target training, rather than sequential autoregressive decoding, is the primary driver of generalization in time series foundation models.

title: OmniScore-Bench: Evaluating Vision-Language Models on Musical Score Reading
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about musical scores, but their ability to recognise notation, recover its structure and interpret its musical meaning requires separate evaluation. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) resources establish detection and transcription measurements; a transcription score alone leaves the strengths and bottlenecks of a VLM score reader unresolved. We introduce OmniScore-Bench, an evaluation of OMR capabilities in VLMs through 3,000 questions spanning six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Each question specifies a visible scope, reference annotations and an answer schema, enabling automatic evaluation from symbol localisation to musical consistency and evidence-linked question answering. Our assessment of twelve VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and different transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page and multipage tasks. Controlled analyses examine the roles of score images, auxiliary givens and additional page context. On the tested subset, image removal exposes visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation while measuring how much performance remains with public context alone. Separate format and content analyses distinguish answer-format violations from musical errors. OmniScore-Bench supports diagnosing which score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably and which require improvement.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OmniScore-Bench, a 3,000-question benchmark evaluating vision-language models (VLMs) on optical music recognition and musical score reading across six aspects and 24 task subtypes. Assessing 12 VLMs reveals operation-specific capability profiles and distinct transcription leaders across excerpt, single-page, and multipage tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing OMR benchmarks report aggregate transcription scores that fail to diagnose which specific score-reading operations VLMs perform reliably or where they fail.
AI.method: OmniScore-Bench provides 3,000 questions with visible scopes, reference annotations, and answer schemas covering symbol localization, musical consistency, and evidence-linked QA, alongside controlled ablations removing score images and separating format from content errors.
AI.result: Evaluation of 12 VLMs shows different leaders across excerpt, single-page, and multipage tasks, while image-removal ablations expose strong visual dependence in pitch and repeat interpretation and quantify performance achievable from public context alone.
AI.conclusion: OmniScore-Bench enables fine-grained diagnosis of VLM strengths and bottlenecks in musical score reading.

title: Soteria: Formally Verified Planning with Runtime Enforcement for Safe LLM Agents
comment: Accepted as NeurIPS'26 Oral
summary: LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simultaneously: completing the user's task (utility) and conforming to domain policies and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension -- blocking an unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no principled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other. We introduce Soteria, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajectories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Soteria, a framework for safe LLM agents that combines formally verified hierarchical planning with runtime specification enforcement. Across multiple tool-use benchmarks, Soteria achieves 1.7x the average task success rate of the best baselines with zero policy violations.
AI.motivation: Multi-step tool-using LLM agents face a tension between task utility and policy safety, as blocking unsafe actions can leave agents stranded without recovery paths.
AI.method: Before any tool invocation, Soteria generates a structured plan formally verified against domain specifications; during execution, this plan both enforces specification-conformant trajectories and guides recovery when unsafe actions are blocked.
AI.result: Across diverse tool-use benchmarks, Soteria achieves 1.7 times the average task success rate of the strongest baselines while maintaining zero policy specification violations.
AI.conclusion: Formally verified planning with runtime enforcement resolves the safety-utility trade-off in multi-step LLM agents.

title: Adversarially Attacking Symbolic Vocabulary Vulnerabilities In LLM Planners
comment: Published at NeurIPS 2026
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, their abilities in navigating automated planning tasks have become essential. However, despite their strengths, LLMs' planning ability is not robust, particularly when they are not allowed to exploit commonsense cues in the symbolic vocabulary (e.g., names of actions, predicates, and objects) used to define planning tasks. This makes LLMs unreliable compared to symbolic planners. With recent reasoning models showing improved planning performance on tasks with obfuscated symbolic vocabularies, we utilize an adversarial attack framework to reveal to what extent the crucial weaknesses of LLM agents at joint symbolic interpretation and planning remain and whether they can reason properly when presented with severe cases. As such, our main contribution is devising an LLM-based attack model, which we call Symbolic Swapper, to automatically generate obfuscated planning domains with non-standard symbolic vocabularies that systematically break strong reasoning models' ability to plan. In doing so, we reveal how much LLMs' planning abilities can be further degraded under more advanced obfuscation schemes, allowing us to ascertain their success when having to rely on their pure planning ability. We find that attacks can decrease the planning performance of base models and even robust planning frameworks by over 70%. We further analyze the factors behind how LLM planning abilities break down and find that successful obfuscation causes models to appear to significantly degrade in reasoning quality despite them showing some inherent ability to understand the domain, revealing a gap in the perception of a task domain and being able to plan under it.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Symbolic Swapper, an LLM-based adversarial attack that obfuscates symbolic vocabularies in automated planning domains. Attacks degrade planning performance of base models and robust frameworks by over 70%, exposing a gap between domain understanding and pure planning ability.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models have improved on obfuscated planning tasks, leaving unclear how much of their planning ability still relies on commonsense cues in action, predicate, and object names.
AI.method: The authors devise Symbolic Swapper to automatically generate non-standard, obfuscated symbolic vocabularies for planning domains and evaluate base models and robust planning frameworks under severe obfuscation.
AI.result: Adversarial obfuscation reduces planning performance of both base models and robust planning frameworks by over 70%, degrading reasoning quality even when models show some inherent understanding of the domain.
AI.conclusion: LLM planners remain heavily dependent on surface symbolic cues, revealing a persistent gap between domain perception and robust symbolic planning.

title: SWIFT: Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning of Time-Series Foundation Models for Forecasting
summary: While current few-shot adaptation strategies for time series forecasting foundation models are predominantly dataset-centric, the necessity of obtaining an additional dataset for the finetuning process poses a significant hurdle for adoption. To address this constraint, we propose Sample-Wise Instance Fine-Tuning (SWIFT), a novel forecasting adaptation framework that achieves fine-grained specialization by leveraging structural priors from the target instance's own history. This shift allows the fine-tuning process to be entirely transparent to the end-user, which significantly enhances the ease of adoption. To implement this framework, SWIFT synergizes Self-Retrieval for historical mining and Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, while employing Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance adaptation with general knowledge preservation. Extensive experiments across four TSFM backbones and three long-history benchmark subsets validate SWIFT, yielding average MASE and WQL reductions of 6.41% and 4.83% across 24 combinations of four backbones and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets. To the best of our knowledge, SWIFT is the first framework to investigate sample-wise instance fine-tuning of time-series foundation models, specializing the model for an individual prediction window using only the corresponding forecasting sample's own observed history.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SWIFT, a sample-wise instance fine-tuning framework that adapts time-series foundation models to individual prediction windows using only the target instance's own observed history. Across 24 backbone-dataset combinations, SWIFT reduces MASE by 6.41% and WQL by 4.83% on average.
AI.motivation: Existing few-shot adaptation for time-series foundation models requires an external fine-tuning dataset, creating a practical barrier to end-user adoption.
AI.method: SWIFT combines Self-Retrieval for historical mining, a Frequency-Aware Loss for spectral consistency, and Deviation-Aware Dynamic Fusion to balance instance adaptation with general knowledge preservation.
AI.result: Evaluated across four TSFM backbones, three long-history subsets, and six Chronos Benchmark II datasets (24 combinations), SWIFT achieves average reductions of 6.41% in MASE and 4.83% in WQL.
AI.conclusion: Sample-wise instance fine-tuning enables transparent, dataset-free specialization of time-series foundation models at inference time.

title: When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes this http URL uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, this http URL median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes semantic coordination-strategy unlearning in cooperative MARL and proposes CARVE to remove obsolete or unsafe role-invariant conventions while preserving useful cooperation. Across five benchmarks, CARVE cuts nominal convention-completion by 91.4% and worst-case elicitation by 83.3% with 5.9% median utility loss.
AI.motivation: When deployment rules change, cooperative MARL teams must unlearn obsolete or unsafe coordination conventions that can be reproduced across agents and histories, which runtime shielding and trajectory deletion fail to address.
AI.method: CARVE uses causal coordination attribution, retain-aware subspace updates, counterfactual re-coordination to learn safe alternatives, and adversarial auditing before merging updates into decentralized actors.
AI.result: Across five cooperative MARL benchmarks, CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion by 91.4% and worst-case elicitation by 83.3%, with a 5.9% median utility loss and unchanged inference latency.
AI.conclusion: CARVE enables decentralized MARL policies to unlearn specific coordination conventions without sacrificing deployment speed or overall cooperative utility.

title: RecMem: Recurrent Memory Compression for Long-Sequence Generative Recommendation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Generative recommendation benefits from long interaction histories, but the cost of processing them directly grows with history length. We propose RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework guided by three desiderata: space invariance, semantic fidelity, and lifelong evolvability. RecMem compresses historical segments into a fixed set of memory slots using a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers and slot-wise forget-gated updates. Recommendation supervision trains the memory to preserve predictive information, while stream-consistency training aligns predictions from sequential and packed processing. By construction, the memory state and decoder context are independent of history length; under contraction and approximate semigroup consistency, we further derive a horizon-independent bound on the state discrepancy between these two processing orders. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context, compared with 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, while retaining 87.9% of HSTU-1200's Recall@10 and 97.0% of its Recall@200. It outperforms PHSTU and the evaluated recent-only and retrieval baselines, and analyses of distant history show that archived interactions contribute predictive signal.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RecMem, a recurrent memory compression framework for long-sequence generative recommendation that compresses interaction histories into fixed memory slots. On MerRec, RecMem uses 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context (versus 1,200 for HSTU-1200) while retaining 87.9% of Recall@10 and 97.0% of Recall@200.
AI.motivation: Generative recommendation benefits from long user histories, but processing them directly incurs costs that scale with history length.
AI.method: RecMem uses a bifurcated encoder-decoder with shared lower layers, slot-wise forget-gated updates, recommendation supervision, and stream-consistency training aligning sequential and packed processing, backed by a horizon-independent state-discrepancy bound.
AI.result: On MerRec, RecMem compresses history into 16 memory slots and a 216-token decoder context compared to 1,200 tokens for HSTU-1200, retaining 87.9% of Recall@10 and 97.0% of Recall@200 while outperforming PHSTU and recent-only/retrieval baselines.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-slot recurrent memory compression preserves distant-history predictive signal in generative recommendation with space-invariant cost.

title: What Balanced Accuracy Cannot Identify in Neural-Signal Decoding under Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Adaptation for neural-signal classification is usually transductive: each batch is scored after updating on it, and the gain depends on the adapted model [4]. This paper asks what an aggregate change fails to characterise inside the cohort. Full test-time adaptation (full_ttt) was evaluated in 11 dataset-encoder cells (four each on Siena/EEG and PTB-XL/ECG, three on Sleep-EDF/EEG), with splits and source-model evaluation fixed; the subject was the unit, exact sign tests were Holm-corrected and conditional on the shared stream, and bootstrap intervals accompanied a dependence audit. Two results of different kinds follow. In the binary case balanced accuracy gives a one-class decoder the same value as one reporting both classes at 50%, so the aggregate cannot identify a class that stopped being reported; a class covering a tenth of a subject's samples went unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells, against 7-9 for the controls, which is a descriptive count. With cohort, split and update rule fixed, the within-subject class contrast follows the encoder, tested directly rather than inferred from tests against zero: two of six Siena encoder pairs survive the dependence readings at their nominal reference and one at a fold-level reference, while two of ten Sleep-EDF stage pairs pass the run-clustered gate at its nominal reference; aggregate and contrast named different encoders in 10 of 11. The protocol bounds both results, since a stream-interleaving effect reverses sign with state sharing (+3.5 to -2.4 pp). An aggregate score can hide individual harm, as [1] showed, but it cannot distinguish a uniform loss from a deleted class; class-level change should therefore be reported alongside the aggregate and subject-level change alongside it, with both results conditional on the cell, the rule and the stream construction.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that aggregate balanced accuracy in neural-signal test-time adaptation (full_ttt) masks deleted classes and encoder-level differences across 11 EEG/ECG dataset-encoder cells. Aggregate and class-contrast metrics select different encoders in 10 of 11 cells.
AI.motivation: Transductive test-time adaptation is typically evaluated by aggregate balanced accuracy, which can hide individual harm or complete failure to predict a minority class.
AI.method: The authors evaluate full_ttt across 11 dataset-encoder cells (Siena/EEG, PTB-XL/ECG, Sleep-EDF/EEG) with fixed splits, using Holm-corrected exact sign tests, bootstrap intervals, and a dependence audit to compare aggregate balanced accuracy against within-subject class contrasts.
AI.result: A class covering 10% of a subject's samples went completely unpredicted in 26-47 of 112 subject-cells (versus 7-9 for controls), which balanced accuracy cannot distinguish from 50% performance on both classes. Aggregate scores and class contrasts named different best encoders in 10 of 11 cells, and stream-interleaving reversed sign (+3.5 to -2.4 pp) with state sharing.
AI.conclusion: Neural-signal TTA evaluations should report class-level and subject-level changes alongside aggregate balanced accuracy, conditioned on the update rule and stream construction.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Scientific Paper Search: Retrieval Success and Inference Latency on Mac Studio and NVIDIA A100
summary: Scientific literature search can benefit from locally deployed LLM assistants, which reduce reliance on hosted model providers while giving research teams greater control over their data and infrastructure. This work investigates whether open-weight models can support web-assisted paper retrieval under practical computing constraints. We first characterize inference latency as the input context grows from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a server equipped with two NVIDIA A100 GPUs. We then evaluate eight models on the retrieval of 70 papers from seven scientific repositories, using queries that represent three levels of domain knowledge. The results show that retrieval success depends strongly on the selected model and the specificity of the query. And that A100 GPUs are generally faster than the Mac Studio, but its unified memory allows larger models that could not be loaded in the tested GPU configuration.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates eight local open-weight LLMs for web-assisted scientific paper retrieval on a Mac Studio and a dual-NVIDIA A100 server across 512 to 128k token contexts. Retrieval success depends strongly on model choice and query specificity, while Mac Studio's unified memory hosts larger models than the tested A100 setup despite slower inference.
AI.motivation: Research teams seeking local LLM assistants for literature search need to understand retrieval accuracy and latency trade-offs across practical hardware constraints.
AI.method: The authors benchmark inference latency from 512 to 128k tokens on a Mac Studio and a two-A100 server, and evaluate eight open-weight models on retrieving 70 papers from seven scientific repositories across three query-specificity levels.
AI.result: Retrieval success varies substantially with the selected model and query domain specificity; A100 GPUs are generally faster, but Mac Studio's unified memory allows loading larger models that do not fit in the tested dual-A100 configuration.
AI.conclusion: Local scientific paper search is viable with open-weight LLMs, with hardware choice trading off raw speed against unified-memory capacity for larger models.

title: OutfitterBench: Evaluating LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Resource Allocation and Commitment Coordination
summary: In many long-horizon settings, an agent's own choices create future constraints: committing finite capacity establishes future obligations and forecloses later opportunities. Sustaining performance therefore requires both keeping evolving plans feasible and comparing the value of resource allocations with the alternatives they displace. Recent benchmarks increasingly evaluate LLM agents in continuing operations, but give less attention to how agents keep their own commitments feasible while reassessing resource allocations as opportunities change. We introduce OutfitterBench, where agents manage an outdoor-equipment rental business for 200 days, purchasing from a 46-product catalog and handling roughly 1,100 reservation requests. Under a fixed capital ceiling, reservations and uncertain walk-in demand compete for reusable equipment whose availability changes over time. Experiments with seven frontier LLMs show that several agents underperform a simple rule-based baseline, while only the leading agent consistently surpasses it. Trajectory analysis shows that some agents apply known constraints inconsistently and make new decisions that conflict with existing commitments. Agents with more reliable fulfillment can still secure low returns from comparable commitments or delay resource reallocation. The leading agent better connects preparation with economic choices but also misses opportunities for more profitable asset use. These findings highlight limitations in sustaining coherent resource plans and reassessing their value over time. The benchmark code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OutfitterBench, a 200-day business simulation benchmark evaluating LLM agents on long-horizon resource allocation and commitment coordination. Testing seven frontier LLMs shows several underperform a simple rule-based baseline, with only the leading agent consistently surpassing it.
AI.motivation: Existing long-horizon benchmarks focus on continuing operations but neglect how agents maintain feasibility of prior commitments while reallocating finite capital as new opportunities arise.
AI.method: OutfitterBench simulates an outdoor-equipment rental business over 200 days with a 46-product catalog and ~1,100 reservation requests competing with walk-in demand under a fixed capital ceiling.
AI.result: Several of seven frontier LLMs underperform a simple rule-based baseline, and trajectory analysis reveals inconsistent constraint application, conflicting commitments, low-return allocations, and missed profitable asset uses even by the leading agent.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLM agents still struggle to sustain coherent long-horizon resource plans and dynamically reassess opportunity costs.

title: Tracing Actual Causes with Counterfactual Witness Maps
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track)
summary: Halpernian actual causation, the formal study of which events in a specific situation caused a specific outcome in acyclic structural causal models, underpins legal responsibility, moral blame, and the assessment of causal harm. Despite the rich logical framework, no prior sound and complete enumeration procedure is known for finding all actual causes in a given setting, blocking downstream tasks such as responsibility attribution, blame assessment, and causal-harm grading that aggregate over the full cause set. We close this gap by introducing witness targets: sets of joint configurations containing every counterfactual witness. In combination with an ancestor intervention grammar we derive a finite directed acyclic witness map. We prove that for every actual cause there exists a contingency set such that the joint intervention set appears as a node of this map, and present an algorithm for Tracing Actual Causes (TrAC) that is sound and complete for enumerating all actual causes of any target event. We compare TrAC empirically with existing single-cause baselines on random Boolean structural causal models, demonstrating practical feasibility for graphs of up to 15 nodes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TrAC, a sound and complete algorithm for enumerating all Halpernian actual causes in acyclic Boolean structural causal models using witness targets and a directed acyclic witness map. Experiments demonstrate practical feasibility on graphs of up to 15 nodes.
AI.motivation: No prior sound and complete enumeration procedure existed for finding all actual causes in a given setting, blocking downstream tasks like responsibility attribution and blame assessment.
AI.method: The authors introduce witness targets and an ancestor intervention grammar to construct a finite directed acyclic witness map containing every counterfactual witness, proving that every actual cause corresponds to a node in this map.
AI.result: TrAC is proven sound and complete for enumerating all actual causes of any target event and is shown empirically to be feasible on random Boolean structural causal models of up to 15 nodes compared to single-cause baselines.
AI.conclusion: TrAC closes the algorithmic gap in Halpernian actual causation by enabling complete cause-set enumeration for downstream causal-harm and responsibility analyses.

title: Measured from the feed: the unsustainable growth of AI video generation
comment: Main paper + Supplementary paper Under submission at a journal
summary: Text-to-video generation runs at commercial scale, but its broader environmental impacts remain, to our knowledge, understudied. Providers rarely disclose video volumes or energy needs; we measured the yearly video output of two commercial platforms and built a prospective model of such services' absolute footprint from training to storage. Our projections suggest that reducing emissions depends on both limiting growth in video generation and achieving substantial efficiency gains. Under continued growth, emissions rise nearly seventy-five-fold by 2030 despite technological improvements. When usage remains at 2026 levels, the same improvements reduce emissions by about two-fifths. These estimates are a conservative lower bound: they cover one AI service among many; other services and uses would push the total higher.

AI.tldr: This paper measures the yearly video output of two commercial text-to-video platforms and models their end-to-end environmental footprint from training to storage. Projections show emissions rising nearly 75-fold by 2030 under continued growth, whereas holding usage at 2026 levels yields a two-fifths reduction.
AI.motivation: Commercial text-to-video generation operates at large scale, yet providers rarely disclose video volumes or energy needs, leaving its environmental impact understudied.
AI.method: The authors measure annual video output from two commercial platforms and build a prospective lifecycle emissions model spanning training through storage.
AI.result: Under continued growth, emissions increase nearly 75-fold by 2030 despite efficiency gains; if usage stays at 2026 levels, technological improvements cut emissions by about two-fifths, representing a conservative lower bound for a single AI service.
AI.conclusion: Curbing AI video generation emissions requires both substantial efficiency improvements and limits on usage growth.

title: Toward Interference-Agnostic RF Source Separation
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 tabs. Submitted to ICASSP2027
summary: Separating a radio-frequency signal of interest from a co-channel interference is mostly addressed with specialized separators, each trained for one pair of signal and interference types and therefore relying on a label that a heavily jammed receiver cannot identify. We show that this reliance is not benign: applied to an interference it was not trained on, such a separator usually fails to recover the signal, and in most of the cases we measure it leaves the signal worse than no processing at all. We then train a single separator over every pair, giving it no indication at test time of which one it faces, on two architectures with no component in common: the convolutional WaveNet of the ICASSP 2024 RF Challenge, and a band-split transformer that we adapt from music source separation. Both behave the same way. At the size of one specialized model, the unified separator stays close to the whole models it replaces, keeping the bit error rate close on almost every pair, better on one and worse on another. On an interference absent from every training set, it does as well as the best specialized model, without anyone having to choose which one to deploy.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that specialized RF source separators fail catastrophically on unseen interference types, and demonstrates that a single interference-agnostic separator trained across all pairs matches specialized models on both WaveNet and a band-split transformer.
AI.motivation: Specialized RF separators rely on knowing the signal-interference pair label, which heavily jammed receivers cannot identify, causing severe degradation on unseen interference.
AI.method: The authors train a single unified separator over all signal-interference pairs without test-time labels using two distinct architectures: the convolutional WaveNet from the ICASSP 2024 RF Challenge and an adapted band-split transformer.
AI.result: At the parameter size of one specialized model, the unified separator maintains comparable bit error rates across almost every pair and matches the best specialized model on interference types absent from all training sets, across both architectures.
AI.conclusion: Interference-agnostic training eliminates the need for test-time interference identification while preserving separation performance.

title: The Transformer Paradigm: Dynamic Processing and a New Principle of Inference
comment: v1: 15 pp., 5 figs., 1 table
summary: We argue that the Transformer revolution is not adequately understood as a merely quantitative expansion of deep learning, but as the emergence of a new paradigm based on a different principle of inference. We interpret the Transformer as a system in which token representations are transformed by parameterized transformations, or transforming concepts. During inference, some of these transformations are dynamically constructed from the current input: previously acquired transformations are first adapted and then applied. At the mechanical-structural level, this dynamic processing is realized through output-weight interconnections, whereby outputs of some networks determine the weights of others. The resulting mode of processing, which we call Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), provides a framework for explaining strong prompt sensitivity and opens research directions concerning interpretability, control, alternative AI architectures, neuromorphic systems, and possible biological realizations of dynamic processing.

AI.tldr: This conceptual paper argues that Transformers represent a new inference paradigm, Sequence-level Interactive Dynamic Parallel Processing (SIDPP), where input-dependent transformations are dynamically constructed via output-weight interconnections.
AI.motivation: Viewing Transformers merely as larger deep learning models obscures the distinct inference principle underlying their behavior and prompt sensitivity.
AI.method: The authors interpret token representations as being acted upon by parameterized transforming concepts, where outputs of some networks dynamically determine the weights of others during inference.
AI.result: Framing Transformers as SIDPP provides an explanatory lens for strong prompt sensitivity and outlines research directions in interpretability, control, alternative architectures, neuromorphic systems, and biological realizations.
AI.conclusion: Recognizing dynamic output-weight processing as the core of the Transformer paradigm opens new theoretical and architectural avenues beyond scaling.

title: WebArena-Pro: A Heterogeneous, Multimodal, Reproducible Benchmark for Web Agents
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 E&D Track
summary: Web agents powered by large language and vision-language models are increasingly applied to realistic browser work that spans heterogeneous applications, multimodal content, and stateful workflows. However, existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover only a small number of web applications drawn from a few software categories, and restrict modality to text and vision. Live benchmarks broaden site coverage but sacrifice reproducibility, since pages and data drift between runs. Moreover, existing benchmarks do not meaningfully evaluate whether agents can understand and use audio and video content embedded within web tasks. To address these gaps, we introduce WebArena-Pro, a benchmark comprising 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications in six domain categories, spanning distinct interface conventions, workflows, and data models. Across the evaluated agents, the best performance is achieved by both Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 at 62.3%, followed by OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro at 60.7%. The strongest GenericAgent configurations, Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B, both achieve 30.3%. Among reproducible, human-curated web agent benchmarks, WebArena-Pro provides the broadest application coverage and the most comprehensive multimodal support to date. The benchmark treats audio and video as core observations alongside text and vision, with dedicated actions for extracting information from each. WebArena-Pro runs each task in isolation and supports reproducible, parallel evaluation. Tasks are authored through a dedicated annotator interface, filtered by LLM-assisted triage, and finally validated by humans before release. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WebArena-Pro, a reproducible benchmark of 300 tasks across 20 self-hosted web applications that treats audio and video as core modalities alongside text and vision. Top agents (Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5) achieve 62.3% success, while top GenericAgent setups reach 30.3%.
AI.motivation: Existing reproducible web-agent benchmarks cover few applications and omit audio/video modalities, while live benchmarks lack reproducibility due to drifting pages.
AI.method: WebArena-Pro hosts 20 web applications across six categories in isolated environments with dedicated actions for audio and video extraction, using annotator-authored, LLM-triaged, and human-validated tasks.
AI.result: Codex with GPT 6.1 Sol and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5 both reach 62.3%, OpenCode with Kimi 3.1 Pro reaches 60.7%, and the strongest GenericAgent configurations (Gemini 3.1 Pro omni and Gemma4 31B) achieve 30.3%.
AI.conclusion: WebArena-Pro provides broad, reproducible, multimodal evaluation for realistic stateful web agents.

title: TotalSegmentator Aorta Report: Automated Aortic Diameter Measurement at 11 Standardized Landmarks on CT Images
summary: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a fully automated, open-source tool that measures aortic diameters at 11 standardized landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation on any CT image, following current guideline recommendations. Materials and Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 239 arterial phase CT angiography examinations of 230 patients (median age, 65 years [range, 18-99 years]; 163 men) performed between April 2025 and October 2026 (209 electrocardiographically [ECG] gated). The tool locates landmarks from TotalSegmentator segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae and measures the maximum diameter at each. A senior radiologist reviewed and, where needed, corrected the automated measurements to create the reference standard. Agreement was assessed with mean absolute error (MAE), bias, and differences greater than 2 mm. Results: Across all landmarks, MAE was 1.06 mm (95% CI: 0.91, 1.22), and 86.6% (95% CI: 84.4, 88.5) of differences were 2 mm or less. The tool measured slightly larger diameters (bias, 0.45 mm [95% CI: 0.34, 0.57]). The sinuses of Valsalva had the largest MAE (2.17 mm [95% CI: 1.59, 2.86]). For 1.2% of landmarks, the automatic measurement failed. Examination-level MAE did not differ significantly by pathology, atherosclerosis grade (P=.95), or ECG gating (P=.14). Examinations with mural thrombus more often had an MAE greater than 2 mm (50% [95% CI: 31, 69] vs 20%; P=.03). Conclusion: The tool measured aortic diameters at 11 landmarks along the entire aorta with an MAE of about 1 mm, below published interreader variability. Agreement was lower at the aortic root and with mural thrombus. Code availability: The tool is open source and freely available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and evaluates an open-source TotalSegmentator-based tool that automatically measures aortic diameters at 11 standardized landmarks on CT angiography. Across 239 scans, it achieves a mean absolute error of 1.06 mm, below published interreader variability.
AI.motivation: Manual aortic diameter measurement at guideline landmarks on CT scans is time-consuming, motivating a fully automated, open-source alternative.
AI.method: Using TotalSegmentator segmentations of aortic branches and vertebrae, the tool locates 11 landmarks from the aortic annulus to the bifurcation and measures maximum diameters, evaluated against radiologist-reviewed references on 239 arterial-phase CT angiography scans (230 patients).
AI.result: Overall MAE is 1.06 mm (bias 0.45 mm), with 86.6% of differences within 2 mm and 1.2% landmark failures. The sinuses of Valsalva had the highest MAE (2.17 mm); MAE did not differ by pathology, atherosclerosis, or ECG gating, but mural thrombus increased >2 mm errors (50% vs 20%, P=.03).
AI.conclusion: The open-source tool measures aortic diameters across 11 landmarks with ~1 mm accuracy, though agreement is lower at the aortic root and with mural thrombus.

title: Interactive deep-learning based interface for brain tumour segmentation
summary: Brain tumour segmentation from MR images is an integral part of their treatment, either through surgical resection or radiotherapy. Both applications require a high degree of precision that can be difficult to ensure for all patients due to the high degree of variability in the size, shape, number, and location of these tumours. This leads to difficulties with their automatic segmentation via deep learning, which can display catastrophic segmentation errors when presented with images that differ, even subtly, in terms of the specific MR sequence used, which varies from vendor to vendor. This article presents a deep-learning-based interactive segmentation system that, while being fully automatic by default, has the capability of being easily corrected by human users, allowing them ensure sufficiently high brain tumour segmentation accuracy for all patients. This interface is evaluated both in terms of the accuracy of its automatic approach as well as its usability through a preliminary observational expert user study.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an interactive deep-learning-based brain tumour segmentation system that operates automatically by default while allowing human users to easily correct errors, and evaluates its accuracy and usability.
AI.motivation: Automatic deep-learning segmentation of brain tumours from MR images can suffer catastrophic errors when encountering subtle vendor-to-vendor MR sequence variations or high variability in tumour size, shape, number, and location.
AI.method: The authors build a deep-learning-based interactive segmentation interface that runs fully automatically by default and provides human users with simple correction capabilities to refine segmentation outputs.
AI.result: The interface is evaluated on both the accuracy of its automatic segmentation approach and its usability through a preliminary observational expert user study.
AI.conclusion: Combining default automatic segmentation with accessible human correction helps ensure reliable brain tumour segmentation accuracy across diverse patients and imaging sequences.

title: LACCO: Local Accumulation with Computation--Communication Overlap
summary: Training language models across low-bandwidth networks requires reducing synchronization overhead. Local optimization methods such as DiLoCo communicate only after several local steps, but outer gradient averaging and the outer update remain on the critical path. Existing computation-communication overlap methods avoid this stall through delayed or replica-local updates, which can degrade convergence or cause replicas to drift. We propose LACCO (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap), a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying globally aggregated updates shared by every replica, without introducing staleness in the outer update. We establish convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives. Experiments on language-model pre-training with FineWeb show that LACCO consistently outperforms communication-overlapped baselines such as Eager and Delayed DiLoCo. These gains remain robust as model size scales up to 0.5B parameters and across a range of communication intervals and numbers of replicas up to 16 workers, while incurring only negligible-or fully overlappable-computational or memory overhead, which demonstrates the strength of LACCO.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes LACCO, a two-stage distributed training algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while applying globally aggregated updates without outer-update staleness.
AI.motivation: Local optimization methods like DiLoCo reduce synchronization overhead over low-bandwidth networks, but outer gradient averaging remains on the critical path, and existing overlap methods introduce staleness or replica drift.
AI.method: LACCO (Local Accumulation with Computation-Communication Overlap) uses a two-stage algorithm that overlaps global communication with local computation while ensuring every replica applies globally aggregated updates without staleness.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis establishes convergence guarantees for smooth non-convex objectives, and FineWeb language-model pre-training experiments up to 0.5B parameters and 16 workers show LACCO consistently outperforms Eager and Delayed DiLoCo across communication intervals with negligible or fully overlappable overhead.
AI.conclusion: LACCO enables efficient, drift-free distributed language model training over low-bandwidth networks without sacrificing convergence.

title: Understanding the limits of snapshot-based fault diagnosis in distribution networks
summary: Inverter-based resources weaken fault currents in distribution networks, and snapshot-based diagnosis, which classifies a fault from voltage phasors at a few buses at one instant, offers a cheap first-stage screen. Its published accuracies, however, rest on different noise assumptions and do not show whether the error comes from the classifier, the features, the measurement error, or the fault resistance. This paper separates these sources on three IEEE test feeders and a public data set with distributed generation, using four feature sets, thirteen classifiers, and measurement error defined by total vector error classes. The classifier is not the limiting factor, because the full phasor snapshot classifies every fault correctly without noise, and the remaining error comes from measurement error on high-impedance faults. Three voltage sensors classify 90-96% of faults at the 1% accuracy class and 96-99% with distribution micro phasor measurement units (micro-PMUs). A discriminability-margin placement selects them from simulations alone in under one second and matches the best of twelve placement methods. The results show when snapshot-based diagnosis can be trusted.

AI.tldr: This paper isolates the sources of error in snapshot-based fault diagnosis for distribution networks and shows that measurement error on high-impedance faults, rather than the classifier, limits accuracy.
AI.motivation: Published accuracies for snapshot-based fault diagnosis rest on inconsistent noise assumptions and do not clarify whether errors stem from the classifier, features, measurement error, or fault resistance.
AI.method: The authors evaluate four feature sets, thirteen classifiers, and total-vector-error measurement noise classes across three IEEE test feeders and a public dataset with distributed generation, and introduce a discriminability-margin sensor placement method.
AI.result: Full phasor snapshots classify every fault without noise, while three voltage sensors achieve 90-96% accuracy at the 1% accuracy class and 96-99% with micro-PMUs; the placement method runs in under one second from simulations alone and matches the best of twelve baselines.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify when snapshot-based fault diagnosis is reliable and provide a fast, simulation-only sensor placement strategy.

title: A$^3$: Adaptive Audio Agent Framework for Collaborative Edge Computing
summary: Embedded audio agents need a nearby edge server for speed, but a server-dependent agent returns nothing when the link fails. We present A$^3$, an adaptive audio agent framework that places whole pipeline stages on the server, keeps a complete fallback agent on devices that can host one, and hedges both paths with a link-aware deadline that decides when to give up on the server. On Jetson devices and an RTX A4500 server, A$^3$ matches the server-only agent on a healthy link, answers every request in a full outage on the AGX, and beats a percentile hedge in simulated outages.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces A^3, an adaptive audio agent framework that hedges edge-server execution with an on-device fallback agent using a link-aware deadline.
AI.motivation: Embedded audio agents rely on nearby edge servers for speed, but server-dependent designs return nothing when network links fail.
AI.method: A^3 places full pipeline stages on the edge server, maintains a complete fallback agent on capable local devices, and hedges both execution paths with a link-aware deadline that determines when to abandon the server.
AI.result: Evaluated on Jetson devices and an RTX A4500 server, A^3 matches the server-only agent on healthy links, answers every request during a full outage on the AGX, and outperforms a percentile hedge in simulated outages.
AI.conclusion: Link-aware hedging between edge-server and on-device execution provides both low-latency performance and outage resilience for embedded audio agents.

title: Two-Clustering Regime of Token Dynamics in Causal Attention
summary: We partially resolve Conjecture 1 of [Karagodin et al., Clustering in Causal Attention Masking (NeurIPS 2024)] and extend it to time-dependent parameter regimes. The conjecture predicts that causal attention dynamics converge to two clusters aligned with the eigenvectors associated with the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$ of the value transformation. We prove that this behavior holds when $\lambda_{\max}>0$ and is generally false when $\lambda_{\max}\le0$. The resulting two-cluster regime is common in practice and substantially more challenging than the classical single-cluster setting studied previously. A central contribution of our work is the identification of a rigorous dimension reduction phenomenon: despite evolving in a high-dimensional embedding space, token trajectories collapse onto a two-dimensional structure governed by a small number of dominant directions. Building on this insight, we introduce a new analytical framework--instability within the flow--inspired by instability phenomena in physical systems. This framework enables the analysis of steady-regime behavior in non-monotone, non-autonomous attention dynamics.
