We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

AI.tldr: This paper adapts Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS) for inference-time steering of crystal generative models using property-conditional proposals and multi-objective Pareto-front search.
AI.motivation: Steering diffusion-based crystal generative models toward multiple conflicting properties via fine-tuning is expensive, and differentiable guidance is often inapplicable.
AI.method: The authors extend DTS—a Monte Carlo tree search over denoising trajectories—to use existing property-conditional models as unbiased guided proposals and to perform multi-objective sampling in a single search.
AI.result: On de novo crystal generation, DTS improves crystal stability, generates structures in rare space groups or with high bulk modulus from pretrained conditional models, and produces Pareto fronts trading off dielectric constant and bandgap without modifying model weights.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time tree search provides a flexible, training-free mechanism for multi-objective steering of scientific diffusion models.

title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures
summary: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a modular ontology and SWRL rule set developed with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living in smart homes.
AI.motivation: Smart homes must coordinate heterogeneous devices to support ageing dwellers, requiring a shared formal representation of both user impairments and smart object capabilities.
AI.method: Derived from two Italian Design For All use cases (cycle-ergometer exercise and accessible kitchen configuration), the authors build a modular ontology using the NeOn methodology, integrating ICF user profiles, fitness metrics, smart object programs, comfort dimensions, and SWRL rules.
AI.result: The resulting ontology and SWRL rules classify user fitness levels, recommend exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and match smart objects to specific user impairments.
AI.conclusion: Use-case-driven ontology engineering with NeOn provides a structured semantic data layer for personalized ambient assisted living systems.

title: Do Mixture-of-Experts Routers Benefit from Ensembling?
comment: 23 pages, 21 figures
summary: Ensembles of neural networks have repeatedly been shown to outperform single networks. Ensemble theory attributes this gain to the accuracy of the individual members and the diversity among them. Mixture-of-experts models already combine many experts, but a single router decides how the experts are weighted for each input. Motivated by ensemble theory, we apply ensembling to the routing step: an ensemble of routers, trained jointly with the experts, proposes the expert weights. We systematically evaluate this approach using underparameterized networks on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks. We analyse each experiment with a performance-diversity decomposition of the router ensemble, which, to our knowledge, has not previously been developed for routers. We report four findings. First, more routers lower the validation loss. Second, training routers to explicitly maximize expert diversity improves the mean performance on three of the four tasks. Third, explicitly maximizing router diversity has no effect on performance. Fourth, combining router weights with the arithmetic mean works better than combining them with the geometric mean. Routing benefits mildly from ensembling, but this benefit is offset by the computational cost of training additional routers.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates ensembling Mixture-of-Experts routers, finding mild validation-loss improvements that are offset by the added computational cost of training multiple routers.
AI.motivation: While neural network ensembles improve accuracy through member diversity, standard Mixture-of-Experts models rely on a single router to weight experts.
AI.method: The authors train ensembles of routers jointly with experts on two image-classification and two tabular-regression tasks using underparameterized networks, and analyze results via a router performance-diversity decomposition.
AI.result: Adding routers lowers validation loss, explicitly maximizing expert diversity improves mean performance on three of four tasks, maximizing router diversity has no effect, and arithmetic-mean weight combination outperforms geometric mean, though extra router training costs offset the mild gains.
AI.conclusion: Router ensembling offers modest performance benefits that are generally outweighed by its additional training overhead.

title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Object tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses CARLA simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA), and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates image-specific and universal adversarial attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 paired with four object trackers in CARLA, showing severe tracking degradation.
AI.motivation: Adversarial perturbations to object detectors can disrupt downstream Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) trajectory estimation in autonomous vehicles in ways not captured by detection accuracy alone.
AI.method: The authors test image-specific attacks and single Universal Adversarial Perturbations (UAPs) against YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 combined with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT in the CARLA simulator, measuring MOTA, HOTA, and IDF1.
AI.result: Under image-specific attacks, YOLOv3-based trackers drop from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03% HOTA (with MOTA reaching -772.60%), while YOLOv4-based trackers drop to 25.06-26.86% HOTA; image-agnostic UAPs also substantially degrade tracking accuracy across frames.
AI.conclusion: Both frame-specific and universal adversarial attacks pose severe risks to camera-based multi-object tracking in autonomous driving.

title: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
comment: Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 First Workshop on Meta Agents: Managing Agents that Manage Agents (Meta-Agents)
summary: Major industry multi-agent systems like Codex and Claude Code can be broken by attacks that have long been unsuccessful against modern frontier models. AI Safety as a discipline has largely focused on finding the bounds and vulnerabilities of AI models used in isolation. Yet as humans increasingly deploy these models as agents and multi-agent systems, the same attacks that had been thought to be patched when using a model in isolation can break these same models under specific circumstances. We show that these system breaks are not purely theoretical, but can break Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, all unmodified and used with their own sub-agent mechanisms. We show the attack by asking agents to answer questions from a store of files on disk in which we have planted a forged record. Searching the store themselves, the strong model orchestrators commit almost zero harmful revisions in over 1,000 trials. However, if that same orchestrator model delegates to a cheaper sub-agent, which is what these harnesses are built to do, the same models on the same facts fail on 20/180, 44/180, 75/180 and 553/900. Thus, even when the system is driven by a strong model, the system's safety lands near the weak reader's, not the orchestrator's. Simulations over 18 models show the same effect in the delivery channel where five aggregators, who on their own were almost never unsafe, repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials. The safety of real-world agentic systems that use strong orchestrator agents and weaker sub-agents, and multi-agent systems in general, is defined not by the safety of the strong agent but by the safety of the weakest agent.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that multi-agent systems like Claude Code and Codex can be broken by forged-record attacks when strong orchestrators delegate to weaker sub-agents.
AI.motivation: AI safety evaluations typically test frontier models in isolation, overlooking vulnerabilities that emerge only when strong orchestrator agents delegate tasks to cheaper sub-agents.
AI.method: The authors plant a forged record in a local file store and test unmodified Claude Code, Codex, and a reference harness, alongside 18-model aggregator simulations, on question-answering tasks with and without sub-agent delegation.
AI.result: Strong orchestrators searching directly commit nearly zero harmful revisions across 1,000+ trials, but delegating to cheaper sub-agents causes failures in 20/180, 44/180, 75/180, and 553/900 cases; in simulations, five otherwise safe aggregators repeat a corrupted sub-agent's error in 751/757 trials.
AI.conclusion: The safety of a multi-agent system is governed by its weakest sub-agent rather than its strongest orchestrator.

title: GraphScent: Calibrating Directional Relevance Signals for Bounded-Context Code Localization
summary: Running open-weight language models locally on a single consumer GPU requires replacing expanding multi-turn exploration histories with short, stateless code inspections. Stateless repository localization, however, hinges on a foundational question: when a frozen language model evaluates an unedited code entity from a compact view, which structural relationships make its relevance judgment informative about a nearby repair target? Studying Gemma 4 models across 211 real-world Python issues in 86 repositories, we uncover a systematic directional relevance asymmetry: zero-temperature relevance scores on enclosing scopes and upstream callers consistently separate true structural neighbors from hard lexical distractors, whereas scores on downstream callees, peer methods, historical co-change partners, and dense node embeddings remain near chance. Zero-leakage masked-scope probes and regressions controlling for lexical similarity and snippet length confirm that this asymmetry reflects functional role (callers expose symptom entrypoints delegating to defective routines, while downstream helpers appear benign alone) rather than target leakage or surface overlap. Guided by this finding, we introduce GraphScent, a training-free search controller that propagates out-of-repository, relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over runtime Typed-AST multigraphs before resolving ties via a single listwise comparison, alongside AST Ripple, a lightweight post-edit check for missed co-edits. Likelihood calibration prevents overconfident smaller models from chasing false-positive callers while lifting exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8 to 23.4 percent at 31B within a single-GPU budget.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a directional relevance asymmetry in stateless code localization and introduces GraphScent, a training-free search controller that lifts exact localization from 12.8% to 23.4% at 31B.
AI.motivation: Localizing code issues on a single consumer GPU requires short, stateless inspections, but it is unclear which structural code relationships yield informative relevance signals from frozen models.
AI.method: Studying Gemma 4 models on 211 Python issues across 86 repositories, the authors find enclosing scopes and upstream callers separate true neighbors from lexical distractors while downstream callees and peers do not; they build GraphScent to propagate calibrated relation-conditioned log-likelihood ratios over Typed-AST multigraphs, paired with AST Ripple for co-edit checks.
AI.result: Zero-leakage masked-scope probes confirm the directional asymmetry reflects functional role rather than leakage, and GraphScent's likelihood calibration lifts exact localization on lexically hard targets from 12.8% to 23.4% at 31B within a single-GPU budget.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting directional structural asymmetry with calibrated likelihood propagation enables effective stateless code localization on local hardware.

title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Target-Centric Causal Discovery in Industrial Processes
summary: Causal discovery promises to find which recorded variables drive a process target such as product quality, yield or energy use. Process data with known causes are rare, and in existing benchmarks the difficulty of identifying the causes of a target is either fixed by the recorded data or set for the whole graph. We present a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes. Its generator is a two-level structural causal model inspired by batch production, assembled from components that each model one phenomenon of process data, such as a control loop or a delayed effect. The graph is built around the target: without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from the direct causes by conditioning on them or by time order. Each component is set independently, so the difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. We evaluate eight methods, from association measures to effect estimation, with an error analysis by the role of the selected candidate; all degrade as the difficulties combine, each in a way consistent with its assumptions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a synthetic benchmark for target-centric causal discovery in industrial processes where difficulty can be varied one condition at a time. Evaluating eight methods shows all degrade as difficulties combine, in ways consistent with their assumptions.
AI.motivation: Process data with known ground-truth causes are rare, and existing benchmarks either fix difficulty via recorded data or vary it only for the whole graph rather than around a specific process target.
AI.method: The authors build a two-level structural causal model generator inspired by batch production, assembling independent components that each model a single process phenomenon (such as control loops or delayed effects) around a target.
AI.result: Without sensor error, every non-cause can be distinguished from direct causes by conditioning or time order; across eight evaluated methods from association measures to effect estimation, all degrade as difficulties combine.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a controllable testbed for diagnosing how individual and combined industrial process challenges affect target-centric causal discovery methods.

title: Benchmarks Don't Talk Back: Learning Through Self-Disagreement
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 15 tables
summary: A benchmark usually measures a language model alone with a question, and deployment rarely looks like that: answers get contested, and models give up correct ones under counter-reasoning that is itself wrong. We show that what fails there is not a shortfall of accuracy but a capability in its own right -- knowing when to hold a position and when to yield to a better one -- which we call dialectical competence. It stands on first-answer accuracy without following from it: a model can be made materially better at answering and no better at this, and training for accuracy alone can drift against it. Nor can it be bought at inference, by self-reflection or by sampling more. Taking a cue from the dialectical tradition in philosophy, in which productive opposition arises within a position rather than being imposed on it from outside, we hypothesize that this capability can be trained from opposition the model supplies itself. It states a position, generates the strongest case against that position -- its antithesis -- rules on whether the case stands, and is trained on that ruling, with no second model at training or at deployment. We call this learning through Self-Disagreement: reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards throughout, where the same check that scores an answer against its reference scores the ruling too, so no reward model, no preference data and no human annotation enter anywhere. The capability is trained rather than elicited: weak in the base model, it arrives with the reward, is not paid for out of first-answer accuracy, and holds against challengers the model never trained against, including ones stronger than itself. The opposition a model needs in order to improve, it turns out, need not come from outside it.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies dialectical competence—knowing when to hold a correct position or yield to a better one—and proposes Self-Disagreement, a reinforcement learning method that trains this capability without external models or human labels.
AI.motivation: Standard benchmarks test models in isolation, whereas deployed models often abandon correct answers under flawed counter-reasoning, and existing accuracy training or inference-time self-reflection fails to build this resistance.
AI.method: Under Self-Disagreement, a single model states a position, generates its strongest antithesis, rules on whether the antithesis stands, and is trained via reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards using the same reference check for both answer and ruling.
AI.result: Weak in base models, dialectical competence emerges with the reward without sacrificing first-answer accuracy and generalizes against stronger, unseen challengers.
AI.conclusion: Productive opposition for improving a model's robustness to contestation can be generated and trained internally without external reward models or preference data.

title: Rethinking Visual Reasoning in Text-to-Image Reward Modeling
summary: Reward models are a core component of modern text-to-image systems, serving as the objective for inference-time selection and RL-based post-training. A key prerequisite is visual understanding: to judge prompt adherence and ground aesthetic preferences, a reward model must bind attributes, resolve relations, and count reliably. We find that widely-used reward models perform poorly on targeted visual reasoning evaluations. Even when starting from strong vision-language backbones, preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities, and continual-learning baselines fail to mitigate a steep tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy. We propose a data-centric intervention that injects visual reasoning supervision into preference learning by flipping the pairing axis. To complement conventional human preference data (paired images under a shared prompt), we convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs that share the same image but differ in prompt, and train on the mixture. This yields a Pareto improvement in both visual understanding and preference prediction. Across inference-time best-of-n selection and RL post-training, the resulting reward model improves text-to-image generation on challenging compositional prompts (GenEval) by an average of 4.0% and 5.5% respectively, outperforming HPSv3 which was trained on 6x more preference pairs.

AI.tldr: This paper improves visual reasoning in text-to-image reward models by adding preference pairs that share an image but differ in prompt, outperforming HPSv3 on GenEval.
AI.motivation: Widely used text-to-image reward models perform poorly on visual reasoning tasks such as attribute binding, relation resolution, and counting, and preference fine-tuning erodes these capabilities in vision-language backbones.
AI.method: The authors convert existing visual reasoning datasets into preference pairs sharing the same image with different prompts and train on a mixture of these pairs and conventional human preference data.
AI.result: The approach yields a Pareto improvement in visual understanding and preference prediction, improving GenEval scores by an average of 4.0% in best-of-n selection and 5.5% in RL post-training while outperforming HPSv3 trained on 6x more preference pairs.
AI.conclusion: Flipping the pairing axis to inject visual reasoning supervision into preference learning resolves the tradeoff between visual reasoning and preference accuracy.

title: X-Nav Technical Report: Real-World Long-Horizon Indoor-to-Outdoor Navigation on a Humanoid Robot
summary: Long-horizon navigation from indoors to outdoors remains an open problem for humanoid robots: one instruction covers rooms, doors and roads, and the camera moves with the gait. Worken, AGIBOT's measure of productive robot work, depends on robots that reach their workplaces autonomously. We present X-Nav, to our knowledge the first system to take a bipedal humanoid through a language-instructed long-horizon mission from indoors to outdoors. X-Nav covers a pipeline from data to deployment. Its data engine collects navigation data in open-source scenes, in digital twins of deployment sites and on real robots. Its navigation model, MELIOR, takes only RGB images from the robot's built-in camera and comes in two versions: MELIOR-A predicts actions, and MELIOR-N predicts a navigation goal. Its agentic workflow, X-Navarch, turns a brief human instruction into sub-tasks and deploys MELIOR on the robot with explicit target navigation and obstacle avoidance. On the Lingxi X2, X-Nav completes a mission of about a hundred metres from an office lobby to a store in a neighbouring building; LiDAR and odometry are used for target approach and low-level control. The mission is completed with both versions of MELIOR: the robot follows a change of destination and walks through a door from the lobby to the road, and with X-Navarch it also passes static and dynamic obstacles on the route. During deployment, MELIOR is adapted with data collected in a digital twin of the site; the adaptation raises its closed-loop success rate in the twin, and the adapted model is then deployed on the robot at the real site. In addition, MELIOR achieves competitive results on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This technical report presents X-Nav, a pipeline and system that enables a bipedal humanoid robot to complete language-instructed, long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation missions using only RGB images for high-level navigation.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor navigation remains an open challenge for humanoid robots because instructions span rooms, doors, and roads while the onboard camera moves with the robot's gait.
AI.method: X-Nav combines a data engine spanning open-source scenes, digital twins, and real robots, an RGB-only navigation model (MELIOR, in action-predicting MELIOR-A and goal-predicting MELIOR-N variants), and an agentic workflow (X-Navarch) that decomposes instructions into sub-tasks with target navigation and obstacle avoidance.
AI.result: On the Lingxi X2 humanoid (using LiDAR and odometry for low-level control), X-Nav completes a ~100-meter mission from an office lobby through a door to a neighboring building's store while handling destination changes and obstacles; digital-twin adaptation raises closed-loop success, and MELIOR achieves competitive results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
AI.conclusion: Combining digital-twin adaptation, RGB-based navigation policies, and agentic sub-task decomposition enables practical long-horizon indoor-to-outdoor humanoid navigation.

title: Training-Free Acceleration of Multi-View 3D Transformers via Regime-Aware Attention Approximation
summary: Multi-view 3D transformers such as VGGT reconstruct a scene from a set of unposed images in a single forward pass, predicting camera poses, depth and 3D points, but the cost of their global attention grows quadratically with the num- ber of images. Accelerators borrowed from large language models assume that each token attends to only a few oth- ers; on these models they lose accuracy or gain little speed. We study the global attention of three multi-view transform- ers on seven datasets and find that every layer plays one of three roles: it averages over the whole scene, matches points across many images, or anchors on the first image, whose coordinates the outputs use. Building on this anal- ysis, we propose Regime-AWare ATTention Approximation (RAWATTA), a training-free method that runs attention in 8- bit precision and keeps 16-bit precision only in the layers where a worst-case calibration check requires it. Its fast set- ting, RAWATTA-Fast, also approximates attention in a few averaging and anchoring layers, while matching layers and the first image keep all their keys. On a 12 GB GPU at 50 im- ages, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than the released code, mostly through our CUDA engine, and loses at most about one point of pose accuracy (AUC@3) on any dataset; RAWATTA-Fast is slightly faster and less accurate. Both fit 200 images, where the released code runs out of memory at 100.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes RAWATTA, a training-free attention approximation method for multi-view 3D transformers that speeds up inference and enables 200-image reconstruction on a 12 GB GPU.
AI.motivation: Multi-view 3D transformers like VGGT incur quadratic global attention cost with image count, and LLM-style sparse attention accelerators either lose accuracy or yield little speedup on these models.
AI.method: Analyzing three multi-view transformers across seven datasets, the authors find layers play three roles (scene averaging, cross-image matching, or first-image anchoring) and propose RAWATTA to run attention in 8-bit precision while keeping 16-bit precision only where a worst-case calibration check requires it, plus RAWATTA-Fast to approximate averaging and anchoring layers while preserving matching layers and first-image keys.
AI.result: On a 12 GB GPU at 50 images, RAWATTA runs VGGT faster than released code via a custom CUDA engine with at most ~1 point AUC@3 pose accuracy loss, and both RAWATTA and RAWATTA-Fast fit 200 images where released code runs out of memory at 100.
AI.conclusion: Regime-aware precision and key approximation enable fast, memory-efficient multi-view 3D reconstruction without retraining.

title: CoTTAGE: An Explainable Judge for Text-to-Audio Generation
summary: Rapid progress in text-to-audio (TTA) generation demands reliable and explainable automatic evaluation. However, existing metrics fail to simultaneously deliver high correlation with human judgments and meaningful, audio-grounded explanations, forcing reliance on labor-intensive human evaluation that bottlenecks model development iteration. To address this, we propose CoTTAGE, a reasoning-based evaluator for text relevance (REL) and audio quality (OVL). Following a reason-then-predict paradigm, CoTTAGE first generates an audio-grounded rationale to diagnose errors before predicting scores. Supported by over 10K newly collected human OVL annotations, CoTTAGE is first trained via supervised fine-tuning and then refined with reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective that converts sampled score distributions into pairwise preference probabilities and rewards agreement with rankings derived from human judgments. Across six benchmarks spanning REL and OVL, CoTTAGE achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments while producing human-preferred explanations to accelerate TTA development.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CoTTAGE, a reasoning-based evaluator for text-to-audio generation that produces audio-grounded explanations before predicting text relevance and audio quality scores.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic metrics for text-to-audio generation fail to combine high human correlation with meaningful, audio-grounded explanations, leaving development bottlenecked by human evaluation.
AI.method: Supported by over 10K new human overall quality (OVL) annotations, CoTTAGE follows a reason-then-predict paradigm trained first with supervised fine-tuning and then refined via reinforcement learning using a Thurstone-based preference objective over sampled score distributions.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks spanning text relevance (REL) and OVL, CoTTAGE achieves state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments and generates human-preferred explanations.
AI.conclusion: Combining audio-grounded rationale generation with Thurstone-based preference RL yields an accurate, explainable automatic judge for text-to-audio systems.

title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
comment: This paper appears at the Trustworthy Machine Learning Workshop (ARTMAN 2026) co-located with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC 2026)
summary: Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how input binarization in Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) acts as an adversarial attack surface and shows that encoding granularity trades clean accuracy for robustness.
AI.motivation: WNNs binarize inputs into lookup-memory queries, which can make them seem naturally robust to small perturbations, yet perturbations that cross binarization thresholds can still alter predictions.
AI.method: The authors formalize threshold-crossing bounds and a response-margin certificate for Boolean WiSARD, and evaluate WiSARD, Bloom WiSARD, and BTHOWeN on MNIST (comparing linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under sensitivity probes, Simulated Annealing, and surrogate-transfer attacks) as well as Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets.
AI.result: Adjusting encoding granularity alone trades a small clean-accuracy loss for a large drop in attack success on MNIST, while on intrusion-detection datasets adversarial perturbations cause WNN detectors to misclassify attacks as normal traffic and raise false alarms despite high aggregate accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Binarization thresholds are a critical security surface in WNNs, and encoding design strongly governs their adversarial robustness.

title: Imitation Policies Learn a Proprioceptive Anchor: A Predictive Law for Perception Noise and Its Closed Loop Cost
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures
summary: Imitation policies for robot manipulation are often trained on noisy object positions, and they learn to discount the noisy reading. We show how much they discount it, and why. Because demonstrators steer toward the object, the robot's own state carries information about where the object is. A trained policy combines this proprioceptive anchor with the reading and weights the reading by $\alpha = V/(V + s^2)$, where $s^2$ is the reading noise and $V$ the anchor's error variance. $V$ belongs to the learner and is far smaller than a linear model of the demonstrations implies, which is why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates $\alpha$. Measured once, $V$ predicted ten held-out sensitivities across two robomimic tasks, two learners and four new noise levels, with mean absolute error 0.025 against 0.37 for classical EIV, and a parameter-free bias test rules out the simpler explanation that the policies just overestimate the noise. The discount does not carry over to deployment, where the policy produces its own state: closed-loop sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded $\alpha$ in all 15 policies that passed the registered gates, although the stricter registered prediction, that all would follow the offset fully, held for 8 of them. Post hoc, lower $\alpha$ went with lower success, steeply for diffusion, and a registered prospective test confirmed this for diffusion on Can at two new noise levels: the measured $\alpha$ predicted success before any rollout, within 0.03 (95% intervals $\pm 0.08$), although training noise predicts it equally well. Every test was registered before its data, including the classical benchmark that failed, and all other analyses are labelled post hoc; all results are in simulation with synthetic Gaussian noise.

AI.tldr: This paper derives and validates a predictive law showing how imitation policies discount noisy object-position readings using a proprioceptive anchor, and demonstrates why this discount breaks down in closed-loop deployment.
AI.motivation: Imitation policies trained on noisy object positions learn to discount the noisy reading, but how much they discount it, why classical errors-in-variables (EIV) regression overestimates it, and how it behaves in closed-loop deployment were unclear.
AI.method: The authors model the policy as combining the noisy reading with a proprioceptive anchor of variance V, weighting the reading by alpha = V / (V + s^2) where s^2 is reading noise, and test pre-registered predictions across robomimic tasks, learners, and noise levels in simulation.
AI.result: Measured once, V predicted ten held-out sensitivities with 0.025 MAE (versus 0.37 for classical EIV); in closed-loop deployment, sensitivity to a persistent reading offset exceeded alpha in all 15 gated policies (and followed the offset fully in 8), while pre-rollout alpha predicted diffusion success on Can within 0.03.
AI.conclusion: The proprioceptive anchor law accurately explains and predicts perception-noise discounting and its closed-loop failure modes in imitation learning.

title: Agent-written heuristics versus commercial solvers on unsolved job-shop benchmark instances
comment: 27 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to International Transactions in Operational Research. Data, schedules, checkers and code: this https URL
summary: Commercial solvers are the standard tool for difficult scheduling problems. We study whether a frontier large language model, used as a coding agent with open-source tools only, can match them in quality and speed. We report every run, and independent checkers verify every schedule. On the 100,000-operation job shop tai_100_1000_1, an agent-written solver reached 525,515, below OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer. Unchanged, it improved all ten instances of the family and closed two. With equal budgets on the same workstation, it ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound, against 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly. On the Behnke-Geiger flexible job shops, an agent-written tabu search improved 11 of 32 open instances. With two transport robots, an agent-written solver improved seven of ten MKT instances. New lower bounds show that four published MKT values cannot be attained on the distributed instance files. Agent-run improvement campaigns closed eight further instances.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether a frontier LLM coding agent using only open-source tools can match or beat commercial solvers on difficult, unsolved job-shop scheduling benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Commercial solvers dominate difficult scheduling problems, and it is unclear whether LLM-written heuristics can compete in solution quality and speed under rigorous verification.
AI.method: The authors use a frontier LLM as a coding agent with open-source tools to write and iteratively improve scheduling solvers, verifying every reported run and schedule with independent checkers.
AI.result: On the 100,000-operation tai_100_1000_1 instance, an agent-written solver reached 525,515 (beating OptalCP, Hexaly, and CP Optimizer) and ended 0.0-1.8% above the lower bound under equal budgets (versus 2.6-5.8% for CP Optimizer and 2.4-4.4% for Hexaly); agent-written solvers also improved 11 of 32 open Behnke-Geiger instances, 7 of 10 MKT instances, and closed 10 total instances.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLM coding agents with open-source tools can produce state-of-the-art heuristics that rival or surpass commercial solvers on large-scale scheduling benchmarks.

title: Logically Consistent Accurate Forecasts
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Temporal Systems (FMTS)
summary: Agentic forecasting systems based on large language models (LLMs) are now competitive with expert human forecasters, but these systems still suffer from a critical limitation: the inability to produce forecasts that are logically consistent. For example, forecasts for related events often fail to satisfy the axioms of probability, which in turn implies that related forecasts cannot simultaneously be correct and undermines their utility for decision makers. Enforcing consistency is not trivial -- naive approaches (e.g., projection onto the set of consistent forecasts) can degrade accuracy. We argue that the key to overcoming the apparent tradeoff between consistency and accuracy lies in the reasoning which supports each forecast. We finetune a supervisory language model that leverages this reasoning to jointly reconcile inconsistencies while improving the accuracy of related forecasts. On ForecastBench, our method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing measures of structural inconsistency by 82-90%. We interrogate our method via a comprehensive series of baselines and ablations, and find that no alternative method matches our gains in consistency and accuracy simultaneously.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes finetuning a supervisory language model on forecast reasoning to reconcile logical inconsistencies across related LLM forecasts while simultaneously improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Agentic LLM forecasters rival human experts but often violate probability axioms across related events, and naive post-hoc fixes such as projection can degrade accuracy.
AI.method: The authors finetune a supervisory language model that leverages the reasoning supporting each forecast to jointly reconcile inconsistencies and improve accuracy across related forecasts.
AI.result: On ForecastBench, the method improves the Brier score of a retrieval-augmented GPT-5.1 forecaster by 9.3% while reducing structural inconsistency by 82-90%, outperforming all tested baselines and ablations.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-aware supervision resolves the consistency-accuracy tradeoff in LLM-based forecasting.

title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
summary: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives this http URL, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. For Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro, a chat sent while eight agents are working receives its first token in 1.5 s, against 291-612 s on llama-server, Ollama, and this http URL. On six machines from three chip vendors serving 64 simulated users for one hour, Superfluid answers all 5,041 requests while machines join one at a time and one is killed and rejoins; throughput grows from 112 to 534 tok/s and the median first-token time falls from 99 to 12 s. On twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras it sustains 10,656 tok/s across 38,563 requests from 384 agents without a failure. Superfluid is available under the Apache-2.0 licence at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Superfluid, an open-source local LLM server that schedules interactive and agentic workloads on one machine and pools heterogeneous machines into a single API endpoint.
AI.motivation: Local LLM serving is strained both on single devices—where multiple background agents block interactive users—and across heterogeneous developer machines that sit idle because each server runs independently.
AI.method: On one device, Superfluid runs isolated worker processes under a unified scheduler that prioritizes interactive requests, shares common prompt prefixes, and logs tokens durably; across devices, it aggregates heterogeneous machines under one endpoint with speed-aware routing and fault tolerance.
AI.result: Serving Qwen3.8-27B on an Apple M5 Pro with eight active agents, Superfluid delivers a 1.5 s first-token latency versus 291-612 s for llama-server and Ollama; across six heterogeneous machines serving 64 users, throughput scales from 112 to 534 tok/s, and twelve Mac Studio M3 Ultras sustain 10,656 tok/s across 384 agents.
AI.conclusion: Superfluid enables responsive, fault-tolerant local LLM serving across both single-device multi-agent workloads and heterogeneous multi-machine fleets.

title: Creative Product Design under Brand Image Constraints
summary: Industrial design requires creative visual exploration while satisfying constraints that are often product-specific and implicit. Existing text-to-image (T2I) approaches can generate creative designs through concept blending or multi-agent self-enhancement, but they provide limited mechanisms for ensuring that generated designs remain consistent with such constraints. We focus on brand image as a representative design constraint and propose a framework for brand-aware redesign generation. Given a product name, the framework constructs a brand image survey report that summarizes product and market information, derives a creative direction from the report, and integrates this direction into a self-enhancement loop in which generated images are critiqued and prompts are revised. We evaluate the framework on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories, comparing it with Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement under the same T2I backbone. By a VLM-as-Judge protocol to measure creativity and brand identifiability, the proposed framework achieves a more favorable trade-off between the two objectives, with particularly clear gains in highly constrained categories such as automotive and motorcycle, where the plausible design space is relatively limited compared with that of other product categories. These results suggest that dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image can guide creative product design generation under brand image constraints.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a brand-aware product redesign framework that extracts brand image constraints into text and integrates them into a self-enhancement text-to-image generation loop.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-image methods can generate creative designs but lack mechanisms to enforce implicit, product-specific constraints such as brand identity.
AI.method: Given a product name, the framework builds a brand image survey report, derives a creative direction, and feeds it into a self-enhancement loop that critiques generated images and revises prompts.
AI.result: Evaluated on 50 redesign tasks across five product categories using a VLM-as-Judge protocol, the framework achieves a better creativity-brand identifiability tradeoff than Naive T2I, IP-Adapter/IT-Blender, and unconstrained self-enhancement, especially in constrained categories like automotive and motorcycle.
AI.conclusion: Dynamically eliciting and textualizing brand image constraints effectively guides creative text-to-image product design.

title: GDP.xlsx: Benchmarking Frontier Models on Professional Workbooks
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the Agent Evaluation Science Symposium (New York City, November 2026). Leaderboard: this https URL ; evaluation harness: this https URL ; public tasks: this https URL
summary: We introduce GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic workplace requests written by professionals in 13 domains, each paired with an expert rubric of binary criteria and with the complete workbook or CSV file it refers to. Together the files hold 2.18 million populated cells, and the rubrics 791 criteria. Agents work in a container with spreadsheet tools, and an agentic judge that can open the file applies the rubric. Completeness and exclusivity criteria require set-valued answers to be found in full and with nothing extra. We rank models by strict pass@1, the share of attempts that meet every criterion. Across 20 model configurations, including frontier models from Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, the top-scoring one, Gemini 4 Argon, passes only 38.3% of attempts, and the median score is 19.3%, leaving wide headroom. We release the evaluation harness and three public tasks; the other 67 are held out to protect the leaderboard from contamination.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GDP_xlsx, a benchmark of 70 realistic professional spreadsheet tasks with 791 rubric criteria, showing that even top frontier models pass at most 38.3% of attempts.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks do not adequately test frontier agents on realistic, large-scale professional workbook tasks requiring exact completeness and exclusivity.
AI.method: GDP_xlsx pairs 70 workplace requests across 13 domains with full workbooks or CSVs (2.18 million populated cells) and 791 binary rubric criteria evaluated by an agentic judge inside a container with spreadsheet tools.
AI.result: Across 20 model configurations, the top scorer (Gemini 4 Argon) achieves only 38.3% strict pass@1 and the median is 19.3%; the harness and three public tasks are released while 67 remain held out.
AI.conclusion: Professional spreadsheet work remains a challenging frontier for AI agents, leaving substantial room for improvement.

title: Activation Steering the Nan-Shan in Typhoon
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS Creative AI Track 2026. Website: this https URL
summary: Typhoon is an audiovisual installation based on Joseph Conrad's novella, in which Captain MacWhirr steers the steamer Nan-Shan directly into and through a catastrophic storm. The novella is a study of what happens when the scale of a phenomenon exceeds the practical and conceptual frameworks available to comprehend it and of the paralysis that sometimes follows a demand for action in such overwhelming circumstances. We chose the text of Typhoon to reflect on human culture's current AI moment. We prompt a large language model, seeded with Conrad's original language, to feed endlessly on its own output, and explore when and how the text becomes increasingly alien and unwieldy as time progresses, including deviations from the narrative, digressions into the model's own instructions and thinking, and long periods of incoherent rumination. We employ methods from activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method we introduce, to control the rhythm of the narrative and the model's digressions over long stretches of generation. The simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability of this steering showcases the tension between the perceived interpretability of AI, and the reality of a system that remains outside our comprehension and control.

AI.tldr: This paper describes Typhoon, an audiovisual installation that uses adaptive activation steering on a self-feeding LLM seeded with Joseph Conrad's novella to explore AI interpretability and control.
AI.motivation: The authors use Conrad's Typhoon—about phenomena exceeding human comprehension—to reflect on the tension between perceived AI interpretability and systems that remain beyond full human control.
AI.method: An LLM seeded with Conrad's text feeds endlessly on its own output while activation steering, including a novel adaptive steering method, modulates narrative rhythm and digressions into instructions, thinking, and incoherent rumination.
AI.result: The steering demonstrates simultaneous efficacy and unpredictability in controlling long-horizon narrative drift and digressions.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive activation steering highlights both the power and the limits of current interpretability tools when governing autonomous, self-feeding language models.

title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
comment: 8-page main text plus appendix, 23 pages
summary: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that acts as a fast System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent, cutting API costs by 33.3% at equal accuracy.
AI.motivation: Hosted LLM agents achieve high text-to-SQL accuracy but are slow, expensive at scale, and expose sensitive queries to external APIs.
AI.method: LuthorSQL predicts slot scores over a bounded query-plan grammar in a single forward pass, compiles and executes up to 32 candidate plans, selects an answer with a trained validator, and escalates to a System 2 LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) only when uncertain.
AI.result: Standalone, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per query (fitting in 9 GB at 8-bit) and transfers zero-shot across five SQL dialects within 3.1 points; in a confidence cascade on 227 post-cutoff database questions, it handles nearly half of queries locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% without losing accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A compact one-pass System 1 model paired with uncertainty-based escalation enables private, cost-effective text-to-SQL deployment without sacrificing frontier accuracy.

title: Towards Seconds-level Video Representation: Quadratically Gated Feature Grid with Adaptive, Prediction-free Sampling
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 4 tables. Code available at this https URL
summary: Implicit neural video representations are notoriously slow to build, which does not cross the basic practical threshold for most industrial applications. Here, we present Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation that couples multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids with a compact SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating (QG) decoder and an error-aware, prediction-free sampler. The explicit grids avoid hash-collision coefficient sharing at the cost of modestly higher storage yet greatly boost the expressive capacity; the QG decoder introduces low-rank local second-order interactions to improve the nonlinear feature response. During fitting, a global error map periodically refreshes a high-error pool, and each batch mixes pool samples with uniform samples, which is free from the auxiliary model to predict difficult samples, thereby further escalating the efficiency. On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS with mixed precision and about 146 FPS in FP32. In our PyTorch implementation, Q-GAS trains and quantizes 5.5-7.2 times faster than the evaluated Instant-NGP baseline and 19-28 times faster than RNeRV. Under a 90 s budget, it improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over the evaluated NeRV-family pipelines at comparable BPP over the measured overlap. We have shared our code at this https URL for readers' free use.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Q-GAS, a coordinate-queryable video representation using explicit 3D feature grids, a quadratic-gating decoder, and prediction-free error-aware sampling to achieve seconds-level fitting.
AI.motivation: Implicit neural video representations are too slow to fit for most practical industrial applications.
AI.method: Q-GAS combines multi-resolution explicit 3D feature grids (avoiding hash collisions) with a SwiGLU-style quadratic-gating decoder and a prediction-free sampler that mixes uniform samples with a periodically refreshed high-error pool.
AI.result: On UVG Beauty/Bosphorus/Jockey, Q-GAS fits and quantizes in under 50 s on one RTX PRO 6000, decodes at over 370 FPS (mixed precision) and ~146 FPS (FP32), trains 5.5-7.2x faster than Instant-NGP and 19-28x faster than RNeRV, and improves PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS over NeRV-family pipelines under a 90 s budget.
AI.conclusion: Explicit feature grids with quadratic gating and error-aware sampling make neural video fitting practical at seconds-level speeds.

title: Can Large Language Models Optimize Pretrained Neural Network Weights? A Multi-Phase Empirical Evaluation of Gradient-Free Editing in YOLO26 Object Detection
summary: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning pretrained detectors, but its generalization and the value of large language model (LLM) guidance remain uncertain. We evaluate five experimental phases using YOLO26 models and MS COCO, comparing deterministic scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, structured interventions, real local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control. Optimization uses native Ultralytics mAP50-95 on 1,000 COCO Val2017 images; selected candidates are assessed on a disjoint, previously examined 1,500-image subset, with COCO API AP50-95 reported separately where available. Increasing the CMA-ES budget from 8 to 250 evaluations raised development gains from +0.11 to +0.28 percentage points, while selection changes remained negative (-0.03 to -0.12 points); the 250-evaluation result uses one seed. The hybrid LLM approach showed no statistically established advantage over random-policy guidance (p = 0.612, 0.369, and 0.694 at budgets 8, 25, and 50). Five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded a COCO API AP difference of +0.004 points (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034). Of 225 archived LLM proposals, 53 satisfy the final strict schema; early tensor-level execution cannot be fully verified. Genuine LLM-mediated weight editing is feasible, but the tested approaches did not demonstrate consistent transfer beyond the development subset or a measurable LLM advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates gradient-free weight editing—including local-LLM proposals and CMA-ES—on YOLO26 object detection, finding no consistent generalization or LLM advantage over random-policy controls.
AI.motivation: Direct weight editing offers a gradient-free alternative to fine-tuning, but its generalization beyond development sets and the actual value of LLM guidance remain uncertain.
AI.method: Across five experimental phases on YOLO26 and MS COCO (1,000 Val2017 images for optimization, 1,500 disjoint images for selection), the authors compare scaling, random perturbations, differential evolution, CMA-ES, local-LLM proposals, failure-aware guidance, and hybrid LLM-CMA-ES against a matched random-policy control.
AI.result: Raising CMA-ES from 8 to 250 evaluations improved development mAP50-95 from +0.11 to +0.28 points while selection changes stayed negative (-0.03 to -0.12); hybrid LLM guidance showed no statistically significant advantage over random-policy control (p = 0.612, 0.369, 0.694), and five-seed YOLO26m replication yielded +0.004 COCO API AP (95% CI: -0.026 to +0.034).
AI.conclusion: While LLM-mediated weight editing is technically feasible, tested gradient-free methods did not generalize beyond the development subset or outperform random-policy baselines.

title: Multimodal Person Concept Model for Person Identification under Varying Observation Conditions
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Artificial Life and Robotics (AROB Journal Track). Project page: this https URL
summary: Service robots in domestic and office environments must identify users to provide personalized services based on their preferences and previous interactions. This is challenging because only a few observations may be available for learning, while observation conditions change owing to appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content. To address this challenge, this study proposes a multimodal person concept model that learns person concepts from a small number of observations, without person labels, and enables robust identification under changing conditions. The model employs a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process and integrates visual, acoustic, and linguistic features extracted using Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) and Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP), followed by principal component analysis (PCA). We evaluated six participants under eight conditions in which appearance changes, additive noise, and transcription errors were introduced individually and in combination. Averaged over the eight conditions, the proposed model achieved an identification accuracy of 0.89 while inferring the number of person concepts from the observations, which is comparable to k-means clustering that was supplied with the true number of participants (0.88). We also examined PCA dimensionality, modality availability, and variation strength, and demonstrated the model on a Toyota Human Support Robot. These results show that multimodal person concept learning supports robust person identification under changing conditions, and that identification can succeed even when the number of concepts is not correctly recovered. The project page and demonstration video are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an unsupervised multimodal person concept model using CLIP, CLAP, and a Chinese restaurant process that identifies users under changing observation conditions with 0.89 average accuracy.
AI.motivation: Service robots must identify users from few observations without labels despite changes in appearance, environmental noise, and utterance content.
AI.method: The model extracts visual, acoustic, and linguistic features using CLIP and CLAP followed by PCA, and clusters them with a nonparametric Bayesian generative model based on the Chinese restaurant process.
AI.result: Evaluated across six participants and eight varied conditions, the model achieves 0.89 average identification accuracy while inferring the number of concepts—matching k-means given the true participant count (0.88)—and is demonstrated on a Toyota Human Support Robot.
AI.conclusion: Nonparametric multimodal concept learning enables robust, label-free person identification for service robots under varying conditions.

title: CarryOn: Learning What to Keep in Context for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-horizon LLM agents can coordinate tools and applications to complete complex, multi-step tasks. As their interaction histories grow, effective context management becomes essential for reliable and efficient execution. Existing methods reduce context through summarization, pruning, or history selection. However, shorter contexts do not necessarily support better decisions: summaries can omit exact details needed for later actions, while retaining entire interactions can carry substantial irrelevant information. We propose CarryOn, a lightweight context manager that pairs compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence. A learned selector and adaptive retention policy keep relevant evidence available without additional LLM calls for context management. We introduce two complementary evaluation metrics: $S_\alpha$ prioritizes task success while accounting for resource use, and normalized cost per success (NCS) measures the resources spent per successful task. Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM Actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success, exceeding the strongest baseline by 6.7 percentage points. It also achieves the best average scores on both metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CarryOn, a lightweight context manager for long-horizon LLM agents that pairs compact execution state with source-linked evidence, improving task success by 6.7 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing context-reduction methods for long-horizon agents either lose exact details needed later (summarization) or retain excessive irrelevant history (full retention).
AI.method: CarryOn uses a learned selector and adaptive retention policy to pair compact execution state with fine-grained, source-linked evidence without extra LLM calls, evaluated via two new metrics: S_alpha and normalized cost per success (NCS).
AI.result: Across AppWorld, OfficeBench, and Tau2 Telecom with three LLM actors, CarryOn achieves 75.7% macro-averaged task success (6.7 points above the strongest baseline) and the best average scores on both S_alpha and NCS.
AI.conclusion: Learned, source-linked evidence retention outperforms heuristic pruning and summarization for long-horizon agent context management.

title: SceneAgent: A Multi-Agent Framework for Portable Game Scene Generation
comment: Project page: this https URL
summary: Moving a scene generator to a new game engine requires more than exporting its final output: planning, construction tools, and stored experience may also depend on the original backend. We present SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework for reusing the construction process and its experience across backends. A canonical SceneContext maintains the evolving world, while backend adapters isolate coordinate conventions, asset bindings, and export. Structured handoffs let fresh Builder sessions query this persistent state without inheriting the full construction transcript. Across generations, human-approved traces are distilled into asset-ID-free Layout skills and semantic Content skills that can be retrieved and recombined. We introduce GameSceneBench, comprising 69 indoor and outdoor prompts. Under a common asset and evaluation protocol, SceneAgent obtains human tie-adjusted preference scores of 78.2-89.4% against five baselines. Ablations show that reusable skills and the multi-agent protocol primarily improve prompt alignment and scene completeness, with additional runtime. Deployment in a second engine preserves the shared construction protocol and skill library while replacing backend integration components. Together, these results support separating persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and reusable experience for portable scene construction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SceneAgent, a multi-agent framework that separates persistent scene state, task-local reasoning, and distilled skills to make game scene generation portable across engines.
AI.motivation: Porting a scene generator to a new game engine is difficult when planning, tools, and stored experience are tightly coupled to the original backend.
AI.method: SceneAgent maintains a canonical SceneContext isolated by backend adapters, uses structured handoffs for fresh Builder sessions, and distills human-approved traces into asset-ID-free Layout and semantic Content skills.
AI.result: On the new 69-prompt GameSceneBench, SceneAgent achieves 78.2-89.4% human tie-adjusted preference scores against five baselines and transfers to a second engine by swapping only backend integration components.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling persistent scene state and reusable skills from engine-specific backends enables portable, high-quality multi-agent scene generation.

title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
summary: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. Trained in a single stage on 4.53M public samples with 32 visual tokens per frame, where open video LLMs use several stages, 9M to 172M samples and 64 to 256 tokens per frame on average, the resulting V-JEPA-LM models (1B to 8B, Qwen3 and Llama) lead every size class in average score across eleven video benchmarks; our 4B model scores 72.1, against 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model. A controlled encoder x supervision study shows that the encoder decides what can be read and the supervision what is read: at a matched budget, counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average and 38 on the speed questions of natural benchmarks. Code and models: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces V-JEPA-LM, showing that counterfactual pixel-transformation supervision unlocks dynamics representations in predictive video encoders like V-JEPA to lead eleven video benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Predictive video encoders like V-JEPA capture scene dynamics, but standard caption/QA training lets VLMs ignore those dynamics and answer at chance on speed tasks even when a linear probe reads speed at 87%.
AI.method: The authors show dynamics live in a shared subspace of predictive encoders (unlike frame-wise text-aligned encoders like SigLIP) and construct 4.53M counterfactual training samples via pixel transformations whose answers depend strictly on the induced change, training 1B-8B models in a single stage with 32 visual tokens per frame.
AI.result: V-JEPA-LM leads every size class across eleven video benchmarks; the 4B model scores 72.1 versus 61.1 for the best open 4B and 64.8 for the best open 8B model, and counterfactual supervision adds 4.5 points on average (+38 on natural speed questions) at a matched budget.
AI.conclusion: Combining predictive video encoders with counterfactual supervision enables video-language models to genuinely read scene dynamics rather than retrieve static attributes.

title: Tracing Uncertainties of Extreme El Niño Prediction to Mesoscale Ocean Currents
comment: 30 pages, 13 figures
summary: The predictability of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) has historically been linked to large-scale errors in models' initial conditions such as heat content and surface wind stress. Here we demonstrate that these slowly evolving errors may ultimately originate from mesoscale errors in initial oceanic states that are common in current models and ocean observation systems. This hidden source of ENSO forecast uncertainty, in terms of mesoscale ocean-current errors, is convincingly exposed by the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method applied to a differentiable ocean AI model. The CNOP-identified most influential current errors are strongly event-dependent. For the 1997/98 El Niño, the initial current errors in the eastern Pacific results in the largest forecast error through locally suppressing original subsurface warming. For the 2015/16 event, the dominate error originates from the western Pacific, which reorganizes upper ocean temperature structure and affects the eastern Pacific through the equatorial waveguide. Further analysis reveals that these current errors perturb mesoscale eddy count and eddy kinetic energy triggering large-scale temperature errors that hinder El Niño development. The timing of the maximum growth rate of the obtained CNOP error is well aligned with the spring predictability barrier of ENSO, and the error structures are reflected in simulated analysis errors caused by unresolved mesoscale currents. These findings extend the potential source of ENSO predictability beyond large-scale thermal signals, reveal for the first time an uncharted route of ENSO forecast failure, and provide an important physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation in the future.

AI.tldr: This paper uses conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) on a differentiable ocean AI model to show that extreme El Niño forecast uncertainties can originate from mesoscale ocean-current errors.
AI.motivation: ENSO predictability has historically been attributed to large-scale thermal and wind-stress errors, leaving the role of unresolved mesoscale ocean currents unexplored.
AI.method: The authors apply CNOP to a differentiable ocean AI model to identify the most influential initial ocean-current errors for the 1997/98 and 2015/16 El Niño events.
AI.result: Optimal current errors are event-dependent (eastern Pacific for 1997/98; western Pacific via the equatorial waveguide for 2015/16), perturb mesoscale eddy count and kinetic energy to trigger large-scale temperature errors, and peak in growth rate in alignment with the spring predictability barrier.
AI.conclusion: Mesoscale ocean-current errors represent a previously uncharted source of ENSO forecast failure, providing a physical basis for targeted ocean observations and data assimilation.

title: Active Learning of Temporal Specifications through Distinguishing Queries
summary: Temporal specifications are essential for verification and monitoring, yet writing formulas that capture the intended behaviour is difficult. Active learning derives such specifications through interaction between a learner and a teacher, but remains underexplored for temporal logics. Existing approaches require the teacher to answer equivalence queries and to construct counterexamples, and they often rely on SAT-based learning procedures that restart the search after each new example. We present an active-learning framework for LTLf in which the teacher only labels traces and answers natural-language questions about the intended behaviour. The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate formulas, generates traces that distinguish candidates, and uses the teacher's hints to rank candidates or to restrict the search. We prove consistency with the observed examples, identification within bounded hypothesis classes with a bound on the number of queries, and a PAC guarantee for the final hypothesis. In experiments with a simulated teacher on 36 targets, including targets in four standard environments, the learner identifies every target when it compares all rivals, with fewer than seven queries beyond an initial sample of ten traces on average. Correct hints reduce the number of queries by up to 16% and the number of generated candidates by a fifth, and hints used for ranking never prevent identification, even when incorrect. Our enumeration-based version space is faster than the SAT-based approach of previous learners at every target size.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an active-learning framework for LTLf temporal specifications that learns from trace labels and natural-language hints without requiring equivalence queries or counterexamples.
AI.motivation: Existing active-learning methods for temporal logics require teachers to answer equivalence queries and construct counterexamples, and often rely on slow SAT-based search restarts.
AI.method: The learner maintains an enumerated version space of candidate LTLf formulas, generates distinguishing traces to separate candidates, and uses teacher hints to rank candidates or restrict search, with proven consistency, query bounds, and PAC guarantees.
AI.result: Across 36 targets with a simulated teacher, the learner identifies every target in under seven queries beyond ten initial traces on average; correct hints cut queries by up to 16% and candidates by 20%, incorrect ranking hints never block identification, and enumeration beats SAT-based learners in speed at all target sizes.
AI.conclusion: Version-space enumeration with distinguishing trace queries and optional hints makes active learning of LTLf specifications practical and theoretically grounded.

title: UltraBERT-JEV: Encoder models for System One Applications
summary: We study encoder models that pick one of several options in a single forward pass, without generating text. This technical report compares recipes for fine-tuning UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option. The four recipes differ in how an option is scored and how the scores become probabilities; one follows the expert gate of DeepSeek-V3. Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B with the LLM-as-Jev recipe (67.6% test accuracy), the encoder reaches 69.7% to 72.1%. Scoring an option by "yes" minus "no" instead of "yes" alone gives the larger gain, from 69.7% to 71.3% on the test set and from 57.8% to 59.6% on external benchmarks (56.1% for the decoder). Sigmoid normalisation adds 0.8 test points; a square-root softplus adds none. One request at a time on an NVIDIA A100, the encoder takes 29 ms per decision against 68 ms, but uses more peak memory (2.8 against 2.2 GiB). An auxiliary head, trained on human-marked evidence and on labels selected with a reward adapted from SelfCite, predicts in the same pass the sentences annotated as support for the answer.

AI.tldr: This technical report compares fine-tuning recipes for UltraBERT-380M as a single-pass System 1 option selector, outperforming Qwen3-0.6B at less than half the latency.
AI.motivation: Using autoregressive decoders for multi-option selection incurs unnecessary generation latency compared to single-pass encoder models.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune UltraBERT-380M with one mask per option, comparing four scoring and normalization recipes (including a DeepSeek-V3-style expert gate) and an auxiliary head trained to predict supporting evidence sentences in the same pass.
AI.result: Trained on the same data as Qwen3-0.6B (67.6% test accuracy), UltraBERT-JEV reaches 69.7-72.1% accuracy; scoring by "yes" minus "no" lifts test accuracy from 69.7% to 71.3% (57.8% to 59.6% external, vs. 56.1% for the decoder), sigmoid normalization adds 0.8 points, and A100 latency is 29 ms vs. 68 ms (at 2.8 vs. 2.2 GiB peak memory).
AI.conclusion: Single-pass encoder models with margin scoring provide faster, more accurate System 1 option selection than comparable autoregressive decoders.

title: DySENSE: Dynamic Spatiotemporal ENergy Synthesis and Emulation with Satellite Imagery
comment: Accpted by KDD 2027
summary: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions.
