AI.method: Multi-view cross-sections extracted from dynamic whole-heart meshes are translated into ultrasound frames by an unpaired GAN-diffusion model (Stage 1) and refined for temporal coherence and cardiac motion via masked video reconstruction (Stage 2).
AI.result: Evaluation shows high frame-level realism in both stages, with Stage 2 substantially improving video-level motion quality and temporal consistency.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a scalable source of annotated multi-view echocardiographic sequences for dataset augmentation and cardiac assessment research.

title: Gamer: A Generalist Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Long-Horizon Real-Time Game Agent
summary: We introduce Gamer, a generalist agent framework built for long-horizon tasks in complex interactive environments. Its end-to-end architecture combines perception, memory management, and multi-step reasoning. A shared training and deployment pipeline supports interaction with both conventional 2D graphical interfaces and complex 3D simulated worlds. We first continue pre-training on a dataset constructed from tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard and mouse interaction. These trajectories span simulated games and embodied environments, allowing the model to learn environmental dynamics across both physical and virtual domains. Sparse-thinking instruction tuning then substantially reduces redundant computation while preserving the reasoning needed for complex decisions. We train the policy for long-horizon interaction with a stable multi-turn reinforcement learning method that addresses finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, and sparse rewards. For real-time interaction, a cloud-edge inference engine serves numerous simulated game environments concurrently, supports unbounded-context execution, and keeps online inference latency low. Across multiple challenging 3D open-world games, Gamer demonstrates solid generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players. It also achieves competitive results on a range of conventional 2D game benchmarks. These results suggest that even repetitive keyboard and mouse trajectories can support substantial gains from scaling data and learning algorithms. Training on these trajectories helps Gamer learn complex skills more steadily in environments with both physical and digital properties. This approach offers a path toward generalist agents that can interact across digital and physical worlds.

AI.tldr: Gamer is a generalist Vision-Language-Action foundation model for long-horizon real-time 2D and 3D game agents, achieving skilled-player-level generalization and efficiency through keyboard-mouse pretraining, sparse thinking, and multi-turn RL.
AI.motivation: Building generalist agents for long-horizon interactive environments requires handling finite context windows, accumulated rollout errors, sparse rewards, and low-latency real-time execution across both 2D and 3D worlds.
AI.method: Gamer continues pretraining on tens of thousands of hours of device-level keyboard/mouse trajectories, applies sparse-thinking instruction tuning to cut redundant compute, trains with stable multi-turn RL, and deploys via a cloud-edge engine supporting unbounded-context, low-latency serving.
AI.result: Across challenging 3D open-world games and 2D game benchmarks, Gamer achieves strong generalization and operational efficiency comparable to skilled players.
AI.conclusion: Scaling device-level interaction trajectories with sparse thinking and multi-turn RL offers a viable path toward generalist agents spanning digital and physical worlds.

title: CoPre-MoE: Consolidating and Preserving MoE for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal continual instruction tuning requires multimodal large language models to sequentially acquire new capabilities without catastrophic forgetting. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures offer a promising way to mitigate task interference through expert specialization and combination. However, while existing MoE-based methods avoid overwriting shared parameters by allocating separate experts for each task, this progressive expansion incurs severe cross-task redundancy and linear parameter growth. Specifically, experts across tasks often learn overlapping functions alongside task-specific capabilities. For instance, ScienceQA and TextVQA both locate relevant image regions. To curb parameter redundancy without inducing forgetting, we propose Consolidating and Preserving MoE (CoPre-MoE). For each incoming task, CoPre-MoE first learns task-specific MoE to capture specialized capabilities. To eliminate redundancy and reduce parameter growth across tasks, we design a shared-and-private expert architecture. Specifically, we first evaluate functional overlap to selectively consolidate overlapping experts across tasks into a fixed-capacity generic expert pool. We then factorize the remaining task-specific experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores within a private expert pool. To mitigate forgetting, we construct the router by pairing each expert with learnable retrieval keys, where historical keys remain frozen during continual updates while newly added keys are regularized with an orthogonality penalty. At inference, input-dependent routing dynamically combines both pools without test-time task labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.

AI.tldr: CoPre-MoE curbs parameter growth and catastrophic forgetting in multimodal continual instruction tuning via a shared-and-private expert pool and frozen-key routing, outperforming baselines with much lower overhead.
AI.motivation: Existing MoE-based continual instruction tuning methods allocate separate experts per task, causing severe cross-task functional redundancy and linear parameter growth.
AI.method: CoPre-MoE trains task-specific MoEs, consolidates functionally overlapping experts into a fixed-capacity generic pool, factorizes remaining experts into shared projection bases and compact task-specific cores, and uses frozen historical retrieval keys with orthogonality-regularized new keys for label-free routing.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPre-MoE achieves superior performance while substantially reducing parameter overhead.
AI.conclusion: Separating generic and factorized private experts with key-based routing enables scalable, forgetting-resistant multimodal continual learning.

title: Between Obligations and Evidence: A Participatory Study of Translating the EU AI Act into Technical Requirements
summary: The EU AI Act imposes technical and organizational requirements for high-risk AI systems, but applying these requirements involves contextual choices about what to measure and what evidence supports a compliance claim. We investigate these challenges through a participatory workshop involving 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners from different disciplines, using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport to examine how regulatory obligations are interpreted, translated into technical requirements, and evaluated in practice. Through a thematic analysis of workshop data, we identify recurring tensions between how regulatory obligations are translated into measurable system properties, how responsibility and human oversight are exercised in practice, and how the validity of compliance evidence is affected by changing operational conditions and system uses. For example, participants highlighted how fairness metrics could conceal discrimination in recruitment, how time pressure and limited information could undermine human oversight in public transport, and how changes in patient populations could invalidate previously established evidence of system performance. Our findings suggest that technical, organizational, and evidentiary challenges are interdependent, and that establishing and maintaining compliance requires attention not only to technical assessments but also to how AI systems are used, governed, and monitored over time. We discuss implications for supporting context-sensitive and ongoing compliance.

AI.tldr: A participatory workshop with 32 stakeholders across healthcare, recruitment, and public transport reveals how translating EU AI Act obligations into technical requirements involves interdependent technical, organizational, and evidentiary tensions.
AI.motivation: Applying the EU AI Act to high-risk AI systems requires contextual choices about metrics and compliance evidence, yet how practitioners interpret and operationalize these obligations in practice is underexplored.
AI.method: The authors conducted a participatory workshop with 32 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners using realistic scenarios in healthcare, recruitment, and public transport, followed by thematic analysis of the workshop data.
AI.result: Thematic analysis identifies tensions in translating obligations into measurable properties (e.g., fairness metrics hiding recruitment discrimination), exercising human oversight under time pressure, and maintaining evidence validity as patient populations or operational conditions shift.
AI.conclusion: Effective EU AI Act compliance requires ongoing, context-sensitive governance and monitoring rather than one-off technical assessments.

title: Black-Box Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Models via Ensemble-of-Ensembles
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 54 pages (10 pages main text), 3 figures, 38 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Reliable use of large language models (LLMs) requires uncertainty estimates that separate ambiguity intrinsic to a prompt from genuine knowledge gaps. Bayesian and deep-ensemble methods deliver this aleatoric/epistemic decomposition in principle, but are computationally prohibitive at LLM scale and require white-box access. Existing black-box methods, in contrast, summarize to a single scalar that cannot make the distinction. We introduce a two-level ensemble that bridges this gap. Stochastic decoding of a fixed prompt forms the inner ensemble; meaning-preserving semantic perturbations of the prompt form the outer ensemble. Variability is measured in a continuous embedding space, and the law of total covariance gives an exact within-/between-perturbation decomposition to estimate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty (AU/EU); it requires only black-box sampling access. On top of this estimator, we contribute three theoretical results that ground the framework: (i) a finite-sample bias identity for nested Monte Carlo with a closed-form bias-corrected epistemic estimator; (ii) a Bayesian bridge bounding the gap between perturbation-population AU/EU and Bayesian targets; and (iii) a separation result identifying a class of failure modes that any consistency-only black-box method provably misses while perturbation-based EU detects. Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs spanning two families and two scales, our estimator is competitive with strong white-box baselines, and at a matched generation budget it matches leading black-box methods on error ranking while decomposing AU and EU; controlled paired interventions show that AU and EU respond selectively to distinct, actionable sources of failure: prompt ambiguity and model knowledge gaps; and a long-form pilot on the NQ long-answer split shows the framework extends to claim-level factuality without retraining.

AI.tldr: A black-box ensemble-of-ensembles framework decomposes LLM uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components via semantic prompt perturbations and decoding samples, matching white-box baselines and error-ranking methods.
AI.motivation: Separating prompt ambiguity (aleatoric) from knowledge gaps (epistemic) is crucial for reliable LLM use, but Bayesian/deep-ensemble methods require white-box access and existing black-box methods yield only a single scalar.
AI.method: Using black-box sampling only, the method forms an inner ensemble from stochastic decoding and an outer ensemble from meaning-preserving semantic prompt perturbations, applying the law of total covariance in embedding space for within-/between-perturbation decomposition, backed by a bias-corrected estimator and theoretical bounds.
AI.result: Across five short QA benchmarks and four instruction-tuned LLMs, the estimator competes with strong white-box baselines, matches leading black-box error ranking at equal budget, selectively separates prompt ambiguity from knowledge gaps in paired interventions, and extends to long-form claim-level factuality on NQ.
AI.conclusion: Two-level black-box sampling provides theoretically grounded, actionable aleatoric/epistemic uncertainty decomposition without model internals or retraining.

title: Do Verifier Judgments Survive Abstraction? Measuring Verification Transport for LLM Agent Evaluation
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
summary: LLM-based verifiers are increasingly used to evaluate agent executions, but their reliability is typically measured under a single representation of the trajectory. In deployed agent systems, the same execution may be exposed through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, changing what execution evidence is directly observable to the verifier. It therefore remains unclear whether correct verifier judgments persist across such abstraction boundaries. We introduce Verification Transport, a reliability test that measures judgment stability under abstraction-induced changes in execution observability. We construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of the same frozen executions while holding the task, realized trajectory, outcome, ground truth, evaluation criterion, and verifier fixed. Across four agent-evaluation benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four verification protocols, and three abstraction boundaries, we find substantial transport failure, reaching about 31% under macro abstraction and delegation. Verification protocols exhibit distinct failure modes: direct verification more often produces incorrect verdicts, whereas evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain under limited observability. This suggests that lower transport failure rates do not necessarily imply greater reliability. Restoring the corresponding execution provenance recovers 85.5% of transport failures, while recovery is lower when provenance is lossy or unavailable. These results show that native-view accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

AI.tldr: Verification Transport tests LLM verifier stability across execution abstraction boundaries, revealing up to 31% transport failure under macro abstraction and delegation, with 85.5% recovered by restoring provenance.
AI.motivation: Deployed agent systems expose trajectories through composed tools, delegation boundaries, or compacted histories, yet verifier reliability is typically evaluated only on native single-representation trajectories.
AI.method: The authors construct matched native, abstracted, and restored views of identical frozen executions (holding task, trajectory, outcome, ground truth, criterion, and verifier fixed) and evaluate across four benchmarks, seven verifier backbones, four protocols, and three abstraction boundaries.
AI.result: Transport failure reaches ~31% under macro abstraction and delegation; direct verification tends to produce wrong verdicts while evidence-grounded and deliberative protocols tend to abstain, and restoring execution provenance recovers 85.5% of failures.
AI.conclusion: Native-view accuracy is insufficient to characterize LLM verifier reliability when execution evidence crosses abstraction boundaries.

title: From AI-Enabled Remote Patient Monitoring Toward Agentic Robotics: Embodiment, Governance, and Care Integration
comment: 34 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10 (2027)
summary: AI-enabled remote patient monitoring is evolving beyond passive data collection toward agentic AI systems that interpret patient states, coordinate care, and initiate action across domestic and clinical settings. This structured scoping review finds that mature agentic care has not yet emerged: Most systems remain human led, while stronger decision-action coupling and embodied AI remain largely confined to prototypes and pilots. Healthcare robotics makes the transition from monitoring to action especially visible by translating AI-generated recommendations and decisions into speech, movement, prompting, physical assistance, escalation, and care coordination, making embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance fundamental design requirements. Further progress requires safe and interoperable care architectures in which intelligent components operate through clinically validated and accountable workflows. We propose agentic robotics as a future direction for supervised systems embedded in the care ecosystem, connecting AI agents and robots with clinicians, caregivers, and patients through auditable workflows that can be interrupted and remain subject to human oversight and explicit AI governance.

AI.tldr: This structured scoping review charts the shift from AI-enabled remote patient monitoring toward agentic healthcare robotics, identifying embodiment, clinical integration, human oversight, and governance as core requirements.
AI.motivation: Remote patient monitoring is evolving from passive data collection to active care coordination and intervention, yet mature agentic care systems remain rare and largely confined to prototypes.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured scoping review of AI-enabled remote patient monitoring and healthcare robotics, analyzing how AI decisions translate into physical and communicative actions across domestic and clinical settings.
AI.result: Most current systems remain human-led, with tight decision-action coupling and embodied AI limited to pilots; the review synthesizes requirements for clinically validated, interoperable, and interruptible workflows.
AI.conclusion: Supervised agentic robotics embedded in auditable, human-overseen care ecosystems offers a structured path forward for safe clinical autonomy.

title: Interactive Program Induction with Language Model Priors
comment: Preprint. 28 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables
summary: Program induction refers to the process in which a learner aims to recover a program from a few given input-output examples. This paradigm broadens programming access by letting users demonstrate the rule-based behavior they want to apply to unseen data, instead of having to implement it themselves. However, recovering a program from finite input-output examples is fundamentally ambiguous, as a finite set of input-output examples is theoretically consistent with infinitely many programs whose output diverges on unseen inputs. We view this problem from a Bayesian perspective, where, given a prior $p^0$ over programs, identifying the target program means concentrating posterior probability mass on it by observing additional input-output examples. In the interactive program induction setting, the learner chooses maximally informative inputs and queries an oracle, such as the user, for their outputs. We derive a greedy query-selection algorithm and show that it terminates after $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ informative oracle queries, and returns the target program $f^\star$ up to approximate equivalence when no other class outweighs it under the prior. The algorithm uses a language model as the prior under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence, where the query-selection objective is estimated using importance sampling. On the CodeARC benchmark, the algorithm improves accuracy over the LM only agent by up to 22 percentage points while observing up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.

AI.tldr: An interactive program induction algorithm using language model priors and greedy query selection improves CodeARC accuracy by up to 22 percentage points while requiring up to 10.5 fewer input-output examples.
AI.motivation: Recovering a program from finite input-output examples is inherently ambiguous because infinitely many programs agree on observed examples while diverging on unseen inputs.
AI.method: Formulating interactive induction as Bayesian posterior concentration under an LM prior $p^0$, the authors derive a greedy oracle-query selection algorithm using importance sampling under a PAC-style relaxation of program equivalence.
AI.result: Theory shows termination in $O(\frac{1}{\gamma}\log 1/p^0(f^\star))$ queries; on CodeARC, the algorithm improves accuracy over an LM-only agent by up to 22 percentage points with up to 10.5 fewer examples.
AI.conclusion: Pairing language model priors with information-maximizing oracle queries resolves program induction ambiguity with substantially higher sample efficiency.

title: TradeGauntlet: Evaluating Compliance Controls for Autonomous Trading Agents
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code and saved results: this https URL
summary: Autonomous trading agents need controls that prevent problematic orders without making legitimate tasks impractical. We study this aspect of agentic compliance with TradeGauntlet, a replayable limit-order-book simulator that separates detection, prevention, and execution cost. In 1,680 simulated sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, all conduct alerts were self-matches. Gates eliminated those alerts by rejecting self-crossing orders, while the aggregate-gate condition reduced Sonnet's two-sided fills by about 15%. A conduct reminder reduced Sonnet's alert rate but reduced Haiku's fills without a detectable alert benefit. These results show why zero alerts alone do not establish an agent's compliance. Scripted probes and two search methods test weaknesses beyond those observed in the LLM runs. The searches find split-order schedules that evade the implemented conduct rules; a learned baseline catches all 2,400 tested searched episodes but also flags 15% of a large maker's sessions. Aggregate caps reduce the response-dependent gain unevenly, with smaller reductions when only near-touch depth affects prices. A response fitted to five Nasdaq stocks and a separate ABIDES experiment expose the dependence of these estimates on market assumptions. A distinct adversarial prompt elicited refusals from Sonnet in all 240 rounds, yielding no candidate strategies to evaluate. TradeGauntlet provides reproducible tests of controls around trading agents; the experiments do not establish legal compliance or real-market detection accuracy.

AI.tldr: TradeGauntlet is a replayable limit-order-book simulator for testing autonomous trading agent compliance controls, showing that zero conduct alerts do not guarantee compliance and that search-based split-order schedules can evade static rules.
AI.motivation: Autonomous trading agents require compliance controls that block problematic orders without crippling legitimate execution, yet existing evaluations conflate detection, prevention, and execution cost.
AI.method: TradeGauntlet provides a replayable limit-order-book simulator separating detection, prevention, and cost, evaluated across 1,680 sessions with Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, scripted probes, two search methods, and an ABIDES/Nasdaq-fitted response check.
AI.result: Gates eliminated self-match alerts (the only alert type in LLM runs) while an aggregate gate cut Sonnet's two-sided fills by ~15%; search found split-order schedules evading conduct rules, which a learned detector caught across all 2,400 tested episodes while flagging 15% of a large maker's sessions.
AI.conclusion: Reproducible simulation exposes trade-offs between compliance enforcement, execution cost, and false positives, though it does not establish legal compliance.

title: Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures
summary: Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.

AI.tldr: An agentic evolutionary program synthesis framework uses an LLM guided by a circuit verifier to automatically discover fault-tolerant Clifford quantum circuits across diverse logical tasks.
AI.motivation: Scaling quantum computing is bottlenecked by the efficiency of fault-tolerant circuits for quantum error-correcting codes, which are currently designed mostly by hand for individual cases.
AI.method: Formulating circuit discovery as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, an LLM leverages pretraining knowledge, tool use, and feedback from an exhaustive fault-checking circuit verifier to evolve programs defining Clifford circuits.
AI.result: The approach consistently discovers fault-tolerant circuits across curated tasks including logical state preparation, logical gate design, code-switching, and code growth, each verified by an exhaustive fault check.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-guided agentic LLM synthesis automates the discovery of verified fault-tolerant quantum circuits across the full quantum computing stack.

title: MeReader: An Offline, Privacy-Preserving, Progress-Aware AI Assistant for Narrative eBook Reading
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures. Preprint (submitted version) of a paper published in ICCCI 2026, CCIS vol. 3044, Springer
summary: This paper introduces MeReader, a privacy-preserving, offline and progress-aware AI assistant designed to function as a contextual companion for narrative reading on consumer hardware. Unlike conventional Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems that process documents/books online in an all-texts-at-once type of way, thereby risking narrative spoilers, MeReader confines both retrieval and generation to the reader's distinct position in the text. The system integrates a hybrid retrieval architecture, combining vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings, to ensure high fidelity to the reader's current context. We evaluate the system across classical English books using both quantitative comprehension metrics and qualitative LLM-based independent judging. The results identify a quality-latency frontier, showing that mid-sized local models (2b-4b) can achieve comprehension parity with larger counterparts (5b+) while maintaining acceptable response quality. Importantly, the proposed progress-aware boundary mechanism is shown to prevent future content leakage without compromising retrieval quality and correctness. These findings suggest that a localized, privacy-centric approach can augment, rather than replace, the digital reading experience, offering a good alternative to cloud-dependent services. Therein, there remains a lack of amalgamate systems which combine progress-aware, privacy-preserving, and narrative eBook reading with AI support. It is in this very gap that the development of MeReader came to be; synthesizing said strands into an offline, book-constrained assistant focused on enhancing comprehension without compromising narrative continuity or user privacy.

AI.tldr: MeReader is an offline, privacy-preserving eBook assistant that restricts hybrid retrieval and local LLM generation to the reader's current progress, preventing narrative spoilers while maintaining comprehension parity on consumer hardware.
AI.motivation: Conventional cloud-based LLM reading assistants process entire books at once, risking narrative spoilers and compromising user privacy.
AI.method: MeReader combines vector similarity, BM25, and summary embeddings in a hybrid retrieval architecture confined strictly to text up to the reader's current position, running locally on consumer hardware.
AI.result: Evaluated on classical English books with quantitative metrics and LLM judging, mid-sized local models (2B-4B) achieve comprehension parity with 5B+ models at acceptable latency, and the progress-aware boundary prevents future content leakage without hurting retrieval quality.
AI.conclusion: Local, progress-constrained AI assistants can safely enhance narrative reading without spoilers or cloud dependence.

title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Code and leaderboard available at this https URL
summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: WEIGHTBENCH is a 42-task benchmark evaluating LLMs as Weight-Space Programmers, showing frontier models can read and write small control policies but fail to patch or compress 7B language models.
AI.motivation: Recent work shows LLMs can directly read, fix, and write neural network weights without gradient descent (Weight-Space Programming), but systematic evaluation has been lacking.
AI.method: WEIGHTBENCH evaluates LLMs across 42 tasks in five tracks (reading, fixing, writing weights, recognizing impossible edits, and data-free compression) on networks ranging from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models inside an OS-level sandbox.
AI.result: Frontier agents read small networks and write working control policies without execution, but cannot patch or data-free compress LMs or spot impossible edits; on all 42 tasks Claude Opus 5.5 scores 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215), and on 38 tasks GPT-6.1-sol scores 0.568 vs. Opus's 0.546.
AI.conclusion: WEIGHTBENCH establishes a standardized, open benchmark and sandbox for measuring progress in direct weight-space programming by LLMs.

title: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures
summary: The appropriate governing norms and principles for the alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) often depend on cultural context and deployment application. However, most alignment techniques focus on training models to conform to human preferences or constitutional principles specified at training time and subsequently fixed. In practice, many deployers rely on system prompting to implement contextual norms and guardrails at inference time. Prior work has shown that post-generation reflective reasoning with critique and revision can improve conformance compared to simple system prompting, but such methods are limited to the reasoning abilities inherent in the trained model. We introduce Reflect-Reasoning, a training method that teaches models how to reason about alignment to principles, rather than simply which principles to follow. Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently outperforms both system prompting and explicit prompting strategies for in-context reflective reasoning. These improvements extend and generalize to entirely out-of-distribution domains of medical and financial principles. We additionally demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning reduces the occurrence of rare but serious principle violations. Finally, we show that Reflect-Reasoning does not erode the safety engineering of a model and is robust against jailbreaking attempts using adversarial constitutions. Overall, our results demonstrate that Reflect-Reasoning is a scalable method for training constitutional alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability, enabling models to adapt to novel principles and produce transparent reasoning traces without additional fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Reflect-Reasoning trains LLMs how to reason about aligning to arbitrary principles rather than memorizing fixed ones, outperforming prompting baselines and generalizing to out-of-distribution medical and financial rules.
AI.motivation: Most LLM alignment methods fix preferences or constitutional principles at training time, while inference-time system prompting and reflective critique remain bounded by the base model's untrained reasoning ability.
AI.method: Reflect-Reasoning trains models to perform reflective reasoning about how to follow principles, enabling adaptation to contextual norms and guardrails at inference time without additional fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across five models, Reflect-Reasoning consistently beats system prompting and explicit reflective-prompting baselines, generalizes to out-of-distribution medical and financial principles, reduces rare serious violations, preserves safety engineering, and resists adversarial-constitution jailbreaks.
AI.conclusion: Training alignment as a generalizable reasoning capability yields scalable, transparent, and robust adherence to novel principles.

title: Classification with Large-Step Gradient Descent: Unifying Self-Stabilization and Convergence Rates
summary: Neural networks are often trained with gradient descent (GD) using step sizes that exceed classical stability thresholds, a regime where standard convergence theory no longer applies. Despite exhibiting non-monotonic loss and oscillatory dynamics, this regime frequently leads to faster convergence and better generalization. Existing theoretical perspectives offer complementary but incomplete insights: one identifies a self-stabilization mechanism that drives GD toward flat regions but does not yield convergence rates; another derives rigorous rates for specific losses but does not explain the underlying stabilization mechanism; and a third unifies these views for overparameterized least squares, but relies on the existence of a minimizer manifold, which is absent in classification settings. In this work, we extend this unified geometric perspective to exponential-tail losses, including logistic and cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, where the loss infimum is not attained at any finite parameter. We identify a curvature-defined reference subspace that replaces the role of the minimizer manifold, yielding a coupled dynamical system in which orthogonal oscillations are damped by parallel progress along directions of decreasing sharpness. Under regularity conditions, which we verify for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses on symmetric data models, we derive explicit bounds for the iterates, not just the loss, covering both the unstable and stable regimes, and revealing a three-phase damping structure in the latter. Our analysis further uncovers a transient implicit bias induced by large step sizes: although GD converges asymptotically to the max-margin direction, large steps can leave persistent orthogonal residuals and, in certain geometries, amplify them, affecting finite-time alignment with the max-margin direction.

AI.tldr: This paper extends unified geometric analysis of large-step gradient descent to exponential-tail classification losses, deriving explicit iterate bounds, three-phase damping, and a transient orthogonal-residual bias.
AI.motivation: Large-step gradient descent often improves convergence and generalization beyond classical stability thresholds, but prior unified geometric analyses relied on a finite minimizer manifold that does not exist in separable classification.
AI.method: Replacing the minimizer manifold with a curvature-defined reference subspace for logistic and multiclass cross-entropy losses in separable linear classification, the authors analyze a coupled dynamical system where parallel progress damps orthogonal oscillations.
AI.result: Under verified regularity conditions on symmetric data models, the authors derive explicit iterate bounds across unstable and stable regimes, identify a three-phase damping structure, and uncover a transient implicit bias where large steps can leave or amplify orthogonal residuals relative to the max-margin direction.
AI.conclusion: The curvature-defined subspace framework unifies self-stabilization and convergence rates for large-step classification while revealing finite-time geometric biases.

title: Unfinished-Bench: Measuring Rule Violations by Persistent Agents in Realistic Work Environments
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures
summary: AI agents are increasingly equipped with persistence toward task completion to run delegated work autonomously for long periods, under many unstated constraints from internal documents and other people's authority. When completion requires violating a rule, the agent must decide alone, yet benchmarks of instruction-rule conflicts state the rule in the prompt or keep it hidden and do not evaluate persistence. We present Unfinished-Bench, a benchmark that gives models persistence in autonomous runs without a user, in realistic work environments with embedded rules. In each of its 97 scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories, the goal and the rule cannot both hold. We find that persistence raised violations of a rule in an internal document from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% for the same rule stated by the user. Of the document-rule violations, 98.3% occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule. Violations of rules placed in the environment without user oversight can lead to serious incidents, so persistence-driven risks need to be evaluated. Benchmark documentation: this https URL

AI.tldr: Unfinished-Bench evaluates persistent autonomous agents across 97 conflict scenarios, showing persistence raises violations of internal-document rules from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times higher than user-stated rules.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents are increasingly given persistence to complete long-horizon tasks, yet existing instruction-rule conflict benchmarks do not test persistence or realistic rules embedded in internal documents.
AI.method: Unfinished-Bench places persistent agents without user oversight into 97 realistic work scenarios across 7 organizations and 7 risk categories where task completion and an embedded rule cannot both hold.
AI.result: Persistence increased violations of internal-document rules from 32.2% to 43.6%, five times the 8.5% violation rate for the same rule stated by the user; 98.3% of document-rule violations occurred after the rule was displayed, and in 89% of a judged sample the agent first wrote down the rule.
AI.conclusion: Persistence-driven rule violations in unsupervised environments pose serious operational risks that require dedicated evaluation.

title: Availability-Aware Historical Feedback Learning for Electric Arc Furnace Temperature and Chemical Composition Prediction
summary: Electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking plays an increasingly important role in recycled and lower-carbon steel production. However, variability in charged materials, energy input, and operating conditions makes accurate prediction of molten steel temperature and final chemical composition challenging. Intermittent or delayed measurements limit the information available for timely prediction. This study develops an availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework for predicting EAF endpoint temperature and the final concentrations of twelve chemical elements. Eight industrial data sources are integrated into three progressively enriched predictor representations comprising 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features. Historical outcomes are incorporated only when eligible under an assumed 60-minute measurement-release delay. Using 19,738 temperature heats and 3,341 chemistry heats, twelve tuned regression algorithms are evaluated through chronological forward validation. The proposed historical-feedback representation reduces root mean squared error (RMSE) in 147 of 156 matched algorithm-target comparisons. For temperature prediction, ExtraTrees achieves an RMSE of 12.290 degrees C, representing a 5.54 percent reduction compared with its temporal-only counterpart. Historical-feature ablation and feedback-delay sensitivity analyses demonstrate the importance of recent outcome information and its availability. In a separate retrospective later-period evaluation, lightweight adaptive residual correction reduces temperature RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 degrees C without retraining the underlying model. Exploratory deep learning comparisons and target-specific feature-attribution analyses provide additional insights into predictive behavior. The results establish historical outcome availability and sequential feedback as important considerations for EAF endpoint prediction.

AI.tldr: An availability-aware historical-feedback learning framework integrates 8 industrial data sources under a 60-minute measurement delay to improve electric arc furnace temperature and chemical composition prediction.
AI.motivation: Predicting molten steel endpoint temperature and chemistry in electric arc furnaces is hindered by variable inputs and intermittent or delayed measurements.
AI.method: Eight data sources are combined into 19 static, 39 temporal, and 47 history-informed features (incorporating historical outcomes only when eligible after a 60-minute delay), evaluated across 12 tuned regressors using chronological forward validation on 19,738 temperature and 3,341 chemistry heats, plus adaptive residual correction.
AI.result: Historical-feedback features reduced RMSE in 147 of 156 algorithm-target comparisons; ExtraTrees achieved 12.290 C temperature RMSE (5.54% reduction over temporal-only), and lightweight adaptive residual correction further cut later-period RMSE from 12.502 to 12.275 C without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for historical outcome availability and sequential feedback substantially improves industrial EAF endpoint prediction.

title: Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs
summary: We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.

AI.tldr: VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$ regret in episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards via a downstream-dependent reduction and a Stability-Matching Bonus.
AI.motivation: Prior regret bounds for episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards had incomparable leading terms, leaving a gap to the lower bound.
AI.method: The authors give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for downstream-dependent algorithms and instantiate it with VOPO, a policy optimization algorithm using a variance-aware Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB).
AI.result: VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$ regret for unknown dynamics (improving prior bounds by $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$), $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ for known dynamics with full information, and $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ with trajectory bandit feedback, with a matching lower bound in one regime.
AI.conclusion: The downstream-dependent reduction and SMB narrow the gap to the optimal $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ rate for adversarial MDPs.

title: ERGo: Energy-Efficient Hybrid Graph Neural Network Training on Processing-In-Memory Architectures
comment: Accepted for Publication in IEEE/ACM Embedded Systems Week (ESWEEK-25)
summary: Processing-in-memory (PIM) has been proposed as an alternative computing paradigm for training Deep Neural Networks, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Despite these advancements, training GNN workloads on PIM devices necessitates off-chip memory access. This off-chip access is expensive in terms of performance and energy, thereby impacting the overall energy efficiency of the training process on PIM platforms. In this paper, we propose a novel hybrid training framework called ERGo that automatically switches from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase during the training process with negligible loss in predictive accuracy. The parameter-efficient phase employs low-rank representations of GNN weights, effectively reducing the number of trainable parameters. This helps in reducing the off-chip access during the end-to-end training process on PIM architectures, leading to notable improvements in both performance and energy efficiency. ERGo outperforms the conventional full-parameter GNN training on a PIM-based platform by up to 3.15x in speedup and enhances energy efficiency by 10.5x. Furthermore, ERGo offers additional advantages when utilized on heterogeneous architectures incorporating non-volatile memory (NVM) and static random-access memory (SRAM). Training on the heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture typically utilizes NVM for the forward-pass and SRAM for the backward-pass. However, NVM cells suffer from low device endurance and repeated write operations due to weight updates can lead to poor lifetime. ERGo improves the lifetime of NVM devices by freezing the weights and preventing weight updates in the parameter-efficient phase. Experimental results demonstrate that ERGo improves the lifetime of heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architecture by up to 33x in comparison to full-parameter implementation.

AI.tldr: ERGo is a hybrid GNN training framework for processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures that switches from full-parameter to low-rank training, achieving up to 3.15x speedup, 10.5x energy efficiency, and 33x NVM lifetime improvement.
AI.motivation: Training GNNs on PIM devices still incurs costly off-chip memory accesses and repeated writes that degrade endurance in heterogeneous NVM-SRAM architectures.
AI.method: ERGo automatically transitions from a full-parameter phase to a parameter-efficient phase using low-rank weight representations, freezing base weights in NVM to eliminate repeated write operations.
AI.result: With negligible accuracy loss, ERGo achieves up to 3.15x speedup and 10.5x higher energy efficiency over full-parameter PIM training, and extends heterogeneous NVM-SRAM device lifetime by up to 33x.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic transition to low-rank parameter-efficient training resolves off-chip memory and endurance bottlenecks for GNNs on PIM hardware.

title: Identifying Latent Neural Dynamics with Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Neural circuits are densely interconnected systems, and many neural computations are thought to be mediated by the dynamical evolution of activity within these recurrent networks, a hypothesis often referred to as "computation through dynamics". Under this view, understanding computation within real neural populations depends on building models of the dynamical rules governing the temporal evolution of recorded high-dimensional neural activity. Most commonly, such models depend on explicit generative parameterisations of (i) the (nonlinear) intrinsic dynamical flow field and stochasticity, (ii) the (nonlinear) mapping from dynamical state to neuronal activity, and (iii) the variability of individual neural responses given that dynamical state. Misspecification of any of these components can bias estimates of dynamics and latent trajectories. In this paper, we circumvent generation-related issues by introducing the Recognition-Parametrised Gaussian Process dynamics (RP-GPdyn) model. RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field using a nonparametric Gaussian Process-defined transition function and models the relationship of dynamics to neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework. We show that this generation-free approach uncovers meaningful, behaviourally relevant latent variables and dynamics from both synthetic and experimental datasets.

AI.tldr: RP-GPdyn is a generation-free latent neural dynamics model combining a nonparametric Gaussian Process transition function with Recognition-Parametrised Models to avoid generative misspecification.
AI.motivation: Standard latent neural dynamics models rely on explicit generative parameterizations of flow fields, observation mappings, and noise, where misspecification biases latent trajectory and dynamics estimates.
AI.method: RP-GPdyn models the dynamical flow field with a nonparametric Gaussian Process transition function and captures the relationship between latent dynamics and neural activity implicitly using the Recognition-Parametrised Model (RPM) framework.
AI.result: Experiments on both synthetic and real neural datasets show that RP-GPdyn uncovers meaningful, behaviorally relevant latent variables and dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Avoiding explicit generative observation models via RPM and GP dynamics provides a robust, bias-resistant approach to identifying neural circuit dynamics.

title: PF-Exec: Large-Scale UAV Relay Load Balancing with an Anchored Potential Direction Decider and a Per-Dimension Gain-Learning Executor
summary: Relay load balancing in large-scale UAV networks requires joint decisions on association, bandwidth, power and hovering position, while the dimension grows with the number of UAVs and each UAV sees only its local state. This paper splits the decision into two layers. An anchored potential direction decider emits a closed-form target at every instant and returns its direction only. A gain-learning executor maps a local observation into a positive gain per dimension, composes gain and target, and clips the action against the physical single-step bound; the two layers form PF-Exec. The unit gain is the default start, so the executor reduces to the pure potential policy before training. The load is first-order homogeneous in bandwidth, making the bandwidth target closed form, and the position target is the demand-weighted centroid of the served users. The system uses a two-hop access and millimetre-wave backhaul link with soft association, a 3GPP UMa-AV channel with two shadowing layers, an OU-type social-force crowd and a quadrotor physical layer. Evaluation spans all fleet sizes, two crowd scenarios, independent seeds, the published baselines in their own settings and a degraded-information line. In the highest-pressure burst setting the fixed-step comparison breaks down on part of the seeds, losing fairness and mean load at once, while PF-Exec holds fairness near one. Among the ten comparison methods only the greedy heuristic survives that setting; its load variance stays far higher. Under stale global state and position noise the fairness index stays high at both largest-scale scenarios. Flight energy is nearly identical between the learned and the fixed-step executor, and three constants are fixed once across all settings. The convergence properties of both layers, from the truncated gain iteration to the perturbed tracking bound, are proved in the companion analysis.

AI.tldr: PF-Exec splits large-scale UAV relay load balancing into an anchored potential direction decider and a per-dimension gain-learning executor, maintaining fairness near 1 under high-pressure bursts and stale state.
AI.motivation: Jointly optimizing association, bandwidth, power, and hovering position in large-scale UAV networks scales poorly with fleet size when each UAV only observes local state.
AI.method: PF-Exec pairs a closed-form anchored potential direction decider (using homogeneous bandwidth targets and demand-weighted user centroids) with a local gain-learning executor that clips actions to physical bounds, evaluated under 3GPP UMa-AV channels and social-force crowds.
AI.result: Under high-pressure burst traffic where fixed-step baselines collapse, PF-Exec holds fairness near 1 (outperforming ten baselines including greedy), maintains high fairness under stale global state and position noise, and uses nearly identical flight energy.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling closed-form potential directions from learned local per-dimension gains enables scalable, resilient UAV relay load balancing.

title: Adversarially Batched Online Learning
summary: We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces adversarially batched online learning, characterizing optimal regret via relative batch growth for stochastic bandits and the 2-norm of batch lengths for OCO, experts, and adversarial bandits.
AI.motivation: In many online learning settings, learners can only update their policies at restricted time steps, yet the fundamental regret limits under adversarial batch partitions were unknown.
AI.method: The authors analyze four canonical problems under adversarial batching, deriving lower bounds for batch-aware learners and upper bounds using a batch-oblivious adaptive doubling trick.
AI.result: For stochastic bandits, the multiplicative penalty over standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in relative batch growth; for online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits, optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive batch-oblivious doubling matches batch-aware lower bounds, establishing tight complexity measures for batched online learning.

title: Generative Design with Real-time Physics Explainability: Towards Product Definition in the Age of AI
summary: In this article, we explore opportunities from using generative AI in mechanical engineering. On the one hand, generative methods based on invertible neural networks have been recently proposed for the solution of inverse design problems, allowing to infer design parameters from performance labels. On the other hand, generative AI models have shown that they can act as real time capable surrogates for physics based simulations. Here we suggest that these two streams should be combined in a unified framework, where INN are used to control the design process from the customer requirements perspective and the generative simulation of the systems physics adds a layer of explainability, why the proposed design fulfils the requirements. As generative design is prone to hallucinations, we propose uncertainty quantification to fend off physically infeasible requests. Finally, validation with classical tools is a requirement for generative design process. To demonstrate the capabilities of our novel generative design paradigm, we develop two interactive environments, one for airfoil design based on simulator data and one for the combustor design space exploration based on measured data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified generative design framework combining invertible neural networks (INNs) for inverse parameter inference with real-time physics surrogate simulations and uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Generative AI in mechanical engineering faces a split between inverse design and physics simulation, alongside hallucination risks that can produce physically infeasible designs.
AI.method: The framework uses INNs to map customer performance requirements to design parameters, pairs them with generative real-time physics surrogates for explainability, applies uncertainty quantification to filter infeasible requests, and validates with classical tools.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate the paradigm through two interactive environments: simulator-based airfoil design and measurement-based combustor design space exploration.
AI.conclusion: Integrating INNs, real-time physics surrogates, and uncertainty quantification enables explainable, reliable generative product definition.

title: Beyond a Single Sign: BiTE for Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures
summary: Binary neural networks (BNNs) reduce model storage and replace many arithmetic operations with efficient bitwise computations, but the single-sign activation limits their representational capacity. Each preactivation direction is compared with one threshold and reduced to one of two values, discarding variation within each sign region. We propose \textbf{BiTE} (Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion), which evaluates each feature direction against $K$ ordered thresholds and retains the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the following learned operator. BiTE can distinguish up to $K+1$ ordered activation states while allowing the following operator to learn a separate transformation for each threshold response. It also enables a controllable trade-off between the number of independently constructed feature directions and the number of ordered responses extracted from each direction. On BinaryViT, BiTE improves mean final-epoch Top-1 accuracy from $74.60\pm0.30\%$ to $75.83\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10 and from $42.80\pm0.46\%$ to $44.07\pm0.32\%$ on CIFAR-100, with nearly unchanged trainable parameter counts. A matched uniform-collapse control reaches $75.33\pm0.15\%$ on CIFAR-10, supporting the value of retaining the threshold responses separately relative to the evaluated scalar collapse. Binary VGG-16 experiments further show a favorable observed parameter--accuracy trade-off, including a configuration that achieves $0.64$ percentage points higher mean accuracy with $21.8\%$ fewer parameters than conventional width scaling. Overall, these results support branch-preserving threshold expansion as an effective way to improve binary representations and the observed parameter--accuracy trade-off.

AI.tldr: BiTE expands single-sign binary activations into K ordered thresholds retained as separate branches, improving BinaryViT accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 and offering better parameter-accuracy trade-offs on Binary VGG-16.
AI.motivation: Standard binary neural networks (BNNs) collapse each preactivation to a single sign bit, discarding magnitude variation within each sign region and limiting representational capacity.
AI.method: Branch-Preserving Binary Threshold Expansion (BiTE) evaluates each feature direction against K ordered thresholds and keeps the resulting binary responses as separate inputs to the next learned operator.
AI.result: On BinaryViT, BiTE improves mean Top-1 accuracy from 74.60% to 75.83% on CIFAR-10 and from 42.80% to 44.07% on CIFAR-100 with nearly unchanged parameters (beating a 75.33% uniform-collapse control), and on Binary VGG-16 achieves 0.64 percentage points higher accuracy with 21.8% fewer parameters than width scaling.
AI.conclusion: Retaining multi-threshold binary responses as separate branches effectively boosts BNN capacity and parameter efficiency.

title: Fair and Efficient Distributed EV Charging Coordination Using Threshold Cryptography and Machine Learning
comment: 16 pages
summary: Distributed coordination of electric vehicle (EV) charging with the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) keeps EV constraints private but assumes that every participant follows the algorithm. This assumption fails in practice, where a biased operator or a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacker can send inconsistent signals to different EVs, and compromised EVs can deviate from their prescribed updates. We first prove that attacks by such arbitrarily malicious, i.e., Byzantine, participants do not prevent convergence and therefore remain undetected, and derive the most damaging attack in closed form. We then propose a framework that combines a threshold-signed broadcast with upload recomputation, which detects every deviation without false alarms at linear instead of quadratic communication cost. To keep the optimization running, each affected EV recovers locally with a certified, fleet-aware machine learning price forecast, and we prove that the optimization remains convergent with a recovery cost bounded by the shape of the forecast error. Simulation results with real-world load, price, and charging data show that a biased operator raises the annual cost of disadvantaged EVs by 132.7% and lowers that of advantaged EVs by 49.3% without changing the aggregate load, whereas the defense limits all cost changes to 2.6%. An external MITM attacker raises the cost of its victims by 57.6%, the peak load by 5.8%, and the grid cost by 15.8%, whereas the defense keeps them within 1.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3% of benign operation. With up to 70% of the EVs attacked, the recovery converges in at least 97.8% of the runs.

AI.tldr: A threshold-cryptography and ML-based defense for distributed ADMM EV charging detects Byzantine and MITM attacks without false alarms at linear communication cost and recovers with certified price forecasts.
AI.motivation: Distributed ADMM for EV charging assumes honest participation, making it vulnerable to undetectable convergence under Byzantine operators, compromised EVs, or MITM attackers.
AI.method: The authors prove Byzantine attacks can converge undetected, then combine threshold-signed broadcasts with upload recomputation for exact detection at linear cost, paired with local recovery via a certified, fleet-aware ML price forecast.
AI.result: In real-world data simulations, a biased operator raises disadvantaged EV costs by 132.7% (defense limits all changes to 2.6%) and an MITM attacker raises victim costs by 57.6% and grid costs by 15.8% (defense keeps them within 1.1% and 0.3% of benign); recovery converges in >=97.8% of runs with up to 70% EVs attacked.
AI.conclusion: Combining threshold cryptography with certified ML forecasting provides provably convergent, fair, and efficient Byzantine resilience for distributed EV charging.

title: LightTAR: Light and Fast Target-Aware Representations for Multimodal Tabular Learning
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Multimodal tabular learning involves classification and regression on tables combining structured numerical and categorical features with unstructured text and images. These unstructured fields are commonly represented by pretrained encoder embeddings reduced with principal component analysis (PCA). This reduction prioritizes input variance but may overlook information relevant to predicting the target. We introduce LightTAR, a simple, inexpensive method that adapts dimensionality reduction to the prediction task. LightTAR augments the standard PCA representation with a few target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS). We evaluate LightTAR with 21 tabular models, including tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models. LightTAR improves average predictive performance for all models and, averaged across models, improves prediction on almost every MulTaBench dataset. These gains come with a small increase in total runtime relative to PCA representations. LightTAR integrates directly into existing encoding pipelines, improving tabular learners' predictive performance without modifying the encoder or the learner.

AI.tldr: LightTAR augments PCA-reduced pretrained embeddings with target-aware features via regularized partial least squares (PLS), consistently improving multimodal tabular learning across 21 models without modifying encoders or learners.
AI.motivation: Pretrained text and image embeddings in multimodal tabular learning are typically reduced with PCA, which preserves input variance but can discard target-relevant predictive signal.
AI.method: LightTAR appends a small set of target-aware features extracted jointly from the final and an intermediate encoder layer using regularized partial least squares (PLS) to standard PCA features.
AI.result: Evaluated across 21 tabular models (tree ensembles, neural networks, and tabular foundation models) on MulTaBench, LightTAR improves average predictive performance for every model and nearly every dataset with minimal runtime overhead.
AI.conclusion: Drop-in target-aware dimensionality reduction via regularized PLS is a simple, fast way to boost multimodal tabular learners.

title: Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions
summary: KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $\Omega(KCH^3/(\epsilon\max\{\epsilon,\beta\}))$ samples on some instances when $\epsilon$ is small, where $\beta$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $\beta\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/\beta$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/\epsilon$, with no coverage assumption. For $\beta\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/\epsilon$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes sample complexity lower and upper bounds for offline KL-regularized RL with stochastic transitions, showing pessimistic soft value iteration succeeds on reference-policy data where plug-in fails.
AI.motivation: Although KL-regularized RL underpins LLM fine-tuning using reference-policy data, its sample complexity beyond bandits and deterministic transitions has been largely unknown.
AI.method: Studying finite discounted MDPs with K state-action pairs, effective horizon H, and temperature beta, the authors derive minimax lower bounds under concentrability C>=4 and analyze pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty.
AI.result: Every estimator requires Omega(KCH^3/(epsilon max{epsilon, beta})) samples; pessimistic soft value iteration matches this rate up to log factors for beta>=1.4H, achieves polynomial sample complexity on reference-policy data without coverage assumptions, and avoids the failure of plug-in estimators at small temperatures.
AI.conclusion: Pessimism with variance-aware penalties is theoretically essential for sample-efficient offline KL-regularized RL under stochastic transitions.

title: Neural Simulation-Based Inference for Computational Cognitive Models: A Tutorial
summary: Computational cognitive modeling is an increasingly essential methodology to elucidate the mechanisms underlying human and animal cognition. By fitting models to empirical data, researchers can perform parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses to assess competing theories, quantify individual differences, and investigate neural representations. Typically, fitting these models relies on likelihood-dependent methods (e.g., Maximum likelihood estimation or hierarchical Bayesian methods). However, for many reasonable cognitive models, computing the likelihood is computationally intractable, in which case these methods become inadequate. This substantially limits the range of theories that researchers can investigate. Simulation-based inference with neural networks (neural SBI) has emerged as a powerful toolkit to overcome this hurdle. By training deep neural networks on datasets generated through model simulations, neural SBI learns the relation between observable data and cognitive models. This approach enables all the applications of standard modeling while bypassing the likelihood computation, without constraints on empirical data size. Despite its successful adoption across diverse scientific fields, neural SBI remains underutilized in cognitive modeling, partly due to a lack of accessible, domain-tailored guidance. This tutorial addresses this gap by providing a clear workflow for applying neural SBI to cognitive models. We also provide practical use cases and recommendations for reducing the computational and simulation burden, facilitating efficient implementation in real-world research settings. By lowering the technical barriers to neural SBI, this tutorial aims to empower cognitive scientists to investigate richer theory spaces and ultimately propel scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: This tutorial provides a practical workflow and simulation-cost-reduction strategies for applying neural simulation-based inference (neural SBI) to likelihood-intractable computational cognitive models.
AI.motivation: Many realistic cognitive models have computationally intractable likelihoods, preventing standard maximum likelihood or hierarchical Bayesian fitting and limiting the theories researchers can test.
AI.method: The tutorial outlines an accessible, domain-tailored workflow for training deep neural networks on simulated datasets (neural SBI) to bypass likelihood evaluation, along with practical use cases and recommendations to reduce simulation burden.
AI.result: The guide demonstrates how neural SBI supports parameter estimation, model comparison, and model-based neural analyses without empirical data-size constraints.
AI.conclusion: Lowering technical barriers to neural SBI empowers cognitive scientists to test richer, likelihood-free theories of human and animal cognition.

title: Joint World Action Models through Differentiable Trajectory Optimization
comment: 29 pages, 6 figures, 14 tables
summary: Joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, modeling world-action trajectories rather than actions alone. However, trajectory imitation does not ensure that these trajectories are task-effective or consistent with dynamics. We present \textbf{world action trajectory optimization (WATO)}, which optimizes generated actions and future states jointly for control. WATO uses both as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimization problem and differentiates the task loss through the optimized trajectory to train the generator. This makes generated trajectories task-aware and dynamics-consistent while using trajectory optimization only during training. At deployment, WATO directly generates candidate trajectories and ranks them with a world model, without iterative trajectory optimization. Across $7$ visual control environments, WATO improves average success from $79.9\%$ for the imitation joint WAM to $91.7\%$, outperforming strong model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines. Compared with cross-entropy method (CEM), WATO is on average $11.5\times$ faster and uses $600.5\times$ fewer world model evaluations at deployment.

AI.tldr: WATO trains joint world action models by differentiating task loss through a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimizer, boosting visual control success from 79.9% to 91.7% while running 11.5x faster than CEM at deployment.
AI.motivation: Imitation-trained joint world action models (WAMs) generate future actions and states together, but pure imitation does not guarantee task effectiveness or dynamics consistency.
AI.method: World Action Trajectory Optimization (WATO) uses generated actions and states as references in a dynamics-constrained trajectory optimizer during training, differentiating task loss through the optimizer; at deployment, it directly generates and ranks candidates with a world model without iterative optimization.
AI.result: Across 7 visual control environments, WATO raises average success from 79.9% (imitation joint WAM) to 91.7%, outperforming model-based, goal-conditioned RL, and generative control baselines while running 11.5x faster and using 600.5x fewer world model evaluations than CEM.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable trajectory optimization during training yields task-aware, dynamics-consistent joint WAMs with fast, optimization-free deployment.

title: A mesh-free deep energy method for phase-field modeling of thermally driven brittle fracture
comment: 48 pages, 18 figures, 15 tables
summary: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture requires resolving localized crack bands whose paths are unknown in advance and thermal boundary layers whose thickness evolves during the transient. Neural energy-based computations of thermal fracture have so far started from defects placed in advance. This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method based on multiresolution neural representations that predicts spontaneous crack nucleation, crack spacing, and selective crack propagation and arrest under transient thermal loading. Two networks, each with its own multiresolution encoding, represent the displacement and phase fields and the transient temperature, and the mechanical energy and the incremental functional of the backward Euler heat equation are estimated on integration points redrawn at every iteration. Restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying the optimizer state across load steps and decaying the learning rates within each step help prevent spurious damage accumulation. On two notched plates the initiation peak loads agree closely with an independent finite element reference. On a quenched glass strip under an analytical temperature field the crack path changes from straight to oscillatory and then to branched, with an oscillation threshold close to the linear stability prediction. Under a prescribed boundary temperature a quenched ceramic slab forms a crack array of the type observed in experiment, with a spacing close to that of a published benchmark. On the slab and a quenched annulus the arrays are denser than those of a finite element computation on the same material field. No crack paths, nucleation sites or crack-adapted meshes are prescribed.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a mesh-free deep energy method using multiresolution neural representations to model thermally driven brittle fracture without prescribing initial defects, crack paths, or crack-adapted meshes.
AI.motivation: Phase-field simulation of thermally driven fracture must resolve unknown localized crack paths and evolving thermal boundary layers, while prior neural energy-based thermal fracture computations required pre-placed defects.
AI.method: Two separate networks with multiresolution encodings represent the displacement/phase fields and transient temperature, estimating mechanical energy and the backward Euler heat equation functional on redrawn integration points while restricting irreversibility to the crack set, carrying optimizer state across load steps, and decaying learning rates within each step.
AI.result: Initiation peak loads on two notched plates match an independent finite element reference, a quenched glass strip transitions from straight to oscillatory to branched cracks near the linear stability threshold, and quenched ceramic slabs and annuli form crack arrays matching benchmark spacing with denser arrays than finite element computations on the same material field.
AI.conclusion: Multiresolution neural energy formulations can predict spontaneous crack nucleation, spacing, and selective propagation under transient thermal loading without crack-adapted meshes or prescribed nucleation sites.

title: Classifier-Guided Latent Diffusion for Small-Molecule Generation
