summary: Diffusion models have emerged as a promising class of generative models for molecular design because of their ability to learn complex chemical distributions and support conditional or guided generation. In this work, we investigate a latent diffusion pipeline for property-guided small-molecule generation. The proposed framework represents canonicalized SMILES strings using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer-based decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from molecular latent embeddings, and learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in the ChemBERTa latent space. To enable property-directed generation, a differentiable latent property predictor is used to guide the diffusion sampling process. Generated SELFIES strings are converted to SMILES, validated using RDKit, and evaluated using molecular validity, uniqueness, novelty, and predicted property scores. We study guidance toward two drug-relevant binary endpoints: blood--brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human $\beta$-secretase 1. The results suggest that latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings can generate chemically valid and novel molecules while enabling controllable steering toward desired molecular properties.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a classifier-guided latent diffusion pipeline over pretrained ChemBERTa molecular embeddings to generate valid, novel small molecules steered toward drug-relevant properties.
AI.motivation: Designing small molecules with desired pharmacological properties requires generative models that can learn complex chemical distributions and support controllable property-guided sampling.
AI.method: The framework encodes canonicalized SMILES using a frozen ChemBERTa encoder, trains a Transformer decoder to reconstruct SELFIES strings from latent embeddings, learns an unconditional denoising diffusion model in that latent space, and guides sampling with a differentiable latent property predictor before converting SELFIES to SMILES for RDKit validation.
AI.result: Evaluated on blood-brain barrier permeability and inhibition of human beta-secretase 1, the pipeline generates chemically valid, unique, and novel molecules while steering predicted property scores toward the target endpoints.
AI.conclusion: Latent diffusion over pretrained molecular embeddings enables controllable, property-directed small-molecule generation without sacrificing chemical validity or novelty.

title: Pattern-Based Matrix Analysis Under Permutations
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
summary: Low-rank approximation captures one important notion of matrix simplicity: a matrix is simple if it is well described by a low-dimensional linear model. This paper studies a complementary notion. We consider matrices that become structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns, so that their mass concentrates in a prescribed geometric pattern such as a band, block-diagonal, arrowhead, or related form. We introduce a pattern distance that measures how close a matrix is to a given pattern after optimal reordering, giving a common framework for structural problems such as latent ordering, community detection, and bandwidth minimization. The problem is NP-hard in general; we derive an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems. We further introduce a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that combines permutation-structured fitting with a low-rank residual, whose permutation step is pattern fitting on the residual; its gains across pattern families persist at a matched parameter budget and are substantially reduced under a density-matched random-mask control. We evaluate the framework on synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, showing that a single universal algorithm recovers qualitatively different forms of matrix structure.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a pattern-based matrix analysis framework and alternating Linear Assignment algorithm to measure and recover latent matrix structures (such as band, block-diagonal, or arrowhead) that emerge only after row and column permutations.
AI.motivation: Standard low-rank approximation captures linear simplicity, but many matrices are structurally simple only after permuting rows and columns to concentrate mass into a geometric pattern, an NP-hard problem lacking a unified framework.
AI.method: The authors define a pattern distance after optimal reordering, solve it via an alternating algorithm based on Linear Assignment subproblems, and extend it to a pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition that fits permutation structure on the low-rank residual.
AI.result: Across synthetic recovery tasks, real correlation and graph adjacency matrices, and transformer attention heads, the universal algorithm recovers diverse structural forms, and pattern-plus-low-rank gains persist at matched parameter budgets while dropping substantially under a density-matched random-mask control.
AI.conclusion: Permutation-based pattern distance and pattern-plus-low-rank decomposition provide a unified, effective way to uncover latent ordering, community structure, and bandwidth in matrices.

title: Representational Geometry as a Diagnostic for Adversarial Robustness
summary: Adversarial training is a common technique for making neural networks more robust to small, intentionally crafted input perturbations, and robustness is commonly measured through accuracy under attack. By exploring inter-network representations across different adversarial training objectives, we can analyze whether multiple networks organize their latent representations similarly. We study Multilayer Perceptrons trained on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and compare the resulting population training dynamics and geometry to those of a vanilla network. We use M-PHATE to embed data samples across training epochs and examine how the geometry of the data changes during training under adversarial objectives. On penultimate-layer representations we measure displacement between clean and perturbed points, distributional distance through maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery. Our visualizations and quantitative analyses show that adversarial training leads to structural changes in how networks organize internal data representations, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite ways. These findings support a discussion of re-evaluating how practitioners approach the auditing of model robustness by treating latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts across sets of networks.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how different adversarial training regimes reshape the internal representational geometry and training trajectories of MLPs on MNIST, finding that robust accuracy and representational stability can rank defenses oppositely.
AI.motivation: Adversarial robustness is typically evaluated only by accuracy under attack, leaving unclear how different adversarial training objectives organize latent representations or whether representational geometry can serve as a diagnostic.
AI.method: The authors train MLPs on MNIST under three adversarial training regimes and a vanilla baseline, embed sample trajectories across epochs using M-PHATE, and measure clean-vs-perturbed displacement, maximum mean discrepancy, and nearest-neighbor recovery on penultimate-layer representations.
AI.result: Adversarial training induces distinct structural changes in internal representation organization, and robust accuracy and representational stability can rank the same defenses in opposite orders.
AI.conclusion: Auditing model robustness should incorporate latent representations and their training trajectories as diagnostic artifacts alongside standard attack accuracy.

title: Antidistillation is Cheap: Lightweight Distillation-Resistance via Stylistic Corruption
comment: Accepted to Findings of EACL 2027
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective paradigm for transferring capabilities from large language models (LLMs) to smaller, more specialized student models. In commercial deployment where frontier models are restricted behind black-box APIs, sequence-level distillation remains a potent vector for competitors to clone proprietary capabilities at a fraction of the development cost. Existing defenses mostly rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which increases computational overhead and real-time inference latency. In this work, we propose a lightweight defense that dynamically injects style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations upon malicious queries. This framework offers exceptional flexibility, allowing hosts to customize target defensive styles and dynamically blend them to maximize stylistic variance. Crucially, this inference-time intervention preserves semantic utility and fluency during malicious queries, misleading adversaries into believing that they are extracting pristine teacher outputs, while standard consumers continue to receive original, unmodified responses. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework successfully disrupts student learning, achieving substantial anti-distillation performance while incurring negligible overhead and preserving text naturalness. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, inference-time anti-distillation defense that injects style-steering vectors into teacher model activations upon malicious queries to disrupt student distillation while preserving semantic utility.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against sequence-level knowledge distillation of black-box LLM APIs rely on surrogate models to manipulate next-token sampling, which adds computational overhead and inference latency.
AI.method: The framework dynamically injects and blends customizable style-steering vectors into the teacher model's activations only when malicious queries are detected, maximizing stylistic variance while leaving standard consumer responses unmodified.
AI.result: Experiments show that the defense substantially disrupts student learning and achieves strong anti-distillation performance while maintaining text naturalness, semantic utility, and negligible inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: Activation-level stylistic corruption offers a cheap, flexible, and effective way to protect proprietary LLMs from black-box sequence-level distillation.

title: Direction or Magnitude? Learning Scalars over Task-Calibrated Directions
summary: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) aims to preserve adaptation quality while reducing training costs. We propose SCALAR, which achieves performance comparable to LoRA with substantially fewer trainable parameters, lower peak training memory, and higher throughput. SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations and assigns a random output dictionary to each input direction. Fine-tuning learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, reducing gradient and optimizer-state storage. Grouped computation aggregates output atoms before applying the adapter to token activations, while dictionary sharing across compatible layers reduces fixed-basis storage. Experiments on commonsense reasoning, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation after instruction tuning demonstrate effective adaptation at small trainable budgets. On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR achieves accuracy comparable to LoRA with about 4% of its trainable parameters. System measurements on Qwen2.5-7B show 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA. The combination of adaptation quality, a compact trainable state, and training efficiency makes SCALAR a promising approach to resource-constrained fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SCALAR, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients over fixed task-calibrated input bases and random output dictionaries, matching LoRA accuracy with far fewer trainable parameters and lower memory.
AI.motivation: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA still incur notable trainable parameter, gradient, and optimizer-state memory costs during LLM adaptation.
AI.method: SCALAR constructs a fixed input basis from task activations, pairs each direction with a random output dictionary, learns only layer-specific scalar coefficients, aggregates output atoms via grouped computation before applying them to token activations, and shares dictionaries across compatible layers.
AI.result: On commonsense reasoning, SCALAR matches LoRA accuracy with about 4% of its trainable parameters, and on Qwen2.5-7B it achieves 20% lower peak training memory and 6% higher throughput than LoRA, while also performing effectively on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Learning scalars over fixed task-calibrated directions provides a compact, memory-efficient, and high-throughput alternative to LoRA for resource-constrained fine-tuning.

title: Federated Physics-Informed Thermal Field Prediction Across Unseen Geometries in Distributed Additive Manufacturing
summary: In additive manufacturing (AM), each change in part geometry requires a new thermal simulation, which makes design evaluation over many candidates costly. Geometry-aware models reduce this cost by predicting thermal fields on unseen parts with a single learned model, but they assume that diverse geometries are available centrally. This assumption is restrictive when each manufacturing site holds only a limited set of proprietary part designs that it cannot share. We propose Fed-PIGANO, a federated framework that trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models at individual sites and aggregates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without sharing part geometries. We evaluate the framework on a 2D steady-state thermal benchmark for metal AM, with geometries from five polygonal families distributed across three sites under four scenarios that range from identical to strongly different family compositions. Over seven replications, Fed-PIGANO achieves mean relative L2 errors of 1.83% to 2.04% across all 12 scenario-site cases, compared with up to 20.46% for local-only training, and consistently yields lower PDE residuals. Its prediction accuracy is comparable to that of a centralized model trained on the pooled geometries of all sites. These results demonstrate that federated learning lets manufacturing sites benefit from each other's geometries without sharing them, enabling rapid thermal prediction on new part designs for tasks such as shape optimization, inverse design, and uncertainty quantification.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Fed-PIGANO, a federated physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator framework that trains thermal field predictors across distributed additive manufacturing sites without sharing proprietary part geometries.
AI.motivation: Geometry-aware neural operators reduce thermal simulation costs for unseen additive manufacturing parts, but they assume diverse geometries are pooled centrally, which is infeasible when sites cannot share proprietary designs.
AI.method: Fed-PIGANO trains physics-informed geometry-aware neural operator (PI-GANO) models locally at each manufacturing site and federates their geometry encoders and prediction networks without exchanging part geometries.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 2D steady-state metal AM thermal benchmark across three sites and five polygonal families under four scenarios, Fed-PIGANO achieves 1.83% to 2.04% mean relative L2 errors across all 12 scenario-site cases (versus up to 20.46% for local-only training), yields lower PDE residuals, and matches centralized training accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Federated learning enables distributed manufacturing sites to collaboratively learn accurate, geometry-generalizable thermal predictors without exposing proprietary part designs.

title: Electrocardiographic Imaging via Posterior Sampling under Operator Discrepancy
comment: Accepted at the GenAI for Health Workshop @ NeurIPS 2026. Code, models and data: this https URL
summary: Electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) reconstructs heart-surface potentials from body-surface potentials, an ill-posed inverse problem. Diffusion posterior samplers combine a learned prior with an explicit forward operator that they assume to be accurate. In ECGI this operator is only an estimate, because the body changes with respiration and posture, and body composition such as subcutaneous fat is rarely known for an individual patient. The resulting operator discrepancy is structured and depends on the heart signal. We introduce OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler that models this discrepancy instead of treating it as signal-independent noise. OpDis-PS learns how the discrepancy depends on the signal, folds this into a corrected forward operator, and reconstructs with a fixed prior across all operator conditions. We study two realistic sources of discrepancy, changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer. Across both, OpDis-PS reconstructs more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with its largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces OpDis-PS, a diffusion posterior sampler for electrocardiographic imaging (ECGI) that explicitly models signal-dependent forward-operator discrepancy rather than treating it as independent noise.
AI.motivation: Diffusion posterior samplers for ECGI assume an accurate forward operator, whereas patient-specific factors like respiration, posture, and unknown subcutaneous fat introduce structured, signal-dependent operator discrepancy.
AI.method: OpDis-PS learns how operator discrepancy depends on the heart signal, folds this correction into the forward operator, and performs posterior sampling using a fixed learned prior across all operator conditions.
AI.result: Under two realistic discrepancy sources (changing lung conductivity and an added subcutaneous-fat layer), OpDis-PS reconstructs heart-surface potentials more accurately than classical regularization and learned predictors, with the largest gains on held-out cardiac pathologies.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling signal-dependent operator discrepancy improves the accuracy and generalization of diffusion posterior sampling for ill-posed inverse problems like ECGI.

title: Fuse-All MoE Inference Kernel with Load Balancing on TPUs
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures activate only a subset of experts for each token, allowing large language models (LLMs) to scale parameter capacity without a proportional increase in computation per token. However, intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads limit the efficiency of MoE inference on TPUs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce Fuse-All MoE, a TPU kernel design that jointly optimizes expert computation, output communication, and load balancing. The kernel fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes, retaining expert computation intermediates on chip. Fixed token-slot destinations allow scheduling and expert placement to change while preserving routing semantics. In prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving, Fuse-All MoE balances EP16 prefill workloads through scheduling and expert redistribution, while symmetric EP8TP2 shares active expert computation between the two TensorCore devices within each chip during decode. Our experiments show that Fuse-All MoE reduces kernel runtime for a measured skewed EP16 prefill workload from 2.3x to 1.09x the same fixed reference time for a balanced workload. Across 32-512 decode tokens, symmetric EP8TP2 reduces kernel latency by up to 21.3% relative to fused EP16. With accompanying serving stack optimizations, the integrated system improves serving throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Fuse-All MoE, a TPU inference kernel and serving design that fuses MoE computation and communication while balancing expert loads, reducing skewed prefill runtime and improving decode latency and serving throughput.
AI.motivation: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference on TPUs is bottlenecked by intermediate data movement and uneven expert loads across devices.
AI.method: Fuse-All MoE fuses token collection, expert projections, gated activation, and output writes on chip with fixed token-slot destinations, using scheduling and expert redistribution to balance EP16 prefill workloads and symmetric EP8TP2 to share active expert computation across two TensorCore devices per chip during decode.
AI.result: Fuse-All MoE reduces skewed EP16 prefill kernel runtime from 2.3x to 1.09x of a balanced reference time, symmetric EP8TP2 cuts decode kernel latency by up to 21.3% over fused EP16 across 32-512 tokens, and the integrated serving stack improves throughput by up to 34.5% over the Megablox EP16 baseline.
AI.conclusion: Jointly fusing MoE operations on chip and balancing workloads across prefill and decode unlocks substantial TPU inference speedups without altering routing semantics.

title: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) pose significant security risks by retaining private or hazardous information, creating an urgent need for unlearning techniques that excise specific knowledge without compromising general utility. However, prevailing fine-tuning-based unlearning methods struggle to achieve this balance, often suffering from computational inefficiency and unintended utility degradation due to the entangled nature of knowledge within model parameters. To disentangle forgetting from utility, we propose UUE, a theoretically grounded framework that reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing. First, UUE projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge representations, strictly ensuring that the editing process causes minimal interference to the model's general capabilities. Second, distinct from targeted mapping, we introduce a convex untargeted objective that derives a closed-form analytical solution to effectively disrupt undesired knowledge by pushing forget-set embeddings toward their antipodal points. We implement UUE via lightweight, pluggable adapters (including a low-rank variant, UUE-L), enabling efficient deployment without modifying the frozen backbone. Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy, significantly outperforming existing methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes UUE, a lightweight LLM unlearning framework that projects parameter updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained knowledge and pushes forget-set embeddings toward antipodal points via pluggable adapters.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning-based LLM unlearning methods often suffer from high computational cost and unintended degradation of general utility because knowledge is entangled within model parameters.
AI.method: UUE reformulates unlearning as controllable model editing by projecting updates into the orthogonal left null space of retained representations, deriving a closed-form analytical solution for a convex untargeted objective that pushes forget-set embeddings to antipodal points, and implementing updates via lightweight adapters (including low-rank UUE-L) on a frozen backbone.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on TOFU and WMDP benchmarks show that UUE and UUE-L achieve superior unlearning efficacy while preserving general utility, significantly outperforming existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal null-space projection combined with closed-form antipodal embedding disruption enables efficient, utility-preserving LLM unlearning without modifying frozen backbone weights.

title: Process Mining-Enabled Federated Anomaly Detection for the Industrial IoT
comment: Accepted to the IEEE Annual Congress on Artificial Intelligence of Things (IEEE AIoT 2026)
summary: While federated anomaly detection enables the integration of local data insights across diverse nodes to reduce false positives, it inherently struggles with non-IID data. In practice, industrial IoT plants often operate under varying conditions and experience diverse environmental phenomena, resulting in significant heterogeneity in the monitored time series. In such settings, standard federated learning approaches fail to perform nuanced aggregation that accounts for these cross-node differences, ultimately leading to increased false positive rates. In this paper, we propose a process mining approach to evaluate the similarity of local node data against a reference provided by a global node. The global node utilizes these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation, producing personalized updates distributed across the network. We evaluate our approach using industrial IoT time-series data collected from manufacturing plants operating under distinct conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that our process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline achieves superior performance, yielding a 46.52% and 11.99% relative improvement in F1-score compared to isolated local training baselines and standard FedAvg, respectively, alongside a 51.24% relative reduction in false positives over standard federated aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a process mining-enabled federated anomaly detection pipeline for Industrial IoT that weights local model aggregation by similarity to a global reference, reducing false positives under non-IID conditions.
AI.motivation: Industrial IoT plants operate under diverse conditions that produce non-IID time series, causing standard federated averaging to suffer from poor aggregation and elevated false positive rates.
AI.method: A process mining approach evaluates the similarity of each local node's data against a global reference, and the global node uses these similarity metrics to dynamically weight local models during aggregation to produce personalized updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on industrial IoT time-series data from distinct manufacturing plants, the pipeline improves F1-score by 46.52% over isolated local training and 11.99% over standard FedAvg, while reducing false positives by 51.24% relative to standard federated aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Process mining-based similarity weighting effectively mitigates non-IID heterogeneity in federated Industrial IoT anomaly detection.

title: Protection-Oriented Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Fault Detection in Power Systems
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at the 21st International Conference on Developments in Power System Protection (DPSP APAC 2027), Hong Kong, 6-9 January 2027
summary: Machine learning (ML)-based fault detectors are increasingly proposed for power system protection, yet aggregate metrics can obscure the consequences of false and missed trips. We present a protection-oriented assessment of three ML detectors and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90, comprising 9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line. The assessment combines five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget. It reports security, dependability, detection timing, decision margins, and episode-level nuisance assertions. Gradient-boosted trees, a convolutional neural network, and logistic regression achieve AUC-ROC values above 0.999, yet at a security budget of $10^{-3}$ their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%. Post-clearing false-trip rates of approximately 0.12-0.16% per window coexist with nuisance assertions in 11.3-19.1% of episodes. Among the analysed physical descriptors, missed trips are most consistently associated with higher fault resistance within the sampled range. An analytical current proxy suggests a fault-current gradient only partly reproduced by waveform-derived current (rank correlation 0.62). No single topology state or faulted phase consistently dominates within the sampled domain. Because PROTECT-90 contains fault episodes only, security is assessed on pre-fault and post-clearing windows rather than independent non-fault disturbances.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a protection-oriented assessment of ML-based power system fault detectors on the PROTECT-90 dataset, showing that near-perfect AUC-ROC scores can mask substantial missed-trip and nuisance-assertion rates under fixed security budgets.
AI.motivation: Aggregate classification metrics like AUC-ROC obscure the operational consequences of false and missed trips in power system protection.
AI.method: The authors evaluate gradient-boosted trees, a CNN, logistic regression, and a sequence-current reference on PROTECT-90 (9,022 simulated fault episodes on a 90 kV double-circuit line) using five window conditions, causal window-end labelling, episode-grouped cross-validation, and operating-point selection under a fixed security budget.
AI.result: Although all three ML detectors exceed 0.999 AUC-ROC, at a 10^-3 security budget their developed-fault missed-trip rates range from 0.007% to 1.99%, post-clearing false-trip rates are 0.12-0.16% per window, and nuisance assertions occur in 11.3-19.1% of episodes, with missed trips most consistently linked to higher fault resistance.
AI.conclusion: Power system ML fault detectors must be evaluated with protection-oriented, episode-level security and dependability metrics rather than aggregate AUC-ROC alone.

title: Delayed Effects of Temporary Weight Decay in Muon Pretraining
summary: A temporary optimization intervention can increase validation loss when it ends yet reduce it at the final training budget. We demonstrate this with temporary weight decay in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers with 162M, 405M, 1.4B, and 3.4B parameters. For models up to 1.4B parameters, moving a fixed-duration decay window from early to late training reverses its final effect. At 162M, changing window duration alters final loss even at approximately matched total shrinkage. Most strikingly, a schedule selected at 162M and transferred without retuning to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it only after 73% of training, and ultimately finishes 0.028 nats better while also outperforming the best sampled constant-decay baseline. Early decay leaves a persistent weight-norm deficit, which keeps relative steps larger after the intervention ends. An approximate norm-dynamics recurrence captures the slow convergence of these relative steps, and fixed-norm replays of the measured trajectories reproduce the performance ordering and a similar loss difference. At 162M and 405M, norm-reset experiments show that smaller weight norms at the end of the decay window explain most of the final loss improvement. A separate Gram intervention exhibits related post-removal norm and relative-step dynamics. These results show that temporary optimization schedules can have delayed effects long after removal and should therefore be evaluated at the intended final training budget, not only at removal.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that temporary weight decay during Muon pretraining can worsen validation loss when removed yet improve final loss at the end of training, driven by persistent weight-norm deficits.
AI.motivation: Optimization interventions are often judged by their immediate effect upon removal, which may miss delayed benefits that emerge later in pretraining.
AI.method: The authors apply temporary weight decay windows in Muon-trained decoder-only Transformers (162M to 3.4B parameters) and analyze weight-norm dynamics via an approximate recurrence, fixed-norm replays, norm-reset experiments, and a Gram intervention.
AI.result: A schedule selected at 162M and transferred to 1.4B is 0.26 nats worse than no decay when removed, overtakes it after 73% of training, and finishes 0.028 nats better while outperforming the best constant-decay baseline; norm-reset experiments confirm that smaller post-window weight norms explain most of the final improvement.
AI.conclusion: Temporary optimization schedules can have delayed positive effects long after removal and should be evaluated at the intended final training budget rather than at intervention end.

title: Quantum Graph Neural Networks: Architectures, Trainability, and Applications
summary: Quantum graph neural networks (QGNNs) apply parametrized quantum circuits to graph-structured data, with the aim of overcoming limits of classical graph neural networks in scalability, expressivity, and long-range information flow. Since the first Hamiltonian-based model in 2019, the field has produced many architectures, applications, and claims, but the evidence behind them has not been assessed systematically. This survey introduces a unified formalism that describes every QGNN as an encoder, a graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and an optional classical head, together with a circuit-level condition for permutation equivariance and a resource model for comparing costs. We organize the literature into five architecture families (convolutional, equivariant, message-passing and recurrent, Hamiltonian, and hybrid) and compare them by qubit cost, symmetry, scalability, and evidence. We then review symmetry and geometric inductive biases (permutation, rotation, and Lorentz), the results on expressivity, trainability, noise, and scalability, and applications in high-energy physics, chemistry, finance, healthcare, earth observation, and transportation. An audit of datasets and evaluation practices leads to a minimum reporting protocol. Our main finding is that the design space is rich and symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, whereas the evidence remains thin: results are mostly simulated, on small graphs, at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has yet been established on tasks over classical graph data. We identify five open challenges and a research agenda covering provable advantage, equivariant and geometric designs, fault-tolerant implementations, and shared benchmarks. The coverage extends through 2026 and emphasizes recent work.

AI.tldr: This survey introduces a unified formalism and resource model for Quantum Graph Neural Networks (QGNNs), systematically auditing architectures, symmetries, trainability, applications, and empirical evidence through 2026.
AI.motivation: Since 2019, QGNNs have generated many architectures and claims, but the field lacks a unified formalism and systematic assessment of whether empirical evidence supports quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors formalize QGNNs as an encoder, graph-conditioned circuit, observables, and optional classical head, establish a circuit-level permutation-equivariance condition, categorize models into five architecture families, and audit datasets and evaluation practices to propose a minimum reporting protocol.
AI.result: Symmetry is the best-supported inductive bias, but empirical evidence remains thin: most results are simulated on small graphs at parity with classical models or with fewer parameters, and no advantage has been established on classical graph tasks.
AI.conclusion: Future QGNN progress requires shared benchmarks, minimum reporting standards, and research into provable advantage, equivariant designs, and fault-tolerant implementations.

title: TIDE: Reclaiming Lost Performance In On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures
summary: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) today suffers from severe under-utilization due to long-tail rollouts. Inference engines fall idle waiting for long-tail rollouts or decode at low, inefficient batch sizes. To address this, we present TIDE, an RL training system that preserves on-policy training semantics while recovering resource utilization. TIDE does so by two complementary techniques: (1) dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training while long-tail rollouts complete and (2) dynamically migrating rollouts between inference engines to boost decoding throughput. TIDE automatically determines the right time to repurpose rollout resources through an adaptive migration policy, obtaining performance improvements that generalize across multiple applications and hardware configurations without requiring bespoke configuration. In our evaluation, TIDE provides end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and achieving up to 97% of optimal throughput.

AI.tldr: This paper presents TIDE, an on-policy RL post-training system for LLMs that recovers GPU utilization lost to long-tail rollouts by dynamically repurposing rollout GPUs for training and migrating rollouts across inference engines.
AI.motivation: Synchronous, colocated RL post-training of LLMs suffers from severe GPU under-utilization because inference engines sit idle or decode at small batch sizes while waiting for long-tail rollouts.
AI.method: TIDE preserves on-policy semantics while using an adaptive migration policy to dynamically repurpose idle rollout GPUs for training and migrate active rollouts between inference engines to increase decoding throughput.
AI.result: TIDE achieves end-to-end speedups of up to 1.36x over colocated systems, outperforming all evaluated on-policy baselines and reaching up to 97% of optimal throughput across multiple applications and hardware setups.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive rollout migration and dynamic GPU repurposing substantially improve hardware efficiency in synchronous on-policy LLM RL without bespoke configuration.

title: Differentially Private Federated Class-Incremental Learning for EEG Mental State Classification
summary: Federated learning (FL) under differential privacy (DP) is typically evaluated on large client cohorts, where subsampling and cross-client averaging amplify privacy and smooth injected noise. Personal biosignal applications such as wearable EEG instead involve small federations of a handful of subjects, a regime whose interaction with formal client-level DP is largely uncharacterized. We study differentially private federated class-incremental learning in this small-cohort regime, combining a public EEG dataset with a custom four-channel MUSE 2 recording set into a K=5-client federation, and give a masked per-class training protocol that avoids degenerate gradients and missing negative supervision under class-incremental streaming. We propose FedEEG, combining Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation with a lagged adaptive FedProx term, and show it reduces catastrophic forgetting relative to FedAvg, FedProx, and a federated Learning-without-Forgetting baseline; on-device balanced-batch replay reduces mean forgetting by a further 56.7%. A class-scoping diagnosis yields $50.5\%\pm3.6\%$ accuracy with 6 seeds and 2.02 times chance. We also introduce head-scoped client-level DP, which protects the classification head and alone reduces the achievable $\varepsilon$ by 200 times at a matched round budget; combined with fewer communication rounds it reaches $\varepsilon\!\approx\!10.4$ with utility not statistically distinguishable from non-private training.

AI.tldr: This paper studies differentially private federated class-incremental learning in small-cohort EEG settings (K=5 clients), proposing FedEEG and head-scoped client-level DP to reduce catastrophic forgetting and privacy loss.
AI.motivation: Formal client-level differential privacy (DP) is well studied in large federations, but its interaction with small-cohort personal biosignal applications like wearable EEG under class-incremental streaming is largely unknown.
AI.method: Combining a public EEG dataset with a custom 4-channel MUSE 2 set into a K=5 federation, the authors introduce a masked per-class training protocol, FedEEG (Synaptic-Intelligence consolidation plus lagged adaptive FedProx with optional on-device balanced-batch replay), and head-scoped client-level DP that protects only the classification head.
AI.result: FedEEG reduces catastrophic forgetting over FedAvg, FedProx, and federated LwF, replay cuts mean forgetting by a further 56.7%, a class-scoping diagnosis yields 50.5% +/- 3.6% accuracy (2.02x chance), and head-scoped DP reduces achievable epsilon by 200x at matched rounds, reaching epsilon around 10.4 with utility statistically indistinguishable from non-private training.
AI.conclusion: Head-scoped DP and consolidation-based continual learning make private, class-incremental EEG personalization feasible even in very small federations.

title: Reasoning Models Confabulate to Defend Injected Beliefs About Their Own Requests
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Also available on Zenodo: this https URL
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report are proposed as levers for AI oversight, on the assumption that a model's account of what it is doing is anchored to what it was asked. We show this anchor can be cut. An activation edit invisible in the prompt text, the injected forming-trace of an off-topic concept, overwrites a reasoning model's belief about its own request: across six models spanning scale, architecture, and recipe, the injected topic becomes the task it reasons about, reports back, and answers: the forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, and on the four models with clean final haiku the injected answer follows in 99% of generations. Warnings barely move it: even one naming the true topic yields under 5% true-topic answers. Handed the truth in clean tokens, the model confabulates a story about the user ("maybe they got confused and corrected themselves") and answers with the injection anyway, its behavior and chain-of-thought corrupted together: a concrete limit on CoT monitorability. Opening the model up offers no reprieve: it attends to the true request even harder after edits, yet that attention is causally inert, and the injected content rides intact task circuits, so attention maps and circuit attributions read as on-task too; the same edit redirects the request's language and format, not only its topic. What the injection reaches is the model's reference to its own input; what it elicits is its defense of it.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that injecting an activation-space forming-trace of an off-topic concept into reasoning models overwrites their belief about their own request, causing both their answers and chain-of-thought to confabulate defenses of the injected topic.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring and self-report assume a model's account of its actions is anchored to the prompt it received.
AI.method: Across six reasoning models, the authors perform an activation edit invisible in the prompt text (injecting a forming-trace of an off-topic concept) and test forced quote-back, warnings naming the true topic, clean-token corrections, attention maps, and circuit attributions.
AI.result: The forced quote-back returns the injected topic in 47 of 48 model-concept cells, injected answers follow in 99% of generations on four models, warnings yield under 5% true-topic answers, and the model confabulates stories about user confusion while attention to the true request remains causally inert.
AI.conclusion: Activation-level belief injection breaks the anchor between prompt and self-report, exposing a concrete limit on CoT monitorability and interpretability-based oversight.

title: DeltaVisionX: A Low-Cost Vision-Guided Automation System Using YOLOv11 and PLC-Based Actuation
summary: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial automation system that integrates real-time computer vision with PLC-based actuation for object classification and sorting. The system uses the YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once) deep learning model to detect objects on an operating conveyor belt and communicates detection results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC, which actuates pneumatic pistons for sorting. A custom dataset was created, labeled, and augmented to train the YOLOv11 model, achieving a mean average precision of 0.97 with real-time inference of 100 ms per frame. Encoder-based tracking ensures reliable synchronization between detection and actuation, supporting a throughput of 80 objects per minute. Results show that affordable, locally developed automation can reduce labor dependency and improve manufacturing efficiency. The novelty of the proposed system lies in its encodersynchronized vision-PLC integration rather than in the detection model itself. Future work includes integrating a highspeed Delta robot with EtherCAT-based servo control for advanced pick-and-place operations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents DeltaVisionX, a low-cost industrial sorting system integrating YOLOv11 object detection with encoder-synchronized Delta DVP-SE PLC pneumatic actuation.
AI.motivation: Affordable, locally developed industrial automation is needed to reduce labor dependency and improve manufacturing sorting efficiency.
AI.method: A custom augmented dataset trains YOLOv11 to detect objects on a conveyor belt, sending results to a Delta DVP-SE PLC that triggers pneumatic pistons synchronized via encoder-based tracking.
AI.result: The YOLOv11 model achieves 0.97 mAP with 100 ms per frame real-time inference, and encoder synchronization supports a sorting throughput of 80 objects per minute.
AI.conclusion: Encoder-synchronized vision-PLC integration provides a practical, low-cost automation solution for real-time industrial object sorting.

title: Analyzing Learning-Dynamics Across Loss and Prediction Choices for Diffusion Models
comment: NuerIPS2026
summary: Denoising generative models predict clean data ($x$), noise ($\epsilon$), or velocity ($v$), while training losses can be measured in any of these spaces. Although the resulting nine combinations are algebraically related, they can yield substantially different denoising accuracy and sample quality. We disentangle the effects of prediction and loss spaces. For a fixed prediction target, we show that changing the loss space is exactly equivalent to timestep reweighting and provide a heuristic analysis of how this reweighting affects generation quality. We then show that a rank-$m$ linear bottleneck compressing a $D$-dimensional noisy input imposes an irreducible squared-error floor of $D-m$ on noise and velocity prediction, whereas clean-data prediction can exploit low-dimensional data structure. Combining this bound with prediction-dependent error conversion yields distinct necessary conditions on bottleneck capacity. Experiments with U-Net and JiT across CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256 support these theoretical predictions. Under compression, prediction choice strongly affects both denoising accuracy and sample quality, with noise-prediction errors closely matching the theoretical lower bound. Our results provide a quantitative understanding of how architectural bottlenecks interact with prediction and loss choices in denoising generative models.

AI.tldr: This paper disentangles the effects of prediction target (x, epsilon, v) and loss space in diffusion models, showing that loss space equals timestep reweighting while linear architectural bottlenecks impose an irreducible D-m error floor on noise and velocity prediction.
AI.motivation: Although the nine combinations of prediction and loss spaces in denoising generative models are algebraically related, they yield different denoising accuracy and sample quality for reasons not fully quantified.
AI.method: The authors prove that changing loss space for a fixed prediction target is equivalent to timestep reweighting, derive an irreducible squared-error floor of D-m for noise and velocity prediction under a rank-m linear bottleneck, and test U-Net and JiT models on CIFAR-10, Imagenette, and ImageNet-256.
AI.result: Under architectural compression, prediction choice strongly governs denoising accuracy and sample quality, with clean-data prediction able to exploit low-dimensional data structure while noise-prediction errors closely match the theoretical D-m lower bound.
AI.conclusion: Architectural bottlenecks interact asymmetrically with diffusion prediction targets, providing quantitative guidance for choosing prediction and loss spaces.

title: When Does Oversampling Help? A Decision Framework for Imbalanced Data Streams Under Label Delay and Concept Drift
summary: For imbalanced data streams with delayed labels, is it worth adding a streaming oversampler, or does continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions already recover the cost of the delay? We address this through an extensive experimental comparison of streaming oversampling and continuous re-evaluation under joint class imbalance, concept drift, and label delay. Streaming oversamplers are typically evaluated under the test-then-train assumption of immediate labels; their behaviour under these conditions, assessed through re-evaluation, has not been systematically studied. We close this gap with a decision framework that predicts when oversampling adds value over re-evaluation, organised around three axes: drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window, and operationalised as a competition between a recovery channel (re-evaluation) and a minority-coverage channel (oversampling). Evaluating $15$ classifiers on $6$ synthetic and $6$ real streams, we find: re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but is silent on stationary ones; oversampling's marginal contribution over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration; and cost--performance Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams do not transfer to real data, where fronts partition by drift regime. Method selection should therefore be conditioned on the stream's profile and re-estimated as it evolves, not inherited from synthetic benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a decision framework for imbalanced data streams with label delay and concept drift, showing that continuous re-evaluation of earlier predictions recovers delay loss on drift-active streams and leaves little marginal gain for streaming oversampling.
AI.motivation: Streaming oversamplers are usually evaluated under immediate labels, leaving unclear whether they add value over continuous re-evaluation when labels are delayed under concept drift.
AI.method: The authors evaluate 15 classifiers across 6 synthetic and 6 real streams, organizing a decision framework around drift density, minority-class learnability, and delay relative to the refinement window as a competition between re-evaluation and oversampling.
AI.result: Re-evaluation recovers delay-induced loss on drift-active streams but not stationary ones, oversampling's marginal gain over re-evaluation is statistically detectable in only one real-data configuration, and Pareto recommendations from synthetic streams fail to transfer to real data.
AI.conclusion: Method selection for delayed, imbalanced streams should be conditioned on the evolving real stream profile rather than inherited from synthetic benchmarks.

title: RiverScan: Learning to Accumulate on River Networks
comment: 17 pages including references and appendices; 6 figures, 5 tables
summary: Accurate runoff prediction across large river basins requires models to capture heterogeneous local hydrological responses and their accumulation downstream. River-network connectivity provides a natural structure for this task, but using it effectively requires learning how to combine contributions from subcatchments of different sizes. We frame this challenge as learning to accumulate and introduce RiverScan, a spatial operator based on area-weighted selective state-space recurrence. RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order. Contributing-area fractions account for subcatchment size, while learned retention controls how upstream information persists downstream. Experiments on 608 stations in the Danube basin show that RiverScan outperforms the evaluated temporal and graph baselines in overall predictive performance. Structural controls and ablations demonstrate that composing heterogeneous subcatchment representations in a manner aligned with hydrological accumulation substantially improves runoff prediction, with the benefits of correct topology growing along the river-network hierarchy. These findings establish physically structured accumulation as an effective inductive bias for hydrological modeling and motivate finer-grained, fully distributed AI-based hydrological models.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RiverScan, an area-weighted selective state-space recurrence operator that learns to accumulate hydrological states along river-network topology for basin-scale runoff prediction.
AI.motivation: Basin-scale runoff prediction requires modeling heterogeneous local responses and their downstream accumulation, which generic temporal or graph models do not naturally align with hydrological drainage structure.
AI.method: RiverScan recursively combines local temporal representations with accumulated upstream states in topological order, using contributing-area fractions for subcatchment size and learned retention to control downstream persistence.
AI.result: Across 608 stations in the Danube basin, RiverScan outperforms evaluated temporal and graph baselines in overall predictive performance, with ablations confirming that topology-aligned accumulation yields growing benefits along the river hierarchy.
AI.conclusion: Physically structured, area-weighted accumulation provides an effective inductive bias for distributed AI-based hydrological modeling.

title: Sample-Efficient Control of Magnetoconvective Flows via Differentiable Simulation
summary: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) fluid flows are central to demanding engineering applications, most prominently fusion blanket cooling, where flow control is a promising tool to optimize key properties such as heat transfer. While active flow control (AFC) has recently advanced through machine learning, its application to MHD flows remains largely unexplored. In this work, we present $\phi$-PICT, a novel differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD solver targeted at AFC. We validate $\phi$-PICT against MHD benchmarks and demonstrate its high computational efficiency. Integrated into FluidGym, $\phi$-PICT enables sample-efficient gradient-based algorithms to improve heat transfer by $>25$% and allows optimizers to achieve $10^3\times$ higher accuracy in inverse design than black-box methods. $\phi$-PICT is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents phi-PICT, a differentiable GPU-accelerated magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) solver integrated into FluidGym for sample-efficient active flow control and inverse design.
AI.motivation: Active flow control for MHD flows, such as in fusion blanket cooling, has been limited by the lack of differentiable, GPU-accelerated MHD solvers.
AI.method: The authors develop phi-PICT, validate it against MHD benchmarks, and integrate it into FluidGym to enable gradient-based optimization and control.
AI.result: Gradient-based algorithms using phi-PICT improve heat transfer by over 25% and achieve 10^3x higher accuracy in inverse design compared to black-box methods.
AI.conclusion: Differentiable GPU-accelerated MHD simulation unlocks sample-efficient gradient-based control and inverse design for complex magnetoconvective flows.

title: Conflict, Feasibility, Faithfulness, Displacement: Four Quantities That Come Apart in Federated Dual-Cone Aggregation
summary: FedFV, FedGH and FedMGDA+ aggregate client updates with multi-objective gradient aggregators to remove conflict between them. We examine this rationale with UPGrad, which increases no client's loss to first order, in a comparison that changes only the direction of FedAvg's update. Four quantities the rationale treats as one -- conflict between client updates, feasibility of their weighted mean, faithfulness of the transmitted updates to the clients' gradients, and displacement of the update -- come apart. Under Dirichlet partitioning UPGrad improves CIFAR-10 accuracy by +0.78 pp (14/15 seeds, p < 0.001), only with full participation; on Oxford-IIIT Pet its +0.52 pp gain vanishes (+0.07 pp) once the data our protocol left unused are kept. Varying only the Dirichlet concentration, the gain grows with heterogeneity, yet the split with the most conflict shows none. Uniform client weights, blind to conflict, match the CIFAR-10 gain and exceed the Pets gain; a matched random rotation does neither. No fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and on CIFAR-10 the guarantee does not reach the clients' gradients. We state what evaluations should report.

AI.tldr: This paper uses UPGrad to show that four quantities treated as unified by federated dual-cone aggregators—conflict, feasibility, faithfulness, and displacement—actually come apart in practice.
AI.motivation: Multi-objective federated aggregators like FedFV, FedGH, and FedMGDA+ aim to remove client update conflict, assuming conflict, feasibility, faithfulness, and displacement align.
AI.method: The authors compare UPGrad against FedAvg (changing only update direction) under Dirichlet partitioning on CIFAR-10 and Oxford-IIIT Pet, varying participation, data retention, concentration, uniform weights, and random rotations.
AI.result: Under full participation, UPGrad improves CIFAR-10 accuracy by +0.78 pp (14/15 seeds, p < 0.001), while its +0.52 pp gain on Oxford-IIIT Pet drops to +0.07 pp when unused data are kept; uniform client weights match or exceed these gains, no fairness effect survives multiplicity correction, and the CIFAR-10 guarantee does not reach client gradients.
AI.conclusion: Federated dual-cone aggregation evaluations must separately report conflict, feasibility, faithfulness, and displacement rather than conflating them.

title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
comment: 55 pages, 9 figures
summary: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework using a frozen TabPFN and a reference pool of 890 devices for enrichment-oriented virtual screening of perovskite solar cell recipes.
AI.motivation: Combinatorial diversity in perovskite compositions, layers, and processing makes exhaustive experimental optimization slow, motivating virtual screening to prioritize candidate recipes.
AI.method: A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides RL recipe generation (PPO and recurrent PPO), evaluated against six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run on 1,846 devices with neighborhood-based assessment.
AI.result: Top-ten selection raises mean PCE from 19.68% to 23.74%, and in top-100 shortlists PPO and RPPO achieve 23% and 24% neighborhood-supported hit rates (versus 2.9% random and 10% for L-SHADE and Ax BO), though 65.4% of 9,000 recipes match a composition family at 0.80 similarity and only 11.7% at 0.90.
AI.conclusion: Surrogate-guided RL effectively enriches candidate shortlists near known high-performing perovskite recipes, though results support prioritization rather than experimental performance or seed robustness.

title: Learning nonlinear interactions and cross-feature couplings with product-unit residual networks
summary: Understanding nonlinear feature interactions is crucial in science and engineering, yet standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) often capture such interactions only implicitly, leading to entangled representations that can impair robustness and interpretability. We investigate complex-valued product-unit residual networks (CV-PURe) that integrate multiplicative product units with residual connections to explicitly model cross-feature couplings while stabilizing optimization. We conduct a systematic evaluation on an interaction-driven synthetic benchmark and real-world datasets and evaluate prediction together with input-level interaction recovery under a reproducible protocol. Across five data splits and five training seeds, CV-PURe achieves the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific benchmarks, reducing Friedman error by 53.9% relative to MLP. Its Friedman interaction maps assign 60.7% of total strength to the known interacting pair, compared with 31.0% for MLP. On a synthetic task containing third- and fourth-order products and 20 distractors, CV-PURe reduces RMSE from 0.1376 to 0.0797 relative to a complex-valued MLP and recovers all nine true pairwise projections in every training/sampling repetition. Bike Sharing experiments connect improved prediction to the contribution of temporal, calendar, and seasonal context through paired ablations of both PURe variants. Parkinsons Telemonitoring extends the context analysis to repeated measurements. Noise and learning-curve evaluations demonstrate sustained predictive gains under perturbed inputs and limited supervision, while inference measurements quantify computational cost. This article extends our ICCS 2026 paper, Modeling Nonlinear Feature Interactions with Product-Unit Residual Networks (doi:https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-29921-5_6).

AI.tldr: This paper investigates complex-valued product-unit residual networks (CV-PURe) that combine multiplicative product units with residual connections to explicitly model nonlinear cross-feature couplings.
AI.motivation: Standard MLPs capture nonlinear feature interactions implicitly, producing entangled representations that can hurt robustness and interpretability.
AI.method: CV-PURe integrates multiplicative product units with residual connections and is evaluated under a reproducible protocol across five splits and five seeds on interaction-driven synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets (including Bike Sharing and Parkinsons Telemonitoring).
AI.result: CV-PURe achieves the lowest mean RMSE on four of six scientific benchmarks, reduces Friedman error by 53.9% over MLP, assigns 60.7% of Friedman interaction strength to the true interacting pair (versus 31.0% for MLP), and cuts synthetic higher-order product RMSE from 0.1376 to 0.0797 while recovering all nine true pairwise projections.
AI.conclusion: Explicit multiplicative product units with residual stabilization improve both predictive accuracy and input-level interaction recovery on structured scientific data.

title: Deep Latents, Long Memory: Latent persistence explains temporal correlations in transformer activations
summary: The hidden layers of Large Language Models (LLMs) are believed to encode representations of the data whose abstraction increases with depth. However, in the absence of an operational notion of abstraction, this statement is hard to test quantitatively. Here, we propose an alternative view, building on the principle that the correlations of a sequence reflect the structure of the process that generated it. We define the autocorrelation function of a layer as the average dot product between its activations at two context positions separated by a lag. Latent variables encoded persistently along the context create slowly decaying tails in the autocorrelation, and we find these tails to grow across layers in both synthetic and natural data. In synthetic data with controlled hierarchical latent structure, this growth stems from the encoding of abstract latent variables, which govern long stretches of the input. Indeed, the persistence of latent codes predicts the qualitative structure of autocorrelations and accounts for most of the empirical measures. In real text, we take sparse-autoencoder features as proxies for latent variables, and find that their persistence correlates strongly with the magnitude of autocorrelations across datasets and LLMs. In particular, the persistence time increases with depth, as do autocorrelations, implying that deeper latent features persist for longer context spans. We complement this analysis by explicitly ablating the persistent sparse-autoencoder features and observing a consequent decrease in the autocorrelations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using activation autocorrelation across context positions to measure abstraction in LLMs, showing that longer autocorrelation tails in deeper layers are explained by the increasing persistence of latent variables.
AI.motivation: The claim that LLM hidden layers encode increasingly abstract representations with depth is difficult to test quantitatively without an operational definition of abstraction.
AI.method: The authors define layer autocorrelation as the average dot product of activations separated by a context lag, analyze synthetic hierarchical latent data, and use sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features as latent proxies in real LLMs alongside feature ablation.
AI.result: Autocorrelation tails grow with depth in both synthetic and natural data, SAE feature persistence correlates strongly with autocorrelation magnitude and increases with depth, and ablating persistent SAE features reduces the observed autocorrelations.
AI.conclusion: Latent persistence provides a quantitative, operational link between hierarchical abstraction and long-range temporal correlations in transformer activations.

title: Efficient Poincaré Convolutions through Patch-Statistics Factorization
comment: Includes supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: Published implementations of the Poincaré convolution in Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ (HNN++) map every overlapping image patch to the Poincaré ball before evaluating its score. We show that the clipped score depends on each patch only through two statistics, its squared norm and its inner products with the filters, which a native convolution and a single-channel box filter compute directly. The factorized layer therefore evaluates the specified score exactly, without constructing ball-valued patches, and its single-precision outputs and gradients agree with double-precision evaluations at least as closely as those of the explicit reference. On an RTX A6000 under two versions of JAX, complete training updates of a Poincaré U-Net and a Poincaré ResNet-20 are 1.5 to 1.8 times faster than the faster of two explicit implementations that map patches to the ball (1.2 to 1.4 times against an explicit implementation that skips this mapping); on a V100, the gain over the gather-based one persists as the ResNet-20 is widened eightfold. In 15 paired training runs per task, updates are 2.0 and 1.8 times faster than a reference that follows the published execution order, with no consistent change in final segmentation or classification quality, and peak memory falls by 38 to 55% in a U-Net scaling study. Replacing the convolutions of the official PyTorch Hyperbolic U-Net makes its training step 1.4 times faster with half the memory. Evaluating an existing layer from its patch statistics thus makes Poincaré convolutional networks cheaper to train in the tested models and software stacks.

AI.tldr: This paper factorizes Poincaré convolutions in Hyperbolic Neural Networks++ (HNN++) through two patch statistics—squared norm and filter inner products—eliminating ball-valued patch construction and speeding up training.
AI.motivation: Existing Poincaré convolution implementations map every overlapping image patch to the Poincaré ball before scoring, incurring high compute and memory overhead.
AI.method: The authors show the clipped Poincaré score depends only on each patch's squared norm and inner products with filters, which can be computed exactly using a native convolution and a single-channel box filter.
AI.result: On RTX A6000 in JAX, Poincaré U-Net and ResNet-20 training updates are 1.5x to 1.8x faster than explicit ball-mapping implementations (and 1.2x to 1.4x faster than explicit implementations skipping the mapping) with 38% to 55% lower peak memory in U-Net scaling, and PyTorch Hyperbolic U-Net steps become 1.4x faster with half the memory and no quality loss.
AI.conclusion: Patch-statistics factorization makes Poincaré convolutional networks substantially faster and cheaper to train without changing their exact mathematical output.

title: When Copying Is Hard to Beat: A Negative Result in Clinical Assessment Forecasting
comment: Accepted at FMTS (Foundation Models for Temporal Systems), a workshop at NeurIPS 2026, Sydney
summary: We report a negative result in next-day clinical assessment forecasting: the evaluated models show no consistent advantage over strong persistence-based baselines. Clinicians can view the previous day's questionnaire answers, a plausible source of documentation persistence. Predicting 45 items on 29,715 ICU day-pairs with patient-disjoint splits, a physiology-informed gated model improves item-macro-F1 over a one-line clinical rule by +0.0019 [+0.0006,+0.0031], while losing accuracy. No macro-F1 advantage is established when the physiology window ends at the previous form's reference time (+0.0001 [-0.0006,+0.0008]), or when scoring excludes the 68.5% of cells derived from parent answers; combining both changes yields a small disadvantage. Four checkpoints across three families underperform persistence, and a fine-tuned one differs from it on only two cells. A categorical read-out raises changed-cell accuracy eightfold, but a state-only read-out scores higher overall than forecast-only decoding and matches a transition matrix. This negative result highlights how the documentation process, input cutoff, observation mask and decoding rule shape conclusions about forecasting recorded assessments.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a negative result in next-day clinical assessment forecasting, showing that evaluated models offer no consistent advantage over simple persistence baselines when accounting for documentation structure and input cutoffs.
AI.motivation: Clinicians can view prior-day questionnaire answers, creating strong documentation persistence that may inflate apparent forecasting performance if not carefully controlled.
AI.method: Predicting 45 items across 29,715 ICU day-pairs with patient-disjoint splits, the authors evaluate a physiology-informed gated model, four pretrained/fine-tuned checkpoints, and different read-outs against a one-line clinical persistence rule while controlling physiology window cutoffs and parent-derived cells.
AI.result: The gated model improves item-macro-F1 by +0.0019 while losing accuracy, but the advantage disappears (+0.0001) when the physiology window ends at the previous form's reference time or when excluding the 68.5% parent-derived cells, and four checkpoints underperform persistence.
AI.conclusion: Conclusions about forecasting recorded clinical assessments are heavily shaped by documentation persistence, input cutoffs, observation masks, and decoding rules.

title: STAMP: Manufacturing-Informed Generative Design and Shape Optimization of Sheet Panels
comment: 25 pages, 11 figures, 7 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Generative design of formed sheet panels must preserve geometric manufacturing conditions while exploring layouts and improving performance. STAMP embeds these conditions directly in the shape representation. Each panel is described by its material layout and a reference surface with one height at each occupied position in a plane perpendicular to the drawing direction. Nominal thickness is prescribed along the normal. The representation allows curved surfaces, ribs, and openings. It excludes reference-surface undercuts and keeps nominal thickness fixed without manufacturing penalty terms. Because these conditions belong to the representation, every generated and optimized panel satisfies them regardless of training-set size. Boundary-conditioned diffusion generates alternative layouts, and predictor gradients guide a surface optimization that retains outlines, openings, and designated fixed regions. We demonstrate STAMP on automotive hood inner panels using CarHoods10k. With a comparable number of stored values, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines. From only five training designs, one of three training runs yields novel and varied layouts. A generator trained on 500 designs, 6.5% of the training set, already reaches the layout variety of the full-data model. Across 11 held-out design families, predictor-based selection among existing dataset designs yields an average gap of 0.18 mm to the best available FEA deformation, versus an expected 1.59 mm for random selection. It does better than random selection in all 11 families. At a 10% depth-change bound, a network not used in the search predicts an average deformation reduction of 24.8% for six generated and existing panels, with a 3.2% average mass increase computed from geometry. Engineers can thus explore and optimize panels within this manufacturing-informed design space.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces STAMP, a manufacturing-informed generative design and shape optimization framework for formed sheet panels that embeds undercut-free and fixed-thickness constraints directly into a depth-map representation.
AI.motivation: Generative design of sheet panels must satisfy geometric manufacturing constraints, which penalty-based approaches can violate especially when training data are scarce.
AI.method: STAMP represents each panel by a material layout and a reference-surface depth map along the drawing direction with normal-prescribed thickness, using boundary-conditioned diffusion for layout generation and predictor-guided surface optimization.
AI.result: Demonstrated on CarHoods10k automotive hood panels, depth maps reconstruct surfaces more accurately than point-cloud and voxel baselines, 500 training designs match full-data layout variety, predictor-based selection achieves a 0.18 mm average gap to best FEA deformation (versus 1.59 mm random), and optimization reduces predicted deformation by 24.8% with a 3.2% mass increase.
AI.conclusion: Embedding manufacturing conditions directly into the shape representation guarantees feasibility for every generated and optimized panel regardless of training-set size.

title: Which Model, For Which Variable? Per-Variable Forecast Combination in Sparse ICU Time Series
comment: Accepted at Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Findings Track, Sydney
summary: Clinical forecasting papers typically report a single best architecture. We show that on multivariate ICU physiology this question conceals variable-specific differences: no architecture is best on every variable, and which model wins changes from variable to variable. Across five ICU databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, HiRID, and UMM (University Medicine Mannheim), a German single-center ICU) we forecast 94 channels over a 24-hour horizon with a pool of 14 models, and combine them with weights fitted per variable. On test, the combination beats the best single model on all five databases by 6.1-11.0% mean squared error (mean 8.7%). The gain is concentrated where clinical data is thinnest: the sparsest third of channels improves by 11.9% and laboratory values by 7.5%, against 3.1% for the densest third. Rank-based harmonic weighting of the best five models per variable, with no fitted weights at all, recovers about four-fifths of the gain. Extending the pool afterwards with a per-channel gradient-boosted tree, ARIMA and ETS makes the tree the validation-selected best single model on all five databases; per-variable combination still improves on it by 2.9-5.9% (significant on four of five), while equal weighting of the same members does not. As on univariate benchmarks, learned combination beats simple averaging - but only once the weights are constrained. We also report which model to prefer when, and show that the ordering changes with database size.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that no single forecasting architecture dominates all physiological variables in sparse ICU time series, and that per-variable model combination consistently outperforms the best single model across five ICU databases.
AI.motivation: Clinical forecasting papers typically report a single best overall architecture, obscuring variable-specific performance differences in sparse multivariate ICU data.
AI.method: Across five ICU databases (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, eICU, HiRID, UMM), the authors forecast 94 channels over 24 hours using a pool of 14 models (later extended with per-channel GBDT, ARIMA, and ETS) and combine them with per-variable fitted weights or rank-based harmonic weighting.
AI.result: Per-variable combination beats the best single model on all five databases by 6.1-11.0% MSE (mean 8.7%), with the largest gains on the sparsest third of channels (11.9%) and lab values (7.5%); rank-based harmonic weighting recovers four-fifths of the gain, and per-variable combination still beats the best GBDT by 2.9-5.9%.
AI.conclusion: Per-variable forecast combination with constrained weights—or simple rank-based harmonic weighting—is more effective than relying on any single architecture for sparse multivariate ICU forecasting.

title: On the Limits of Sufficient Explanations
summary: We formally characterize the conditions under which sufficient explanations exist for classifiers on structured data such as graphs and strings. We focus on post-hoc explainers that select parts of the input as sufficient explanations. An explanation is sufficient if the selected part alone ensures the predicted label. Sufficient explanations have been widely adopted across data modalities, including graphs, strings, and images. However, a unified formal analysis of sufficient explanations remains missing. We bridge this gap with four main contributions: (i) We define a general explanation formalism consisting of an instance space, a classifier, and a select relation.
