The select relation specifies which potential sub-instances or feature subsets can be selected as explanations from each instance; (ii) We show that the existence of sufficient explainers is fully characterized by the interplay between the classifier and the select relation; (iii) We extend this analysis to practically relevant variants of sufficiency, including probabilistic sufficiency and deletion sufficiency; (iv) Based on the formal analysis, we devise statistics that bound the maximum achievable sufficiency for a given task. We evaluate these statistics on language, protein, and molecular classification datasets and find that full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them. Since these bounds hold for every explainer, they provide a task-level reference against which any explainer's sufficiency can be judged in absolute terms.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes sufficient explanations for classifiers on structured data, characterizes when sufficient explainers exist, and derives task-level upper bounds showing full sufficiency is unattainable on most tested datasets.
AI.motivation: Post-hoc sufficient explanations are widely used across graphs, strings, and images, but the field lacks a unified formal analysis of when they actually exist.
AI.method: The authors define an explanation formalism (instance space, classifier, select relation), characterize explainer existence via the interplay of classifier and select relation, extend the analysis to probabilistic and deletion sufficiency, and devise statistics bounding maximum achievable sufficiency.
AI.result: Evaluating the derived bounds on language, protein, and molecular classification datasets reveals that full sufficiency is unattainable on most of them.
AI.conclusion: These task-level bounds provide an absolute reference for judging any explainer's sufficiency without relying on relative comparisons alone.

title: MarathonTS: a benchmark of long synthetic time series from window assembly and long-series generators
summary: Many applications of synthetic time series require a series that is much longer than the windows on which a generative model is trained. Such a series can be assembled from a pool of short generated windows, which requires deciding which windows are taken, in what order, and how their seams are processed, or it can be produced directly by a long-series generator. This study presents MarathonTS, to our knowledge the first open benchmark that compares both families under one protocol. Every method produces a series of the same length on 9 open hourly datasets with 10 seeds. The series is evaluated by its fidelity to the real data (83 metrics in 12 groups, against three real references: train, validation and an out-of-time split), by its utility (models are trained on the synthetic series only and tested on real data, TSTR against TRTR, in 14 classification and regression tasks), by its memorisation of the training data and by its computational cost. The statistical analysis is carried out as a separate stage that reads the published tables and gives the rankings of every method in every slice, the answers to the research questions with tests and uncertainty, and the results of a pre-specified confirmatory family. In the main run, the methods differ in both confirmatory cells; the choice of windows matters more than the processing of their seams, which does not improve the series, and no method trains the downstream models as well as the real series. The top tier of the leaderboard is reproduced on other hardware, whereas the exact places within it are not. For the reproducibility of the study, the code, the data hashes and all results are publicly available (links below).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces MarathonTS, an open benchmark comparing window-assembly methods and direct long-series generators for long synthetic time series across 9 datasets, 83 fidelity metrics, and 14 downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Generating synthetic time series longer than a model's training window requires either assembling short windows or using long-series generators, but no open benchmark has compared both families under a unified protocol.
AI.method: Every method generates equal-length series on 9 hourly datasets with 10 seeds, evaluated on 83 fidelity metrics against three splits, TSTR vs TRTR utility across 14 tasks, memorisation, and compute cost, followed by a separate statistical ranking stage.
AI.result: Methods differ significantly in both confirmatory cells, window choice matters more than seam processing (which does not improve series quality), no synthetic method trains downstream models as well as real data, and only the top leaderboard tier reproduces across hardware.
AI.conclusion: MarathonTS establishes a reproducible baseline showing that window selection outweighs seam processing and that synthetic long-series utility still lags behind real data.

title: NeoResearch: Literature- and Experience-Guided Autonomous Time Series Model Discovery
summary: Developing effective forecasting models for diverse time-series domains requires substantial expert knowledge, evidence from scientific literature on the web, and iterative experimentation. However, translating this knowledge and research experience into model designs requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions. In this paper, we propose NeoResearch, a literature- and experience-guided autonomous research framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as researchers to discover lightweight, domain-specific forecasting models. Specifically, NeoResearch establishes an expert-inspired dual-loop research workflow, coupling hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization through experimental feedback. To enable knowledge-grounded discovery, the agent autonomously mines scientific literature from the Web, extracting modeling mechanisms, empirical evidence, and applicability conditions to formulate task-grounded, testable architecture hypotheses. Furthermore, a hierarchical experience memory links literature findings to experimental outcomes and consolidates conditional lessons, guiding architecture discovery and training optimization while supporting reuse across forecasting tasks. Experiments on ten datasets show competitive performance and support dual loops, literature extraction, and memory reuse. Our code is available.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes NeoResearch, an LLM-based autonomous research framework that mines web literature and uses a hierarchical experience memory in a dual-loop workflow to discover lightweight, domain-specific time-series forecasting models.
AI.motivation: Translating web literature and research experience into effective domain-specific forecasting architectures requires preserving source context and testing applicability under task-specific assumptions.
AI.method: NeoResearch couples hypothesis-driven architecture exploration with iterative training and hyperparameter optimization, autonomously mining web literature for modeling mechanisms and storing conditional lessons in a hierarchical experience memory for cross-task reuse.
AI.result: Experiments across ten datasets demonstrate competitive forecasting performance and validate the contributions of the dual-loop workflow, literature extraction, and experience memory reuse.
AI.conclusion: Grounding autonomous LLM research agents in mined scientific literature and structured experience memory enables effective discovery of lightweight forecasting models.

title: Neural Classifiers as Error-Correcting Codes
comment: 40 pages, 6 figures. Submitted version. Published in Information Sciences 766 (2027) 124394
summary: A unified framework is proposed that characterizes supervised deep classification as the decoding of error-correcting codes in the Shannon sense. Cross-entropy optimization is shown to align softmax classifiers with maximum-likelihood decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class-specific codewords. This correspondence explains the emergence of standard divergence objectives (e.g., Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys) and provides a geometric basis for the stability of decision boundaries. Furthermore, the geometries of Neural Collapse and LeJEPA are identified as optimal constellations for decoding under isotropic noise. Unlike classical Error-Correcting Output Codes, deep networks are shown to learn effective codebooks in the feature space implicitly. This insight is leveraged to derive novel criteria for lossless quantization, improved knowledge distillation, and architectural regularization based on code redundancy. Finally, this perspective is extended to self-supervised encoders, offering a cohesive explanation for the geometry of latent representations in modern neural models.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes supervised deep classification as Shannon-sense error-correcting code decoding, where logits map to Hamming distances to class codewords and Neural Collapse and LeJEPA emerge as optimal constellations.
AI.motivation: Deep classifiers and self-supervised encoders exhibit structured latent geometries, but a unified information-theoretic explanation linking cross-entropy, divergence objectives, and representation geometry is lacking.
AI.method: The authors map softmax classifiers to maximum-likelihood decoding of implicitly learned feature-space codebooks, deriving criteria for lossless quantization, knowledge distillation, and code-redundancy regularization, and extending the framework to self-supervised encoders.
AI.result: The correspondence explains standard divergence objectives (Kullback-Leibler, Jeffreys), establishes Neural Collapse and LeJEPA as optimal constellations under isotropic noise, and yields practical criteria for quantization, distillation, and regularization.
AI.conclusion: Viewing neural classifiers as implicit error-correcting codes provides a cohesive geometric and information-theoretic foundation for modern representation learning.

title: Clean Tickets, Wrong Orders: Catching Silent Errors with a Language Model in Your Browser Tab
comment: 4 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Demo: this https URL. Companion paper: arXiv:2611.17169
summary: A small language model that turns a typed order into structure can fail in two ways. It can print something broken, which any system rejects. Or it can print a clean, well formed order that nobody placed. Our companion work calls the second kind a silent error, and it is the dangerous one. We present a web demo in which a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely inside the visitor's browser tab, through this http URL compiled to WebAssembly. No order text leaves the device. The page parses orders as the visitor types, scores every ticket with the PIZZA benchmark's own matcher ported to TypeScript, refuses anything off the menu with "?" so the model can face the open web, and lets visitors hunt for silent errors or try to cause one. Run in the browser on all 1,357 PIZZA test orders, the deployed model writes the same output as the server evaluation for 99.0% of them and reaches the same exact match (0.882); we also report its latency on 3 consumer laptops. Demo: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper presents an in-browser WebAssembly demo of a fine-tuned 0.8B parameter language model that parses typed food orders locally and lets visitors hunt for silent errors.
AI.motivation: Small language models converting typed orders into structured tickets can produce silent errors—clean, well-formed orders that nobody placed—which are harder to catch than broken outputs.
AI.method: A fine-tuned 0.8B parameter model runs entirely in the browser tab via WebAssembly with no order text leaving the device, paired with a TypeScript port of the PIZZA benchmark matcher and an off-menu refusal mechanism ("?").
AI.result: On all 1,357 PIZZA test orders in the browser, the deployed model matches server evaluation outputs on 99.0% of cases and achieves the same 0.882 exact match, with latency reported across three consumer laptops.
AI.conclusion: Client-side WebAssembly deployment of small language models can match server-side accuracy while enabling interactive, privacy-preserving inspection of silent parsing errors.

title: Emulating physics-based XCO2 retrievals across OCO-2 viewing modes with compact neural networks
summary: Operational full-physics retrieval of the column-averaged dry-air mole fraction of carbon dioxide from satellite spectra is computationally demanding. We use singular value decomposition to compress spectra from the Orbiting Carbon Observatory-2 separately by band. Compact multilayer perceptrons use the resulting spectral scores, prior information, and viewing geometry to predict the difference between the full-physics retrieval and its operational prior. Adding the predicted difference to the prior yields an estimate of the retrieved mole fraction. The models were trained on 2015-2019 observations and validated on 2020 observations. In 2021-2025 tests, the mean annual root-mean-square errors relative to the Atmospheric Carbon Dioxide Observations from Space retrieval product were 0.89, 1.35, and 1.43 parts per million for ocean glint, land glint, and nadir observations, respectively. On East Asian nadir observations screened using the published criteria for the spectral Transformer, our model yielded a lower mean annual error than reported for that model in 2020-2022. These results show that compact neural networks using compressed spectra can efficiently emulate the full-physics retrieval across multiple viewing modes and years.

AI.tldr: This paper uses singular value decomposition (SVD) and compact MLPs to emulate computationally demanding full-physics XCO2 retrievals across OCO-2 viewing modes.
AI.motivation: Operational full-physics retrieval of column-averaged dry-air CO2 mole fraction (XCO2) from satellite spectra is computationally expensive.
AI.method: Spectra from OCO-2 are compressed per band via SVD, and compact MLPs take the spectral scores, prior information, and viewing geometry (trained on 2015-2019, validated on 2020) to predict the difference between full-physics retrieval and the operational prior.
AI.result: In 2021-2025 tests against ACOS retrievals, mean annual RMSEs are 0.89, 1.35, and 1.43 ppm for ocean glint, land glint, and nadir modes, respectively, and the model achieves lower mean annual error than a reported spectral Transformer on screened 2020-2022 East Asian nadir observations.
AI.conclusion: Compact neural networks operating on SVD-compressed spectra can efficiently and accurately emulate full-physics XCO2 retrievals across multiple viewing modes and years.

title: f-Divergence Self-Play for Tabular Anomaly Detection via Large Language Models
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026. 28 pages, 7 figures
summary: Anomaly detection in tabular data poses significant challenges due to heterogeneous feature types-mixing numerical, categorical, and textual attributes, which complicate learning meaningful representations of normality. Recent work has applied large language models (LLMs) to this problem by serializing table rows as text sequences, yet these approaches rely on one-shot supervised fine-tuning that offers limited signal to tighten the model's description of normality. We propose DiSPaT, a self-play fine-tuning framework that strengthens the model's understanding of normal data. Building on the theoretical foundation of f-divergence minimization, we derive a tight approximation connecting our training objective to reducing the distributional gap between real normal data and model-generated samples. DiSPaT operates through an alternating optimization: at each iteration, the current policy generates synthetic samples that serve as pseudo-anomalies, while a critic discriminator learns to distinguish these from real normal samples; this signal drives policy updates that progressively align the model distribution with the true normal-data distribution. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based methods, deep learning approaches, and classical unsupervised detectors for tabular anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes DiSPaT, an f-divergence self-play fine-tuning framework for LLM-based tabular anomaly detection that iteratively tightens the model's representation of normal data.
AI.motivation: Serializing tabular rows for one-shot supervised fine-tuning of LLMs provides weak signal to tightly bound normal data distributions across mixed numerical, categorical, and textual attributes.
AI.method: Grounded in f-divergence minimization, DiSPaT alternates between a policy generating synthetic pseudo-anomalies and a critic discriminator learning to distinguish them from real normal samples, using this signal to align the policy with the true normal distribution.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse tabular anomaly detection benchmarks show DiSPaT consistently outperforms prior LLM-based, deep learning, and classical unsupervised detectors.
AI.conclusion: Self-play fine-tuning via f-divergence minimization substantially improves LLM-based normality modeling for heterogeneous tabular anomaly detection.

title: Where Tree Ensembles Decide: Structural Local Explanation with Decision Predicate Graphs
comment: Code, data and results: this https URL. Supplementary material attached as an ancillary file
summary: Tree ensembles are among the most accurate models for tabular data, yet the computation behind a single prediction is spread over hundreds of decision rules. Feature attributions and counterfactuals explain such predictions through the influence of features or a change of the input, leaving open which of the thresholds applied by the trees a prediction responds to, while structural explanations compress these rules and lose the trees behind them. To address this gap, we propose a local Decision Predicate Graph (local DPG), which gathers the rules executed for a sample into a verifiable record of the computation, with a class support that reproduces every explained prediction. From these rules we select the critical predicate, the executed predicate whose crossing is estimated to move the model most strongly toward a chosen class, which offers the user a concrete threshold and the trees that share it, without an external explainer. Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, it separates differently predicted neighbours better than random and nearest-threshold predicates. A single crossing recovers the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions, against 29-50% when the same rule is applied to the feature ranked first by TreeSHAP, a measure close to the selection criterion, and on planted faults it finds the faulty threshold in 46-71% of the resulting errors, against 6-21% at random. Although training-free edits of these predicates did not reduce the error on unseen data, the critical predicate complements attributions and counterfactuals by naming where a prediction can be changed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces local Decision Predicate Graphs (local DPG) and critical predicates to explain tree-ensemble predictions by identifying the exact executed threshold and sharing trees where a prediction can be changed.
AI.motivation: Feature attributions and counterfactuals do not identify which specific tree thresholds a prediction responds to, while global structural explanations compress rules and lose the underlying trees.
AI.method: Local DPG gathers all rules executed for a sample into a verifiable graph whose class support reproduces the prediction, and selects the critical predicate whose crossing most strongly shifts the model toward a target class without an external explainer.
AI.result: Across 16 datasets and four ensemble families, critical predicates separate differently predicted neighbors better than random and nearest-threshold predicates, recover the true class in 46-69% of wrong predictions (versus 29-50% for TreeSHAP's top feature), and locate planted faulty thresholds in 46-71% of errors (versus 6-21% random).
AI.conclusion: Local DPG and critical predicates complement attributions and counterfactuals by pinpointing concrete, actionable decision thresholds inside tree ensembles.

title: WeatherDreamer: Learning a World Model from Multimodal Earth Observations
summary: Machine learning weather models now rival operational global forecasts but still start from analyses produced by separate, expensive data assimilation (DA) systems, which for global models are typically updated every six hours. Observation-to-observation models avoid this dependence, but most omit the recursive filtering cycle that lets DA systems carry a background state through sparse, irregular observations. We introduce WeatherDreamer, a world model that learns this cycle end-to-end from 18 global observing systems, without reanalysis. It infers a latent state from observations, carries it forward hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it each hour with new observations, and can predict what any of its observing systems would measure at any location. At held-out stations, its ensembles beat NOAA's Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS) for temperature, dew point and wind out to 12 h and are better calibrated than GEFS and the ECMWF ensemble. Precipitation, cloud-top height and solar irradiance, never inputs at inference, are inferred with skill matching or exceeding operational products at short leads. Against the first guess of NOAA's Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI) DA system, WeatherDreamer's short-range departures are within 10% of GSI's at surface stations and within 25% for moisture-sensitive microwave channels, but up to five times larger for temperature-sounding channels. Never given observation errors, its learned update assumes errors close to known instrument and retrieval errors of microwave sounders and scatterometer winds. WeatherDreamer also separates viewing geometry from atmospheric state, recovering 83-96% of observed limb darkening and producing seamless nadir-view imagery. Producing an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU, WeatherDreamer shows that assimilation and forecasting can be learned together directly from observations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces WeatherDreamer, an end-to-end world model trained directly on 18 global Earth observing systems without reanalysis that jointly learns hourly data assimilation and forecasting.
AI.motivation: Machine learning weather models still depend on expensive external data assimilation (DA) analyses, while prior observation-to-observation models omit the recursive filtering cycle needed for sparse, irregular observations.
AI.method: WeatherDreamer infers a latent atmospheric state from observations, propagates it hour by hour with learned dynamics, corrects it hourly with new observations, and predicts measurements for any observing system at any location.
AI.result: At held-out stations, WeatherDreamer ensembles beat NOAA's GEFS out to 12 hours for temperature, dew point, and wind with better calibration than GEFS and ECMWF, infer un-inputted precipitation, cloud-top height, and solar irradiance at operational skill, recover 83-96% of limb darkening, and produce an hourly global analysis in about 1.5 minutes on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: Data assimilation and global weather forecasting can be learned together end-to-end directly from multimodal observations without reanalysis.

title: Deep Neural Networks Training Efficiency: Does Grokking Modify its Dynamics?
summary: We study whether grokking, the delayed emergence of out-of-distribution generalization after apparent overfitting, alters training efficiency in deep neural networks, where efficiency is measured as accuracy per unit energy. Using two canonical settings, modular arithmetic and MNIST, we analyze two neural network models under 16-, 32-, and 64-bit precision and use Orthograd to test whether grokking produces noticeable deviations from the typically decreasing dynamics of training efficiency. We consider both short training runs of up to 500 epochs and long training runs of up to 20,000 epochs, and in both cases identify grokking as a sharp improvement in test accuracy after a sustained train-test gap. In the short-horizon experiments, applying Orthograd at progressively stronger levels during early training does not induce grokking, and efficiency remains smoothly decreasing. In the long-horizon experiments, Orthograd induces grokking, but the efficiency curves remain approximately monotonic and show no appreciable local increase at the grokking transition. These results suggest that, in our setting, grokking does not materially alter overall training-efficiency dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether grokking alters training efficiency (accuracy per unit energy) in deep neural networks, finding that efficiency curves remain approximately monotonic with no local increase at the grokking transition.
AI.motivation: Grokking produces a sharp delayed jump in test accuracy, raising the question of whether it also causes noticeable deviations in energy-based training efficiency dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze two neural network models on modular arithmetic and MNIST under 16-, 32-, and 64-bit precision across short (up to 500 epochs) and long (up to 20,000 epochs) runs, using Orthograd to induce grokking and measuring accuracy per unit energy.
AI.result: Orthograd does not induce grokking in short runs and induces it in long runs, yet in both cases training efficiency remains smoothly decreasing or approximately monotonic without an appreciable local increase at the grokking transition.
AI.conclusion: Within the tested modular arithmetic and MNIST settings, grokking does not materially alter overall energy-based training-efficiency dynamics.
